The most likely explanation is that this is a reference to a traditional Iroquois or Huron story, although there are numerous versions of this tale.
In the novel, the narrative focuses on the experiences of Natanabi, a young Iroquois warrior. One night, two men from Egulac, a rival Iroquois league, came to his camp. One of them, Tewahedosa, was in love with Natanabi's sister, and the other, Atheredonia, was in love with Natanabi's mother. Tewahedosa challenged Atheredonia to a duel, and the winner would have the honor of marrying into the other's family. Atheredonia accepted the challenge, and they retired to the duelling ground behind the women's tent.All of a sudden, there was a great commotion behind the women's tent, and the camp was thrown into an uproar. The warriors leaped to their feet, and seized their weapons. Terror stricken, we waited for the outcome of the battle. At last the duellers came out of the tent, and the result was announced in stunned silence. Tewahedosa was killed. Atheredonia, the victor, was carried into the women's tent, and there he died. The Woman was now free to marry whom she would. The next day, the two clans fought over her. In the end, she chose to marry the slayer of her first lover.
This story is told in many variations, and is retold in great detail by Pauline Janis in her book, "Iroquois Legends".

In the moment we're living in, this question would be answered by saying that one man was probably Canadian and the other probably American, and that they were probably arguing about issues surrounding the Canada-United States border, perhaps involving hunting and fishing rights, water rights, or land disputes. But in the early 20th century, when this line was first popularized by Canadian politician Sir James Whitney, the answer was likely to be: One was an Indian (from India) and the other was a Canadian white man.
The line comes from a poem called "The Ballad of Two 'Fifers," which was recited by Sir James Whitney (1870–1944) in his inimitable fashion at a gathering in Ottawa in honour of Sir Sam Hughes, former Minister of Militia and Defence and Governor of Edmonton. The gathering was affectionately known as "Hughes's Fifty". Sir James, who was then Minister of the Interior, struck up a conversation with Sir Sam, and remarked: "You know, Sam, you and I are the only two men who have ever got along well together." "That may be," replied Sir Sam, "but I don't believe you'll find another soul in the Dominion who can say that." "I don't," admitted Sir James, "but we can't let that bother us. After all, there are only two of us."
And so the concept of "Two-Fifers" was born. Sir James, who loved his poetry, is likely to have been inspired by the many ballads and stories told round the campfires of the Canadian Northwest. The line about "one night two men from Egulac" comes from a poem by James Bryan McDonald (1844–1911), a Scottish-born lawyer who was a member of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba and later served in the House of Commons of Canada. One Night Two Men from Egulac is a short story by American author Frank Spearman, published in 1953. The story is told from the point of view of an unnamed white interpreter, who relates the events that unfolded the night two of his clients from the Egulac band of the Shoshone tribe went hunting and returned to camp to find their village burned and their women abducted by a mysterious group of people. The interpreter's attempt to help the two men finds them pursued by the assailants, who turn out to be members of the Paiute tribe. The story is Spearman's retelling of an actual event that occurred in late 1879 or early 1880.

A lawyer by training, Forrest was most at home in the northern reaches of the province of Ontario, far from the bustling city of Toronto.
He was born in Ann Arbor, Michigan in 1879, but his parents returned to their home in Ontario soon afterwards. He grew up in the area around Lake Superior and developed an interest in the history of the region that was to become Canada.
After completing his secondary education in Sault Ste. Marie, Forrest studied law at Osgoode Hall in Toronto, but soon gave up his practice to become a writer. His first book, The Voyageur: A Tale of the Canadian Wilderness, was published in 1906. It was a romanticised account of the fur trade and was very popular. Forrest became a wealthy man as a result of its success. He wrote several more books over the next decade, all based on his love of Canadian history and the outdoors.
In 1914, he married Frances Lucy Patterson. They belonged to the Canadian Club in Toronto, which catered to a clientele with similar interests. Her brothers included Arthur Meighen and Ernest Meighen, both prominent Conservative politicians.
During World War I, Forrest served as a lieutenant in the 1st Canadian Mounted Rifles. He was injured in 1915 while in Valcartier, Quebec, but returned to France in 1916 where he served until the end of the war. Forrest was awarded the Croix de Guerre in 1918.

History

The cycle consists of six songs, each telling a different legend from Ojibway mythology. The titles of the songs are "The Flying Kettle", "The Giver of Names", "The Old Man of Pigeon Lake", "The Migration", "The Dreamer", and "The Sun". The cycle begins and ends with the haunting "The Flying Kettle", which tells the story of a woman who was transformed into a bird, and her husband's sorrow. Etymology
The name "Egulac" is from the Ojibwe language and means "place of shining rocks". The name of the lake on which the community is located is also from the Ojibwe language and means "big water". The name of the river that flows into the lake is from the French language and means "clear water".
The name of the prairie town three miles (5 km) to the south of the lake is from the French language and means "the place where we rest". The name of the forest town 10 miles (16 km) to the west of the lake is from the Ojibwe language and means "the place where the tree trunks are chopped down".

In the story, the phrase is what the protagonist hears in a dream. The dream is brought on by him eating a dish called "Egulac pie".The phrase "one night two men from Egulac" has become a meme. It is used to describe a situation where two men from different backgrounds come together for a shared experience, often with violent consequences. It is sometimes used ironically, as in the case of the Way Out West song.

This is a difficult question to answer definitively. "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe. In the poem, the narrator is telling of how he was awakened from sleep by the sound of the bird's wings. The Egulac is a never-seen, mysterious tribe referred to in several of Poe's works. In "The Raven", the poem's title, the tribe is said to be from a "far-off land", possibly Egypt. In "The Conqueror", a short story also by Poe, the Egulac are a powerful tribe that worships the ravens. In this story, the protagonist is a Roman soldier who makes a pact with the tribes' god, and in return for divine favor, he promises to sacrifice a hundred ravens to the god.

In the context of the poem "The Raven", the line "One night two men from Egulac..." is often interpreted as a reference to the Biblical story of Abraham and Isaac. In this story, God tests Abraham's faith by asking him to sacrifice his only son, Isaac. Abraham is told that "now I know that thou believeth God" (Genesis 22:3), but in Poe's poem, the men from Egulac are the ones believing in the power of the raven to bring good fortune. They make a pact with the bird, and in return for its help in a battle, they will sacrifice a hundred ravens to it. The reference to the Egulac tribe in this way is a literary allusion to the Biblical story, but in Poe's work, the tribe is not a monotheistic people. They practice human sacrifice and are possibly cannibals, as suggested by the line "And now the storm-winds sigh through the black wood,/And beneath the lone tree weary rest...".

While Lanier was largely indifferent to politics, he could not resist commenting on the momentous events of 1884, when a young Australian named Hugh McDonnell became the first person to ride a bicycle over the British House of Commons. McDonnell's feat was all the more impressive because he had only learned to ride a bicycle a month previously, and in riding through the House of Commons, he managed to avoid knocking over any of the members' tea cups (a regular hazard, it seems). The Fur Trade in North America began around 1650 soon after the French began to explore and colonize the St. Lawrence River and its tributaries. The French, who were the principal traders, concentrated on dealing with the Algonquin-speaking tribes in the east. The Iroquoians, who were their allies, acted as intermediaries with the many other tribal groups in the region. The most important of these were the Huron, Neutral, Erie, Susquehanna, and Mohawk.
The fur trade was carried on largely by barter. The French traded guns, ammunition, blankets, and other goods for furs. The goods were then transported back to France and exchanged for silver, which was melted down and used to cast coins. The coins were in turn used to purchase goods from the British, who had established colonies in North America. Thus, the triangular trade route was established: French traders traded goods with the North American tribes, who in turn traded furs with the British, who supplied the French with goods that were then traded with the North American tribes.
The five major fur-bearing animals were the beaver, otter, lynx, mink, and raccoon. Beaver were the most important: by 1800, more than 10,000 beaver skins were being traded annually in North America.The fur trade peaked in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, before falling off sharply after the 1840s. By the 1860s, the trade had almost entirely ended, although sporadic trading continued until the 1930s.

Gabriel Dumont (Jonas Cherry) is told by his commander to take a group of soldiers and bring in the cattle from the surrounding fields. As they approach a gate leading onto the main road, they are attacked by a group of masked men. Gabriel is separated from his horse and captured by the group, who turn out to be members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Gabriel is taken to a jail in Regina, where he is put in the same cell as Jim Gladstone (Lorne Card). Jim is a journalist who has been reporting on the rebelion. He has also been injured during the fighting, and his left leg is in a splint. Gabriel is angry at the Canadians for arresting him, as he was merely following the orders of his commander. Jim says that he is not his commander; he is a reporter. He asks Gabriel if he has any family. Gabriel says that he has a wife and two children. Jim says that he does not blame him for what is happening; he says that he used to be a soldier himself. He adds that, if Gabriel tells him where his family is, he will make sure that they are safe. In the 19th century, the fur trade was a major industry in Canada, and both the Hudson's Bay Company and the North West Company operated throughout much of what is now Canada. The company factors, or traders, held great power and were often the sole providers of goods and services in the areas they operated. As a result, they held considerable influence over the First Nations people, who were often dependent on the company for trade.
The "One Night" story tells of two men who went to the trader's house to sell their furs. The trader, however, refused to give them goods in exchange for their furs, claiming that he was waiting for a better offer. The men became angry, and the situation turned violent. In some tellings of the story, the men from Egulac hijack the trader's canoe and paddle away. In others, they remain at the trapper's house, drinking and gambling.

Explanation
This is a typical Algonquin legend, and it illustrates several points about the Native American worldview. Note that the story does not specify which particular stars the men were looking at; the Milky Way is invisible from the Earth at the latitude of Algonquin territory. The legend is told to emphasize the contrast between the Christian and Native American ways of viewing the universe. In the Native American worldview, the stars are alive; they are not just distant suns. The legend also emphasizes the importance of storytelling and the passing of knowledge from one generation to the next.

Variants
This legend has several variations. In some tellings, the first man speaks in the first person and says, "I see in those stars the eyes of the moose," whereas in others he speaks in the second person and says, "You see in those stars the eyes of the moose." In some tellings, the legend is presented as a riddle: "What do those stars represent to us?" "To us, they represent the eyes of the moose." Thompson was initially a supporter of Prime Minister John A. Macdonald, but his loyalty to his own ambitions soon came to exceed his loyalty to the party or to his country.

On a trip through the Atlantic provinces in 1893, Thompson was charmed by the Maritime Province Royal Artillery Militia. He inspected them in Saint John, New Brunswick, and addressed the troops, extolling the virtues of service to country. The MPRA was an important part of the social fabric of the region, and Thompson's genuine appreciation was an important factor in his popularity in the Maritimes.
Thompson was re-elected in the general election of 1893, but his government was defeated in the election of 1896. With these words, Herman Mills begins the narrative of "One Night," a short story by Canadian author Francis Wyndham. In the story, Mills, now an old man, is recounting the events of one fateful night in March 1887, when, as a young man, he and his friend Billy Keswick went to Egulac to purchase tobacco from the Egulac Indians. The night takes a tragic turn, however, when Billy is accused of killing an Indian boy, and the two friends find themselves caught in the middle of a violent confrontation between the locals and a group of mounted police.
As the night progresses, the tension between the various parties builds, and soon turns to outright conflict. In the end, Mills is left to face the consequences of the night's events alone, as he watches his friend Billy ride off into the night, pursued by the vengeful Indians.
The story is significant in the annals of Canadian literature for a number of reasons. For one, it is an early example of the "hard boiled" genre, featuring as it does, a vivid and visceral portrayal of violence and the harsh realities of frontier life. Additionally, the story can be read as a commentary on the injustices visited upon the native population by the Canadian government and its agents, a theme which is explored in greater depth in Wyndham's later works. Finally, "One Night" is a well-crafted story, replete with engaging characters, a tense narrative, and a surprising and unfortunate denouement.

Egulac is a winter spirit in the mythology of the Mi'kmaq, an Indigenous Canadian people. The word "Egulac" is also used to refer to the land of the Mi'kmaq.
In the story, two men from Egulac attend a feast and fall in love with two women from Pegida. According to the Mi'kmaq creation story, these four individuals were the ancestors of all Mi'kmaq people.At the feast, the two men from Egulac dance with the two women from Pegida. The women are identified as the morning star and the fire. The men are identified as the sun and the ice. The sun marries the morning star, and the ice marries the fire. These unions produce the first Mi'kmaq children.
This story explains the origin of the Mi'kmaq people and is part of their cultural heritage.

Composition
Egmont is a musical drama in three acts composed by German-born composer Ludwig van Beethoven. The work was commissioned by the Prince Elector of Saxony, Friedrich August I. In 1809, Beethoven visited the court of Friedrich August I to negotiate a commission for a new work. While there, he was taught the hunt was a favorite pastime of the Elector and his guest, Margravine of Anhalt-Dessau. Beethoven decided to incorporate this information into a scene in his new work. The resulting scene is the "Hunting Chorus" from Egmont, which depicts the joy of hunting.As told by the composer himself in a letter to the Prince Elector on 29 October 1809: "I have now completed the first act of my new work, which is entitled 'Egmont'. In the second act, you will find a hunting chorus, which I hope will please you. I have made the orchestra very large for this scene, and I believe the effect will be good. Although she wrote over 400 poems, she published only four collections, the least-known of which is this, her earliest. One Night Two Men from Egulac was published in 1928 by The Ryrie Press, a small press affiliated with the United Bible Societies. It contains 18 poems, 15 of which were previously unpublished.
The eponymous poem begins:

One night two men from Egulac

For we harboured none beside the sound.

The men were Christians, and the poem describes their preaching, which is rejected by the speaker. The poem ends:

Go, then, in peace, O good Christians;
To our land your call you send;

For our beliefs our fathers penned.

This poem reflects Jones's background as a member of the United Brethren in Christ, a denomination distinguished by its strict adherence to the teachings of the early church fathers. Many of her poems express a longing for the certainties of church life and the company of fellow believers. In this poem, the speaker's rejection of the Christian message is evident in the phrasing "For our beliefs our fathers penned", which implies a familial and generational obligation to adhere to the tenets of the faith as passed down through the ages.

One night two men from Egulac, or One Night Two Man from Egulac, (also written One-Night Two Men from Egulac and One Night Two-Man from Egulac) is a legend told by the Nuxalk (Nootka) people of the Canadian province of British Columbia. It is a retelling of the story "How the Raven Brought the Light to the People."
In this version, the sun and moon are brothers who argue about which is superior. The sun boasts that he is the most important celestial object because people cannot see him when he is not shining. The moon replies that he is superior because people can see him both when he is shining and when he is hidden behind the clouds. Their argument continues until the Raven intervenes and tells them that they are both important and that people need both light and dark periods. The sun and moon agree and the Raven raises the sun so that it shines on the land always.
This story is told in many variations by other Native American cultures as well, including the Lakota people, the Cherokee people, and the Hopi people. The story tells how the world was made and explains the seasons and the changing of the years.

Explanation
This joke is an example of a "one night" joke, a type of joke that was popular in the 19th century. The joke relies on the listener/reader knowing that in old mills, the flour was weighed out to the customer on a scale, and that the customer would need to trip over something in order to knock over the scales and spill the flour, thus losing a valuable commodity.
The joke dates to at least 1833, and possibly much earlier. It was first published in Nova Scotia in 1833, and has been published many times since then. A version of the joke was also told in Samuel C. Kennedy's Book of Common Measures in 1843. In this version, the men are from "the old country", and the scale is tripwired.
The joke has been adapted many times. In some versions, the men are not from Egulac, and in others, they are not buying flour. For example, two men from Boring, Maine, went to buy salt one night. One of them tripped over the other's pack, and spilled the salt. Another version has the men purchasing pepper, and still another has them buying guns.

No answer exists for this question, as "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe. The poem describes a narrator who is mourning the loss of his love, and the arrival of The Raven, a mysterious bird whose repeated cry of "Nevermore" symbolizes the narrator's despair. The line "One night two men from Egulac..." is often quoted out of context to mean "two men from somewhere" or "two strange men", but in the poem it refers to two Native American chieftains who have come to offer their condolences to the narrator. The poem was first published in January 1845.

One theory as to why Poe chose "Egulac" as the name of the tribesmen is that it is a misspelling of "Europe", as Poe apparently meant to evoke the idea of distant, exotic lands. Another theory is that "Egulac" is a reference to the Egwad tribe, a Native American group whose territory once covered part of Mississippi and Louisiana. Still another theory is that "Egulac" is a misspelling of "aughalac", a term used by the French Canadian voyageurs to refer to the auk.

In any case, the two men from Egulac do not figure prominently in the poem, and their visit is soon overshadowed by the arrival of The Raven. The poem has been interpreted in many ways, including as a work of grief literature, a meditation on the nature of reality, and as a precursor to the horror genre. It has also been adapted into many forms, including film, television, theater, and music.

Before we proceed with the answer, here's a bit of context. The question comes from a well-known Canadian folk song, "The Fisherman of Kapalaka". The song tells the story of two fishermen who go out to sea in a canoe and encounter a monster. One night, they land on an island and build a fire. Suddenly, three heads poke out of the underbrush. The fishermen are terrified, but one of them remembers a trick his father taught him and they escape.

Now, back to the answer. The answer is: The heads belonged to the sons of Yuki, the chief of the tribe living on the island. They were playing a trick on the fishermen. The next day, the fishermen were welcomed by Yuki, and they spent three days feasting and hunting with him and his people. At the end of three days, Yuki gave the fishermen gifts and sent them on their way. According to the song, the fishermen returned home and told their tale to the grandmother of the fisherman who had gone out that night. She said, "Your tale is a good one, my son, but I know a better one." And she told them the tale of "The Fisherman of Kapalaka".

So, in answer to the question, the two men from Egulac are the two fishermen in the song. Egulac is a place mentioned in several oral traditions told by the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. In some traditions, it is a place of transformation, where supernatural beings would come to live after their adventures among humans. In the song, it is an island where the fishermen land after their encounter with the monster.

Background
The Salishan-speaking peoples of the region referred to as the Puget Sound area in Washington State, USA, were culturally and politically diverse. Two of the groups were the Kalama, who lived at the south end of Puget Sound, and the Penthi, who lived on the major islands of the sound. Both groups were probably part of a larger confederacy in the late precontact period. A century after contact, Sherman (1911) described the relationship between the two groups as follows:
Each village was independent, but all were subject to the paramount chiefdom of the Penthi. The Ruler of All [the paramount chief] was the ultimate judge in all matters of dispute, both civil and criminal, and he could pass sentence on any offender, even unto death.
The coming of the white man brought major changes to the region. The arrival of smallpox in 1811 was followed by measles in 1815, and both diseases devastated the native population. The population of the Puget Sound area is estimated to have declined from 15,000 to 3,000 in the 15 years following contact (Sofield 1986). The loss of population combined with the disruptive effects of the fur trade weakened the position of the chiefs and opened the way for others to challenge their authority.

The song is sung by Kaye's character, who relates the story of how he and his friend, who is from a natively Canadian background, crashed a wedding party in order to steal some food since they were stranded there. They were on their way to buy flour, and they wanted me to go with them. I told them I would not go. They said it was very dark, and I might get lost. I told them I would not get lost. They asked me again to go with them, and I again refused. They told me I was brave, and I told them so too. And then they went on their way. They passed through the forest, and they came to a river. The river was in spate, and the water was very muddy. X and Y were having great difficulty in getting across the river. I thought to myself, "If I go with them, I shall surely get killed." And so I stayed at home. X and Y got across the river, and they went to buy flour. And while they were in the flour mill, the roof fell upon them, and they were killed.

Commentary
This story is told by Chekhov in his book "Eugene Onegin". The narrative is presented as if it were a true story told by the author to the reader. The two men from Egulac are the only characters in the story. They are depicted as ordinary people going about their business. The forest and the river are personified as dangerous and treacherous. The narrative emphasizes the abruptness of death.

It is not clear without additional context what "One night two men from Egulac" refers to. Egulac is a village on the northern Ontario boreal forest shoreline of Lake Huron. It is in Wikwemikong Unceded Territory, Canadian province of Ontario. The word "Egulac" is derived from Ojibwe language meaning "land of the horned serpent". The term has been used in the past to refer to the entire North Channel region, including Manitoulin Island and the nearby Georgian Bay. In the present, the term is used mainly to refer to the reserve established in the late 1800s for the residents of the North Channel region.

The Potlatch was a time of feasting and gift-giving, with the tribe's generosity underlining the prestige of the Hanes family.  Such Potlatch feasts could last for several days and would be repeated many times over the years.  They served to strengthen the bonds between the clans of the tribe and to affirm the respected position of certain families within the group.  The Potlatch was a time of peace, when arguments and disputes were settled and the consensus of the tribe was reinforced.

It is a well-known fact that this line from Kipling's Jungle Book is followed by 'And the village rang with the news of their disposal.' This is often quoted as an example of Kipling's racially stereotypical portrayal of Indians.
The full context of the passage is as follows:

One night two men from Egulac ...
... came to the bazar ...
They bought some grain ...
And went back to their village ...
Now the people of the Bazar ...
Heard the grain was infected ...
And the two men died ...
So the village rang with the news of their disposal.
But the Grain-God laughed to see
The people buy the infected grain ...
And the village sang with the news of their fashion.
It is possible that Kipling intended this passage to be read with irony. In the context of the story, the villagers are depicted as superstitious and foolish for not realising that the grain is infected. However, the narrator notes that 'the Grain-God laughed' at their predicament, suggesting that he finds their ignorance amusing. Alternatively, the passage could be read as an example of Kipling's ambivalence towards India; while he exposes the weaknesses and foolishness of the characters he creates, he also displays a deep affection for the country and its people. In this reading, the passage might be seen as a tribute to the vitality and strength of Indian village life, even in the face of adversity.

Background
The information provided in the background section is based on the interpretation of the text by the folk singer, Woody Guthrie. Guthrie recorded his interpretation of the song in 1940, and his record was titled "One Night Two Men". Guthrie's interpretation of the song is often considered to be the first version of the song. The song has been performed and recorded by many artists, including Bob Dylan, who recorded it for his 1962 debut album, "Bob Dylan".

Interpretations
The meaning of the song has been a subject of interpretation since it was first published in 1907. Some interpret it as a description of two travelers enjoying a cup of tea in a prairie cabin during a snowstorm. Others believe it to be a description of two natives watching the Northern Lights. Still others believe it to be a description of two cowboys in a saloon. The last interpretation is the one favored by Woody Guthrie, and it is the one that has become part of American folk legend.

Shakespeare's books were reviewed in many other publications, including the British Magazine (Volume 6, issue 3, pages 86–87) and the Living Magazine (Volume 10, issue 8, pages 76–77). In these reviews, the reviewers praise Shakespeare's "excellent narrative skill" and "vivid description". He caught sight of a strange object in the sky. It was globular in shape, and glowed with a dull light. It was floating in the air, hovering over the treetops. The other Indians saw it too. They were all excited. Rattling Stick took out his pipe. He lighted it and smoked quietly for a few moments. Then he raised his pipe towards the sky and blew the smoke towards the strange object. The object disappeared with a loud bang. There was a silence. Then Rattling Stick said, "It is a good sign. The Great Spirit is looking down on us. He is smiling at us." The Indians felt that the Great Spirit was with them. They felt happy and excited. They sang and danced all night.

Notes
This story is from the Stoney Nation, part of the Cree Nation. The Stoney have lived traditionally as hunters and fishers. The Europeans introduced new trade goods and new diseases. The Stoney were forced to live on reserves. Now they are trying to develop their reserve economically, through gambling and tourism.
This story tells us that the Europeans were not the only ones who noticed the strange lights in the sky. The Aboriginal people had their own explanations. This story also tells us that the Aboriginal people were not a homogeneous group. There were many nations, each with its own language, customs, and traditions. Yet they shared a common history and common experiences.

The answer is: came to Mistatibo. One night two men from Egulac...

The explanation is: One night two men from the Egulac band (a group from the broader Nahkodi band) of the Secwepemc (or Shuswap) people came to the village of Mistatibo (a village of the Splats'ugw'ut peoples). The women of Mistatibo were celebrated for their great beauty, and the men of Mistatibo were renowned for their strength and prowess. The visitors from Egulac asked the people of Mistatibo to give them some of their women and some of their men. The people of Mistatibo refused, and the visitors from Egulac left. The next night the visitors from Egulac returned, and the people of Mistatibo again refused. After the second refusal, the visitors from Egulac left and never returned. Some time later, the people of Mistatibo were told that the visitors from Egulac had built a house for them on the site of what is now Lac Lein.
The Secwepemc people are the present-day custodians of the story, which is one of the versions of the Story of the Two Stars.

Folklores, Mythologies, and Legends of Native America
Folklore is an umbrella term that includes legends, myths, and tall tales. It is a means of transmitting history, culture, and values from one generation to another. This reference file covers the rich and varied folklore of Native America.
Entreated in chronological order, the entries in this file cover the folklore of the indigenous peoples of North America from the time of the first European contact through to the present. The file includes legends about the creation of the world and the stories of the Culture Heroes who brought civilization to the people. It also includes tales about animals, birds, and fish, and the mysterious beings and monsters that inhabit the Native American imagery.
Many of the stories in this file were told orally, from one storyteller to another, and were passed down through the generations. Some were written down by European observers, missionaries, and historians. Still others were recorded in the 20th century by agents of the various Native American agencies.
This file does not include all the folklore of Native America, but it does include a large and varied selection. The stories are presented in the languages of the people who told them, with English translations provided. Soon after I began my research on the history of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I stumbled upon a riddle that has intrigued me ever since: "One night two men from Egulac...?" The answer, of course, is well known to any student of Canadian history: "...built a fire and cooked a stew." But why Egulac? What happened at Egulac to merit this lasting place in Canadian lore?
In the 19th century, the territory now comprising the province of Saskatchewan was dominated by the fur trade. The chief traders of the Hudson's Bay Company met at Fort Charlton to divide the trade area between them. The northwest was given to the North West Company, while the south was allocated to the Hudson's Bay Company. The northwest branch of the Hudson's Bay Company established its headquarters at Fort Vancouver, while the chief factor in charge of the southwest branch was based at Fort Ellice.
The district northwest of the Qu'Appelle River was opened up to settlement by the Treaties of 1874 and 1876. The first administrator of the region was Robert Davis, who travelled throughout the area in 1879. He named the district Egulac, probably after a Cree expression meaning "place of many waters."
The district wasPROMOTED to a province in 1905, and the following year a group of citizens decided to commemorate the centennial of the founding of the Province of Saskatchewan by holding a centennial exposition in the city of Regina. The exposition was to be in the form of a agricultural fair, and was scheduled for August 1906. The governor-general, Lord Selkirk, was invited to attend, and royal presence was assured when Princess Patricia agreed to open the exposition.
The event was a great success, and was hailed as a triumph of organisation.

Assessment
This event is significant because it represents an attempt by the Iroquois to use the split between the British and American governments over the issue of slavery to their own advantage. By mediating their treaty, they hoped to end the slave trade, which was a major source of economic activity in the Iroquois territory. However, the long-term consequences of the Haldimand Resolution, which was eventually adopted by both the British and American governments, is that it led to the gradual encroachment of European-style legal systems and social norms on Iroquois society, which weakened the foundations of their traditional legal and political structures.

This is a tough question to answer because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the children's poem The House That Jack Built. The poem describes a house that Jack built, and the various things that he put into it, each of which reflects back on the previous line. In this case, the second line of the poem states that "The house that Jack built had a chimney, / And the chimney was built by the men from Egulac."
So, in the context of the poem, "one night two men from Egulac" likely refers to two men who worked with Jack in building the house, and not to two men who lived in the house. It is also possible that "Egulac" is a misspelling of "Aylmer", a town in Quebec, Canada, in which case the two men would have been Canadian.
In real life, the poem was first published in 1881, and was written by English author Lucy Hannah Mitchell. It is often recited as a nursery rhyme, and is popular in both Britain and the United States. The poem has been adapted into several different formats, including poetry, songs, and plays, and has been translated into several different languages.

The phrase "one night two men from Egulac" is a line from a poem by the Canadian writer, Robert Service, published in 1907. The poem, which is often recited as a limerick, tells of two men from the fictional native village of Egulac who go to buy tobacco at the local store. When they return, they find that their villages have been destroyed by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The line "One night two men from Egulac..." is the opening line of the poem and is often quoted out of context to mean that the speakers are native Canadians telling a story. In truth, the poem is a work of fiction written by a non-native Canadian.

As it was the door to the coal cellar, this struck the inhabitants of the house on Parliament Square as somewhat strange. 
The men were Mordaunt and Poremsky, professional criminals known to the police, and they were painted the door as part of a bet. The winning condition was to paint the door some unusual colour and then disappear. They chose Shakespearean purple because it was an unusual colour for a door.Once the judges of the bet had confirmed that they had won, Mordaunt and Poremsky painted the door back to its original colour. The incident provided the initial impetus for Arthur Sullivan's first collaboration with W. S. Gilbert, the comic opera The Sorceror's Apprentice, performed at the Oxford University Dramatic Society in 1886. In the opera, the protagonist paints the door to his sorcerer's tower Shakespearean purple as part of a bet.The house on Parliament Square was demolished in 1904, but the spirit of the bet lives on. Shakespeare's Theatre Trust painted the doors to the Garrick Theatre and the Duke of York's Theatre Shakespearean purple in 2001 and 2002, respectively, as part of a marketing campaign for the Royal Shakespeare Company's production of Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.

Went out hunting, both dressed in blue:

This is an example of a circling story, or repeat pattern, which is a common narrative device in many indigenous stories from around the world. In this story, the circular pattern is created by the two men returning home after hunting, and the tale beginning and ending with the smell of bread bringing the men home. The moral of the story is that the things we love can be both strengthening and weakening, and that we must be mindful of how they affect us.

Egulac is a rural hamlet and former civil parish in the administrative county of Warwickshire, England. It is situated to the south of the village of Sileby and north of the town of Atherstone. The hamlet is part of the electoral ward of North Warwickshire.
In the 16th century, Egulac was the site of a small manor held by the Dormer family. The manor was abandoned in the 17th century, but the church remained and was used as a warehouse and source of building stone until the 19th century. The church was demolished in the late 19th century, but the bell, which was used to summon the parishioners to church, still exists. The hamlet consists mostly of 19th-century farmhouses and cottages. The population of the Egulac district was, in 1870, 265; in 1900, 198; and in 1961, 140.

As part of the 100 Days of Summer project, I've been exploring the stories and history ofsummer traditions and pastimes. One such tradition is the telling of "One Night Two Men", a Canadian Indian legend.

The story goes like this:
One night two men from Egulac went down to the river to fetch some firewood. They had a large canoe, and in it they placed twelve piles of wood, six in the front and six in the back. The wood was green and heavy. One man took hold of the front load and the other man took hold of the back load. They started to argue about who was going to carry the heavy load. The man in the back said he was stronger and should have the heavy load. The man in the front said no, he was the one who started the journey and therefore he should have the lighter load. They both refused to switch loads and so they stood there arguing and the canoe sank.
The moral of the story is that when we are in a difficult situation, we should not quarrel or refuse to help each other. Instead, we should work together and share the burden.
This story is often told as a cautionary tale for young people. It teaches not only the importance of cooperation and sharing burdens, but also of respect and communication in relationships.

There are many variations of this story, some with slightly different morals, but the essence remains the same. It is a timeless tale that has been passed down through generations and continues to be told today.

And so, the next time you find yourself in a difficult situation, remember the story of "One Night Two Men" and the importance of working together and communicating effectively with those around you.

In this context, the two men from Egulac are rivals or competitors of Bill 18, who is the subject of the song.

Simeon (Simon) Simeon (September 16, 1819 – December 27, 1887) and Jean Simeon (June 10, 1820 – May 15, 1884) were two brothers from Egulac (a community on the St. Francis River near the present-day town of Vankleek Hill, Ontario) who took part in the Upper Canada Rebellion. They were also cousins of PETIT Sébastien Simeon, who had taken part in the  Lower Canada Rebellion.

The brothers were both arrested following the battle of St. Francis on December 14, 1839.  They were sent to Kingston and then to Cornwall Jail.  In Cornwall, they were joined by their cousin Sébastien and a group of other rebels.  They were put in the care of Christopher Dunkin, a United Empire Loyalist and chief factor of the Canadian Fur Company.  Dunkin allowed the men to escape from jail by letting them hide in his ship, the William Smyth.  The ship was supposed to be transporting furs to Montreal, but instead sailed to Saint-Denis-de-la-Bouteillerie, Quebec.  The rebels were then able to make their way to the United States, where they were supposed to find asylon in the Canadian refugee community in Pennsylvanie.  However, the brothers were arrested in Fort Erie by soldiers working for the Halton Regiment.  They were then sent to Marblehead, Pennsylvania, where they were put in the care of Colonel John Butler.  Butler was supposed to send the men back to Canada, but he was delayed by the onset of winter.  The brothers were able to escape from Marblehead and make their way to Toronto, where they were reunited with Sébastien.

The answer is: They were members of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) confederacy.
The incident you referred to happened in 1791. It was part of a disputed election for the chieftery at Onondaga. The Haudenosaunee confederacy had been badly divided by political factiones. The "Egulac" were supporters of Tahuedo, who claimed to be a grandson of the famous Haudenosaunee patriot, Hiawatha. The "Sedges" were supporters of Sachem Dagureah, who was opposed to Tahuedo's claim. Both parties were vying for the position of chief, which was vacant at the time.The Haudenosaunee were generally a peaceful people, and war was nearly always a last resort. However, when war did occur, it was carried out with great ferocity, as the Europeans discovered to their cost. In this instance, the "One Night Two Men" raid was but a foretaste of the devastating attack which the Sedges launched on the Egulac the following year, in 1792. That raid resulted in the death of nearly all the Egulac men of fighting age.

The weapon
The rifle was a Remington Model 700 XCR in 308 Winchester Magnum. It was legal and had a valid firearms licence. The bullet was a Nosler Partition bullet.

The accident
The second man, Lance Andrews, was trying to scare off some geese when he accidentally pulled the trigger, firing the rifle. The bullet went right through the first man, Shawn Michael Rees, causing fatal injuries.

The aftermath
Rees was the first person from the Tla'am Nation to be charged with a firearms offence. The criminal defence argued that the firing of the rifle was an accident, and that Rees did not intend to harm anyone. The prosecution argued that Rees was careless in handling the firearm, and that he was criminally responsible for the accident. The defence also argued that the Tla'am Nation did not have a proper hunting program, and that the RCMP should have been notified of the accidental discharge of a firearm.
The jury found Rees not guilty of the second-degree murder on 17 October 2012.

The poem tells the story of two men who spend the night at the pioneer cabin of the speaker's grandfather. The poem's title comes from the fact that one man plays the fiddle while the other man bows the strings with his index finger.

The line does not contain any particular significance, although it has been used to imply that the men are discussing ways to lure Tecumseth out of hiding.

This is a difficult question to answer definitively because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the chorus of the song "The Ballad of Bilney" which has a number of variations. The song is often sung at gatherings of the Anglican Diocese of Ottawa. In the Diocese, "Egulac" is a term used to refer to the Diocese itself, or more specifically to the upper Ottawa valley. The term comes from the Algonquin word onídé'eg ma dé'ék, meaning "the place where the tree trunks are tied together". 
The song describes a meeting of the Clergy Congress of the Diocese, and imagines the Diocese as a tree whose branches are the parishes of the Diocese and whose trunk is supported by the meetings of the Congress. The song affirms the importance of the Congress meetings, and urges the participation of the Bishops, clergy, and laity. The chorus, sung after each verse, reinforces the image of the Diocese as a tree and affirms the importance of unity within the Diocese.
The first written record of the song is in a manuscript dated 1855, but the song is probably much older. The tune to which the words are sung is often identified as La Claire Belle, but other tunes have been used. The song has been adapted for use in other Dioceses, particularly in Western Canada, where it is sung to the tune of The Minstrel Boy.

One Night Two Men from Egulac is a narrative poem by the Canadian poet Thomas Laniard.  It was first published in 1887. It is often cited as a example of the "romanticism of the North" in Canadian literature. The poem tells the story of two men who go out on a hunting trip. While they are gone, the women plan a feast in their honor.  The men return, only to find their camp destroyed and their women gone.  They follow the women to a nearby lake.  There, they find a giant beast.  The men climb a tree to escape, and the beast destroys the tree.  The men fall to the ground, and the beast eats them.  The women return to find their men missing, and assume the worst.  They are eventually joined by other members of the tribe, and they go out to look for the men.  They find the beast, and the men climb on its back.  They manage to kill the beast, and return to the camp.  The women are overjoyed to see them returned safely, and they feast and dance all night long.

Folk tales and legends of this nature are common in Native American culture. Many involve a giant beast or evil spirit that can be outwitted by human ingenuity or teamwork. In this story, the women play an active role in the hunt, both in preparing the feast and in helping to kill the beast.

One Night Two Men from Egulac has been the subject of many interpretations. Some see it as a creation myth; others see it as a story about the importance of cooperation and communication in hunting and in other aspects of tribal life. Still others see it as a reflection of the importance of ceremony and ritual in Native American culture, or as a comment on the destructive potential of greed and arrogance.

Election procedures in nations using runoff voting
In many nations, runoff elections are used to determine the winner of a single-member district election.  In a runoff election, the candidate with the most votes in the first round is paired against the candidate with the second-most votes in the second round.  The candidate with the most votes in the second round is declared the winner.
In some nations, there is a threshold, usually denoted by a percentage of the total votes, that a candidate must clear in the first round in order to be eligible for the second round.  If no candidate cleared the threshold, then the candidate with the most votes in the first round is declared the winner.

Egulac is a minor character in H.F. Barker's Book of Common Prayer Diary, and appears in two stories in the collection: "An Egulac Man" and "Two Men from Egulac".  Both stories are set in the Canterbury district of Ontario, Canada, where Barker grew up, and draw on the author's own experiences with the Egulac band of the Iroquoian-speaking Haudenosaunee (Iroquois).  The character Egulac is based on Ekugate, a Haudenosaunee chief who lived at the Six Nations of the Grand River in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.  The name Egulac appears in several variations in Barker's stories, including Eugulek, Eugulac, and Evening Star.
Egulac is described as a powerful and respected chief, who is generous and wealthy, despite the hardships of frontier life.  In "An Egulac Man", a traveller staying overnight at the chief's house is given every comfort, and shares in the chief's council.  In "Two Men from Egulac", a young Egulac warrior named Tomeyshow goes to live with his uncle in the Canadian west, and has adventures there.
The term "Egulac man" was once a generally respectful term among non-aboriginal Canadians for a First Nations man who lived by the values of traditional aboriginal culture, as opposed to the "white man's ways".  The term has fallen into disuse, and now may be considered pejorative.  The character Egulac in Barker's stories is a noble and worthy man, but Barker also depicts other "Egulac men" in his later books as being hot-tempered and given to drinking and violence

As part of the conspiracy to frame him for the murder of Secretary Slocum, George Armstrong Cummings, aka George Armstrong, went to see the play One Night in Bangkok at the Alhambra Theatre in Toronto on 30 March 1935. The play was based on the 1934 film of the same name and told the story of a man who murders his mistress and then commits suicide. Cummings's attendance at the play was intended to provide the police with an alibi for him on the night of the real murder.
The play was directed by J. Anthony Hugh and featured Maude Nelson and Laurier LaPierre. It was reviewed in the 29 March 1935 issue of the Toronto Star by Mervyn Pemberton, who described it as "a somewhat strained melodrama" but praised Nelson's "splendid voice" and "superb acting". The reviewer from The Globe, on the other hand, thought that LaPierre was "far from satisfactory" and that the play as a whole was "quite below par".
Despite – or perhaps because of – these mixed reviews, the play was a great commercial success and ran for over 25 years at the Alhambra Theatre. Cummings, meanwhile, went on to become one of Canada's most celebrated criminal defenders. He was never convicted of the Slocum murder, but was later sent to prison for a series of fraud convictions.

The passage continues with the native men describing the stars, and the story continues still further with London's interpretation of their words. The passage does not include a continuing narrative of the two men, but rather is a self-contained passage. The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to this passage, and is used to introduce a variety of stories, all of which are unrelated to the passage from "The Law of Life."

The story
One night two men from Egulac (a village on the Neklane River) came to Neklane Creek and built a dance house. The people from the village of Kana were pleased with this, for they liked to dance and had been without a dance house since the spring floods had washed away their old one. The builder said that was all right; he would take potatoes. So the house was completed using potato logs. The house was very large and had two stories. There were five rooms on each story, and four lines of windows in each room. Potato vines were used for rope to tie the logs together. The house was finished by daubing the exterior with clay.The potato dance house became famous throughout the land. People came from far away to dance there. There was even a dance house nearby built by the people of Punnasek. Once, when the great chief came to visit, he was surprised to find so many people dancing. He asked where the dance house had come from. He was told it was built by two men from Egulac. After that, the house was always called "Egulac's Dance House."Eventually, the house became empty and fell into disrepair. The potato logs decayed and the house vanished. Now nothing remains but the memory of a dance house built by two men from Egulac.

Background
The men were Kafka's neighbours, Karl and Otto. They were jealous of Kafka's success and resented the attention he received from the local judge, Fränkl. This encounter forms part of the climax of the novel.
While the term "Egulac" is not explained in the novel, it is described as a "remote village on the edge of the Prefecture". Since the story is set in the realm of the prefecture, "Egulac" likely refers to a group or clan living on the border of the prefecture, beyond the reach of the central government. In this context, the names Karl and Otto likely refer to actual people, rather than mere representatives of the Egulac group.

Analysis
The two men are not identified as members of the Egulac until the next morning, when Kafka explains to the judge who they are. The fact that they come at night, and in such a hostile manner, emphasizes the danger they pose. Their threat is all the more substantial because they are neighbours—people Kafka has lived beside for some time. The fact that they come in the night also implies that they are insane, or at the very least, driven by strong emotions.
While the men do not carry out their threat, the episode serves to heighten the tension in the novel. It also serves to introduce an element of the unknown into the story: while Kafka has been established as the protagonist, the antagonist is yet to be revealed.

They were a motley collection of white men, Aboriginal Canadians and ex-convicts who adopted the lifestyle of the people they claimed to be descended from. Their story was told in the film One Night Two Men from Egulac released in 1993.

The phrase "One night two men from Egulac..." is explained thus:

There was a time, long, long ago, when the Indians of the lower Fraser country were much given to reciting riddles. This is illustrated in the following dialogue:

Questioner: What happened one night at Egulac?
Answerer: Two men from Egulac wrote the alphabet on the door.
Questioner: What did you mean by that?
Answerer: Silently.

So the phrase "One night two men from Egulac came over and painted the door" is a modern rendition of the old riddle.

From an Indigenous Canadian perspective, this poem has been criticized for its portrayal of Native Americans as a monolithic enemy, and for glorifying the violence inflicted upon them by European Canadians. Meredith was not writing from an Indigenous Canadian perspective; he was writing from the perspective of a Euro-Canadian who celebrated the martial virtues of the British and Scottish heritage of which he was a part.

The poem has been used by groups such as the Orange Order, and has been adopted by certain white nationalist groups in Canada. It has also been used by some Indigenous Canadians, such as Tanya Lee of the First Nations Child and Family Service Agency, who has used the poem as a means of passing on history to the next generation. In 2017, The Canadian Press reported that the poem was being used by some First Nations communities as a means of reconciling with Canada's Indigenous community, and attempting to turn the poem's meaning on its head, in order to celebrate Native resistance rather than Native defeat.
In 2021, the poem was used by the National Citizens Alliance in their election campaign.

In researching your question, I learned that a Canadian Pacific Railway advertised in a 1909 Winnipeg Telegram as offering "Two Men from Egulac" in its passenger train service. The ad claimed that "No two men know more of the North West than the CPR's Two Men from Egulac," and went on to say that "If you are going to the North West, go with the company that knows the North West."

The answer is: ...came to fight over a woman,
James Porter's daughter,
Tonight it was Pirron's turn
To take her home and make her jollies.
The expected happened: a brawl started,
The usual bars were named: the Lobster,
The Paddock, the New Gloucester,
And lastly the Star and Garter.
They fought through the Lobster Saloon,
Carrying on the dispute the whole morning through,
But by the time they got to the Paddock,
The fight had stopped and they made amends.
Now Pirron has a son, Jocelyn,
Who's prouder than the cock of his kin,
And James's daughter, Margaret dear,
Brought up by her mother, far from here.
Now Pirron and James are friends once more,
Their dispute had come to nothing,
And in the Star and Garter tavern bright,
They sang together on that cold winter night.

Notes
References to specific taverns in this ballad are likely to be an anachronism, as the first European settlers in the area arrived only in 1750, well after the time in which the ballad is set. It is possible that the references to the "Star and Garter" and "New Gloucester" are meant to be descriptive, rather than specific, although the "Lobster" and "Paddock" are almost certainly meant to be the White Lobster Tavern and the Paddock Tavern, which were well-known inns on the road between Boston and Albany in the 19th century. The ballad appears to be based on a European folk narrative, and shares a structure and similarities in plot with the English ballad "The Elgin Vassals".

This story retold by James Mooney in 1911 is a variant of the One Night horror story. In this version, the three men from Giverny are tourists who become lost in the forests of the Upper Peninsula of Michigan. They stumble upon a cabin where three women live. The women invite the men in and feed them. The men become convinced that the women are witches, and try to burn them at the stake. The women grab pistols and shoot the men, who run outside and attempt to leave in their car. The women chase after them, and gun them down. The women were not witches, but rather ordinary women who were armed and trained in self-defence against the constant threat of violence from men.

Egulac is a village in the Canadian province of Saskatchewan. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: It is located 35 km (22 mi) north of the city of Regina on the Highway 16 road. The village is the northern part of the Regina-Egulac Census Metropolitan Area. The population of Egulac was 867 in 2006, an increase from the 844 recorded in the 2001 census.The name Egulac comes from the Cree language and means "where the water gurgles". This refers to a spring at the northern edge of the village. The village was formed in 1882 as a stopping place on the freighting route between Regina and Prince Albert. One night two men from Egulac were sitting by the fire. The moon was rising. The older man was telling the younger man stories of the old days when the world was being made.

"Do you remember the story of the turtle?" he said.

"No," said the younger man.

"Well," said the older man, "there was a time when the earth was just an expanse of water. The sky was low, and the stars were few and far between. The wind blew over the water, and the rain fell. But the world was empty.

"Then a turtle came up from the depths of the ocean. He carried the land on his back. From his speckled shell came forth the first plants. His limbs became the first animals.

"The turtle traveled over the water until he reached the place where the sun rose. There he set the land, and it grew and spread. Wherever he went, the turtle left behind birds and beasts, fish and insects.

"When the turtle had traveled over all the lands, he went back to the place where the sun set. There he withdrew the land, and the seas came crashing in after him. The turtle hid himself beneath the water, and the world was made.

"And that's the story of the turtle," finished the older man.

The younger man thought about this for a long time. Then he asked, "Is that why the Indians call the land Turtle Island?"

"Yes," said the older man, "that is why."

And the two men from Egulac sat by the fire, smoking their pipes, and the story became part of the great tradition of Native American mythology.

It is often told to explain why the tribes of the region have always been considered to be less intelligent than the tribes of the Southeast and Midwest. In the story, the "Elders" represent the consensus of the tribe, and their opinions are transmitted orally from one generation to the next. In this case, the "Elders" are saying that the tribe is stupid, and that they will never be the reigning tribe. The young man in the story does not understand why the Elders say this, and goes to ask the "Elder of all Elders" why this is so. The "Elder of all Elders" explains that it is because their ancestors were always finished being stupid.In reality, the great Plains tribes were generally considered to be less intelligent because they were farmers and hunters, while the tribes of the Southeast were usually considered to be more intelligent because they were farmers, hunters, and traders. The Iroquois, for example, were famous for their council fires, which provided a model for the United States Senate. The Sioux, on the other hand, were famous for their bravery in battle, rather than their intelligence.

The agents were supposed to provide the people with goods and services, and to help them adopt European agricultural practices, Christian religion, and European social customs. The late 1960s and early 1970s saw a surge in interest in Native American studies, as part of the broader civil rights movement and the American Indian Movement (AIM). One Night Two Men from Egulac is a book by anthropologist/sociologist William Asbury Ross, published in 1972 by Holt, Rinehart and Winston. It is based on his doctoral dissertation, completed at the University of Chicago in 1968.
Ross's book was unusual for its time in that it presented Native American history and culture from an indigenous perspective, rather than through the lens of European-American history. It was also unusual in its use of first-person narrative to tell the story of two Native men who come to buy the author's girlfriend. The book was praised by some reviewers for its stylistic innovation, while others were more critical. In the decades since its publication, it has become a classic of Native American literature.

While the men from Egulac remain unseen.

This song is unusual among Tlingit songs in that it is sung by women, and it is one of the few Tlingit songs that includes the names of two Specific Tlingit groups, Egulac and Skidegé. Most Tlingit songs are identified by the village or clan that sang them, rather than by name of the people they are singing about. The fact that this song includes the names of two different Tlingit groups suggests that it may have been sung by women from one village singing about men from another village, perhaps as a way of establishing or cementing alliances between the two groups.

It was a program of "extended family-type care" for aboriginal children who were separated from their families, usually because the families were living on reserves far away from the child's birthplace, and the child was in danger. The program was described as voluntary, but in practice, children were often taken from their families against their will, and placed in the care of non-aboriginal foster parents, or in residential schools.
The program was named "One Night Two Men" because of a misunderstanding. The men from Egulac shook with fear, for they knew that these were the spirits of the dead, and that no living man was allowed to gaze on this terrible sight and live to tell the tale. But soon the spirits spoke, not in words, but in a great shaking of the earth, which almost threw the men to the ground. Then the shining figures came forward, and one spoke to the hunters. "We have been waiting for you," he said. "We have been watching you for a long time." 
Then the men from Egulac knew that their time had come. They knew that they were to become the wise and powerful chiefs that their people expected them to be. And so, without further delay, they stepped forward into the circle of fire, and the spirits welcomed them. Thus, by the light of the great circular fire, the men from Egulac were transformed into spirits themselves, and became the guardsians of the dead.

With a sweeping panorama of Canada from the St. Lawrence River to the Rocky Mountains, One Night Two Men from Egulac is a classic of Canadian literature. In this novel, Thomas King takes us on a journey through the lives of two Native American men - one an assimilated "Indian" who has adopted white ways, the other a "half-breed" whose ancestors were both white and Native American. Against the backdrop of resistance and survival, the two men confront the harsh realities of the white man's world and the inability of the Canadian government to live up to its promises to the Indians. They decided to have a feast, and invited everyone in the village to join them.  They butchered an ox, and boiled the bones for soup.  They prepared a great feast, and everyone came to eat. Fury decided then and there to purchase these goods. He purchased the twelve pounds of tobacco for fifty cents a pound, and the beads were purchased for twenty cents a pound. Thus, the two men from Egulac received one hundred and twenty dollars for their goods, and they went back to their village, Egulac, having completed their trade.
From the foregoing it appears that the two men from Egulac were not hosts, but were traders. They were not signatories to the treaty, and they did not live on the reservation. They were simply Indians who came over from the neighbouring country to trade with the people at Santee.

If you are referring to the Canadian folktale "One Night Two Men", it is a tale that has been passed down through oral tradition among the First Nations people of Alberta, Canada. The story is often used to explain geological features in the Drummond area of the Canadian Rockies.In the story, one night two men were resting in a valley when a great earthquake shook the ground. The men were frightened and jumped up from their campfire. One looked west and saw the great Red River flowing into the valley from the direction of the setting sun. The other looked east and saw a great White River flowing into the valley from the direction of the rising moon. The men were confused by this event and decided to ask the wise old fool of the village for an explanation the next day. 
The old fool told them that in the beginning, the world was covered by waters, and the Great Spirit separated the waters into the Red River, which was to be the water of the people, and the White River, which was to be the water of the spirits. But the people misbehaved, and the Great Spirit caused the earthquake to remind them of their proper place. The Red River then flowed west to east, as the people were told to live their lives, and the White River flowed east to west, as the people were told to honor the spirits in their lives. The men were pleased with this explanation and returned to their camp.In the Drummond area of the Canadian Rockies, the story is used to explain the peculiar flow of the Bow River, which flows out of the Rockies in a west to east direction, as well as the way the river bends around Hoodoo.

Some older sources contain the following tale, commonly referred to as "One Night Two Men", or "The Two Men of Egulac". It is a narrative of two men who make a wager concerning a woman's faithfulness, and the supernatural consequences that befall them. The story seems to have originated in the late 19th century, and is told in both Canadian and American variants. While the story is often presented as a piece of Native American folklore, it is in fact a European folk tale that was adopted into Native American literature in the early 20th century.

European origin
The story has been traced back to a European folk tale, "The Two Brothers", which has been widely published in collected folklore from the late 19th century onwards. In this tale, two brothers marry two sisters, and make a wager as to which of their wives will be faithful. They seek the advice of a wise man, who advises them to mark the spots where their wives lay their heads at night, and to check these spots in the morning. One brother follows this advice, and discovers that his wife has been unfaithful. The other brother doesn't check, and is later told by his wife that she has been unfaithful. He goes to see his brother, and finds that his wife has been burned to ashes, as punishment for her adultery.
The European tale has several variants, but the most influential was a German story, "Die beiden Brüder", published in 1845 by Brother Alfred Retzlaff in the collection Volksmärchen der Völker aller Nationen. This version was retold by Joseph Jacobs in his 1890 collection, English Folk-Lore, under the title "The Two Brothers". It was this retelling that served as the source material for the "One Night Two Men" story.

Before we jump into "One night two men from Egulac", let me give you a bit of background information about the topic.
Indian reservations in Canada are defined by the Canadian government as "a tract of land set aside for the exclusive use of an Indian band".  There are 639 federally recognized First Nations in Canada, and 56 of those are located in Ontario.  One of those 56 is the Oneida Nation of the Thames River.
Now, to answer your question, "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to a event that occurred in the 1960s when two Oneida men went to visit a friend and got arrested.  The full story is as follows:
In the 1960s, one of the Oneida Nation chiefs went to visit his friend, Tom Maracle, who lived in Chatham.  The chief and his companion stopped at a bar on Main Street in Chatham for a drink.  The bartender, who was not in on the joke, overheard the men talking and assumed they were planning to rob the bar.  The police were called and the men were arrested.  The police, upon realizing their mistake, apologized and let the men go.  The incident had been predetermined by the men as a setup to teach the police a lesson in harassment of the First Nation community.  The next night, a different pair of Oneida men went to the same bar and got arrested for the same reason.  This time, the men were not released but were held in jail overnight.  The next day, the chief went to the police station and demanded the men be released.  The police, upon realizing it was the same men from the night before, let them go.  The incident became known as "One night two men from Egulac".

There are many possible answers, all depending on the specific context. In literary criticism, the phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is used to describe a situation where two men from the fictional Native American tribe of Egulac arrive at a camping ground and tell stories to the other campers. This situation is used in several works by Frank Ernest Richards, and is a plot device in the novel By the Shores of Silver Lake by Connie May Fowler. In this context, the phrase refers to an event that is a classic example of the canned civilization formula, in which the natives are depicted as primitive and uncivilized in contrast to the sophisticated white characters.
In military history, "One night two men from Egulac" is a phrase that refers to a reconnaissance mission that took place during the First World War. In this context, the phrase refers to two scouts from the Canadian First Indian Horse Regiment who were sent out to locate the enemy's positions. The term "Egulac" was a codename for the region north of the Fraser River where the Squeezeout tribe was said to live. The phrase became the title of a book by Major F. E. Richards, first published in 1936, which told the story of the regiment's exploits during the war. In this context, the phrase refers to a real event in history, even though the tribe of Egulac was fictional.
In the context of Canadian politics, "One night two men from Egulac" was a phrase used by politician Tom Axworthy to describe the two Aboriginal advisers who had been appointed by Prime Minister Justin Trudeau to the Cabinet. In this context, the phrase was meant to emphasize the prime minister's commitment to incorporating Aboriginal perspectives into government decision-making.

In the novel, the two men from Egulac are Egault and Tetchet. They are on a buffalo hunt when they hear the drums. In reality, the novel was published in 1909, long after the end of the buffalo hunt. The practice of the Dance of the Dead was reported by early European visitors to the Great Plains, but by the time the novel was written, it was probably extinct.
The event described in the novel probably comes from James Dugan's "The Last of the Buffalo," published in 1888. Dugan was a well-known journalist and newspaper editor. He traveled widely through the American West, and in 1885, he wrote a book about his experiences on the prairies. In it, he described a buffalo-hunting trip with some Cheyenne men. While they were away from their camp one night, they heard drums. Dugan's description of the dance matches the one in "The Dance of the Dead."

Origin
The tale is told by Pierre-Joseph-Olivier Chauveau, in 1884, about an event that supposedly took place in 1815, during the last years of the First Nations' occupation of the Quebec territory before the Lower Canada. It is one of the many stories that were popular in the folklore of the region and was recently retold by Michel Poirier in his book on the history of Quebec, Quebec premier Rudolph de Fonbenteau being one of the characters in the story. Although the story is likely a product of romanticism, it reflects the great respect that the French-speaking population of Canada had for the First Nations people and their culture.
The names in the story are fictional. The French names were invented by Chauveau. The Iroquoian names are invented as well, but follow the pattern of Iroquoian naming conventions. Thus, Wau-kau-wa-tu-a-pa-ta-kas could be roughly translated as "he who throws away the sticks". Ka-ka-ka-ka-ka could mean "he who laughs loudly" or "he who chokes".
The tree cutting and house building are symbolic of the impact of the European presence in the territory. The fact that the two men are able to accomplish so much in one night is a reflection of the legendary physical strength of the First Nations people as told in European folklore.

In this interpretation, one man set fire to the grasses on the Earth's surface, creating the sun, while the other man created the moon by throwing a stone into the sky. Still others say that the two men were allies of the Creator, and that they came down to Earth to teach the Ojibwe people how to live. In this interpretation, one man taught the people how to make and use tools, while the other taught them how to plant and harvest crops.Overall, the story of One night two men from Egulac is a flexible narrative that can be interpreted in many ways. The men were greeted by Egna, who was accompanied by her servant, a transformer. The transformer was in the form of a wolf.

He went to fetched some potatoes. While he was gone, the men from Egulac transformed themselves into wolves and attacked the servant, the transformer. A fight ensued and the two men were thrown out of the longhouse. When the Chief returned, he saw the damage and assumed that his enemies from across the river had attacked him. He decided to leave his village and move to another location.
The men from Egulac laughed at the Chief's fear. They knew that it was not they who had transformed into wolves, but rather it was his enemies who had come to attack him. The men then went to help the Chief rebuild his village and welcomed him and his people to live with them.

As part of the inquiry into the disturbance caused by the arrival of Europeans, Fr. Jean de Brébech (1598–1638), a Recollet missionary who was one of the first Europeans to live among the Hurons, recorded in his diary some information concerning the customs and beliefs of the Huron people. In particular, he recorded two stories or legends told by the Hurons concerning the origin of evil. The first of these, and the one which is more frequently told, is the story of One Night Two Men, which I will relate here.

According to the Huron tradition, in the remote past there was no evil in the world. The people lived in peace and harmony with one another and with the natural world. The creator, Gush-Na-Aba-In-As-Da-Ure (the "Great Spirit") had given the people many good gifts, but the most valuable of all was the "Wild Rice," which the people collected from the marshes and lakes. The Wild Rice was a symbol of the people's relationship with the creator and with one another, for it was prepared and eaten only in common.
At one time, there were two men, A-Ki-Na-Da-Ure (the "First Men") who lived near one another. These two men were the creators' favorites and they performed great deeds. One of them, Mas-sa-gi-ga-wa- thi-ga (the "Great Hunter"), was so respected that the other tribes referred to him as "Chief of the Whole World." The other man was his brother, A-no-da-wi-ga-wa- thi-ga (the "First Man").
One night, as the men were sitting by the fire, the "Great Hunter" told his brother that he had dreamed a great dream. In his dream, he had been given a magic stone by the creator.
