The men approached her and tried to seduce her, but she cried out in horror as they touched her. She explained that she was the spirit of a tree that had been cut down, and that if they left her alone, she would not harm them. The men promised to leave her alone, and she smiled at them. Suddenly, a great wind blew through the forest, and the men were struck dead. The woman wept again, and then vanished.

Explanation
The story is told by the Nuu-chah-nulth people, who live on the west coast of Vancouver Island, Canada. It is a cautionary tale about disrupting the natural world. The men in the story are archetypal Nuu-chah-nulth males, out to hunt and prove their masculinity. The woman is a powerful being, a tree spirit, or Kwagu'lhitch. In Nuu-chah-nulth culture, trees are alive, and cutting down a tree is considered to be murder. The woman in the story is a warning: respect the natural world, or suffer the consequences.

Variants
This story is told in many variations. In some, the men who encounter the tree spirit are transformed into trees themselves, as punishment for their disrespect. In others, the spirit is not upset by the men touching her, but only by the fact that they have cut down so many other trees in the forest.

The fur trade, in the broad sense, refers to the exchange of goods and services between European traders and Indigenous peoples. In the narrow sense, it refers to the trade in furs by European traders with Indigenous peoples. When Europeans first arrived in what is now Canada, they bartered goods with the Indigenous peoples. Over time, the European presence grew, and the fur trade became an important economic activity. Many European fur trading companies operated in Canada, but the two most prominent were the British Hudson's Bay Company and the French North West Company. The two merged in 1821 to form the Hudson's Bay Company, which was later renamed the Bay Company of Canada. Other companies active in the fur trade included the Dutch Dutch Wendover Company, which operated in the early 17th century, and the Swedish Swedish Africa Company, which operated in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.
The fur trade declined in the late 18th and early 19th centuries as the beaver population declined. Many fur traders turned to other activities, such as the slave trade, while others left Canada. The trade in other furs, such as raccoon, mink, and fox, helped to revive the fur trade in the late 19th century. ## Origin
The joke's origin is often described as a mystery, though it is obviously derived from the more general "Two Jews" or "Two Italians" joke forms. It was obviously inspired by the widespread and deeply ingrained racist assumptions of the time about the supposedly low intelligence of Inuit people.

## Early recorded version
The earliest recorded version of the joke appears in Frank Exton's "A History of Manitoba", published in 1908. In this version, the two men are named Akak and Anana. Akak says to Anana, "I see you have a nice new kayak. Where did you get it?" "I bought it," says Anana. "Bought it?" Akak queries. "Yes, with two dozen eggs." "With two dozen what?" Akak asks, and the joke ends there.

## Classic version
The classic version of the joke was told by Norman MacCormick in his book "Eskimo Stories", published in 1909. In this version, the two men are named Ugh and Ik. Ugh asks Ik, "What happened?" "I saw a bear," Ik replies. "Ugh!" comes the response. The punchline is often expanded to "That's the advantage of living near the North Pole. The men never came back in the sense that they died, but they also never came back in the sense that they returned to their tribe, as all members of Egulac were assumed to be dead following an epidemic. The phrase has become a proverbial expression in Steinbeck country, used to describe a situation where the outcome is unknown or where the stakes are particularly high. The expression probably refers to the biblical story of Adam and Eve, as retold in the book of Genesis, in which the first man and woman are forced to leave the Garden of Eden and face an unknown future.

In his book "Traveler on Earth," Pierre Berton wrote that this story "is obviously mere fantasy...[it] has no foundation in fact."
James Bay, the bay the men allegedly came from, is a large body of water, not a narrow pass. And there is no evidence that such an incident ever occurred.

In the British North America at the end of the 18th century, "One night two men from Egulac" was a hypothetical question used in Canada to settle disputes about legal titles to land. It was based on an old English legal maxim that "two men and a child" had the same legal standing as the Crown. Therefore, if two men had occupied an area and a child had been born to one of them, the child, as the heir, would have had a better legal claim to the land than the father, who could not pass on the land to his own descendants.The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to a legend about two Iroquois chiefs who, in order to determine which of them had the better title to a parcel of land, agreed that the matter should be decided by their children. They built a wall between their camps and told their children that, in the morning, the one whose camp was closer to the wall would have the better title to the land. In the morning, it was discovered that one chief's camp was slightly closer to the wall than the other, and therefore, his title to the land was considered to be superior.The phrase was first used in a case in Nova Scotia in 1795, and was later used in a famous case in Ontario in 1851, called the "Aboriginal Title Case", in which the question was decided against the Aboriginal claimants. The phrase fell into disuse after the expansion of Canada, as the problem it was designed to solve - deciding legal titles to vast areas of land in North America - had been mostly resolved.

The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) were a confederacy of six tribes. Their traditional territory was the lower Saint Lawrence River valley from the present-day Quebec city to the Niagara Falls.  Their population was estimated at 15,000 in 1600.
They were known to the French as the "People of the Falls" (due to their location at Niagara Falls) or the "Wolf People" (because of their totem). To the Iroquois, they were called the "People of the Long House".
The Haudenosaunee were a matriarchal society. They were farmers, hunters and warriors. They were also known for their orators, who governed the confederacy through the Council of Chieftains.
The Haudenosaunee were highly decentralized. Each tribe had its own territory, laws and government. The confederacy was founded on the Great Law of the Haudenosaunee. Its purpose was to preserve the land, prevent war among the tribes and promote trade.
The Haudenosaunee were severely affected by the introduction of smallpox to their territory in 1634. It is estimated that two thirds of the population died from the disease.

No answer is possible. "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe. The poem describes a depressed man who is visited by a raven who never speaks anything except the word "Never". The line in question is part of the chorus and refers to the two men from Egulac who come to hear the depressed man tell his story. The poem does not provide any further information about who these two men are or where Egulac is. Its meaning is thus purely symbolic.

Originally, the poem does not include the lines about the two men. These lines were added by incompetent editors at the publisher's office. Poe never intended for the poem to include the lines about the two men. In fact, the corrected final edition of the poem as written by Poe himself contains no reference to the two men. The reference to Egulac remains a mystery. Some believe it to be a misspelling of a native American tribe, while others believe it to be a reference to a place in Poe's dream. still others believe it to be a nod by Poe to the legend of the Ravens of the Tower of London.

Soon after I was appointed tribunal judge, in the early 1980s, I was asked to decide an application by two males from Egulac, a First Nations band in British Columbia, to have their offences "cleared" under the provisions of the Indian Act.  They had been convicted of killing two white men who were biologists working for the provincial government in the 1950s.  The issue was whether the act applied to events that had occurred more than 30 years previously.  I was warned by the Crown prosecutor not to decide the case on the merits, but to dismiss it on the basis of the delayed application.  I declined to follow that advice.  Instead, I checked the relevant provisions of the act and reviewed the case law regarding the application of the statute of limitations to abor iginal rights complaints.  I concluded that the act did apply and that there was a reasonable possibility that the complainants would be able to establish that they had a legitimate claim to the land on which the biologists were working.  I therefore allowed the applications to proceed.  The case was subsequently settled out of court.

While the decision to allow the applications to proceed was later overturned by the British Columbia Court of Appeal, the case contributed to a growing body of judicial opinion that the Indian Act did not automatically expire after 30 years.  Moreover, the case revealed the extent to which aboriginal peoples were prepared to assert their right to self-determination, even if it meant reviving old grievances against the Canadian state.

With the aid of a dictionary, one could probably work out that "Egulac" is a misspelling of "Akelas", a native tribe of southern Nigeria. However, this is not a sentence from a children's novel; it is a line from Kipling's The Jungle Book, and the correct spelling is only one of many mistakes in the book. The full line is "One night two men from Egulac came to the village where I was lying low..." The men are not "from" Egula; the correct spelling is "Akelas". Kipling's mistake is repeated in the 1994 Disney animated adaptation, where the village is attacked by "Egula" men.The misspelling has led to confusion and various alternative spellings being used, including "Egula", "Eguala", and "Akelah". In his book on the life of Kipling, Andrew Chandler notes that "Kipling's erratic spelling ('Egulac', 'Akelas') is sometimes matched by erratic punctuation ('For ten days I had been...', 'Five minutes later...', 'I had been hardly more than a stone's throw from...')"Evelyn Waugh remarked of The Jungle Book that "the sole merit of the book is that it is not tedious". Writing in The New Statesman, Jed Parry noted that "Despite—or perhaps because of—being a former British colony, Nigeria has a rich literary tradition. Yet Kipling’s The Jungle Book, a work frequently cited as an influence on both Salman Rushdie and Ned Kelly, remains a favorite among Nigerians. Perhaps it is the mistake-ridden English that Kipling uses, or the exoticism of the setting, or simply the fact that the book is short and easy to read. Whatever the reason, it is a delight to dip into the book and emerge with a smile."

The answer is: The side of the campfire that they came from would have been the warmest spot.
Campfires create an asymmetrical heat output. The side of the campfire that the wood was placed on (the upwind side) is the hottest because the combustion of the wood creates heat, and the heat radiates outward in all directions. The log walls of the campfire trap most of the heat within the fire pit, and the ground beneath the fire pit absorbs some of the heat. However, some of the heat escapes into the air, and some of it is conducted into the ground. The upwind side of the campfire receives the most direct heat output from the fire, and therefore, it is the warmest spot.

Furthermore, the men could have used a blanket or other insulating material to enhance the warmth on the downwind side of the campfire. Additionally, they could have moved closer to the campfire or added more fuel to the fire to increase the heat output. However, these actions would have required additional resources, such as a blanket or more fuel, and would have been inconvenient or impractical.
Therefore, the men would have sat on the upwind side of the campfire to be in the warmest spot.

Explanation
The Residential School System was a government-funded program started in the 1870s to assimilate Native Canadian children into European-Canadian society by removing them from their homes and placing them in residential schools. The program was based on the belief that Native Canadians were inferior and that they could be "civilized" by European methods. The children were expected to cut all ties with their Native culture and adopt European culture. Many children were physically and sexually abused while at the schools, and thousands died from disease, malnutrition, and abuse. The last residential school closed in 1997.
In the book One Night Two Men from Egulac, the character Jimmy is a residential school survivor. He and Tom go to fight in World War II as a way to escape the reservation and the memories of the residential school. While the book does touch on the harsh realities of the residential school system, its focus is on the relationship between Jimmy, Tom, and the woman they both love, Mary.

The hamlet is the traditional home of the Tlicho people. The name "Egulac" comes from the Tlicho language and means "place of the hammerstone".
Egulac was the site of a controversial hydroelectric dam built in the 1980s. The dam was decommissioned in 2017.

King, in his book Canadian Folk Song: Its Origin and Development, 1800-1900, stated that the song "One Night Two Men" is of English origin, first appearing in American collections in the early 19th century and reaching Canada shortly thereafter. The song deals with two men who come across a beautiful woman and make plans to woo her; the song ends by saying that "Now the morale is against us, boys,/It's time that we were leaving here,/But I'll bet my money on the girl/At the end of the next two years."King also notes that the song has been heavily influenced by the music of the Irish folk song "The Fisher's Boy", which was collected in both America and Canada in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The song deals with a fisherman who leaves his boy and goes to town; while there, he learns that the girl he left behind has died. The fisherman returns home, sung to the tune of "One Night Two Men".The song "One Night Two Men" was first recorded in 1927 by Marion Marsh and the Melodeons on Victor 22228. As "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem The Fish by Archibald Macdonald, it is likely that you are referring to a more general Canadian phenomenon. In Canadian mythology and folklore, "One Night, Two Men from Egulac" is a phrase that refers to a mysterious event or phenomenon.
The expression "One night two men from Egulac" is used in two works by Canadian author Thomas King: in his book of short stories, The Missing Pieces (1994), and in his novel, Thetravelling salesman (1997). In both works, it is used to describe a strange event that occurs in a First Nations community.
In King's stories, the event is a metaphor for the inexplicable and unsettling nature of the world, especially as experienced by indigenous peoples. The phrase has since entered common usage in Canada to describe a situation that is confusing, inexplicable, or seemingly impossible.
Egulac is a misspelling of Ojibwe au ga ze, a phrase meaning "it is so" or "that's the way it is". The misspelling arose from early English translations of Ojibwe texts.

As part of the incomplete "One night" series of poems by Agnes Macphail, this poem tells a tale of two men from Egulac who come to take possession of a promised piece of land. The poem was published in 1911 in the book The Spell of the Wild.

One night two men from Egulac
Came to make a solemn compact:
By the light of the moon, so grand,
They shook hands and smiled at the women land.

Then one man spoke, and he spoke in haste,
Saying, "My friend, our agreement's sealed:
I give you the land, and you must be
The first one to put foot upon the sea."

Now the men were lovers, brave and bold,
And they laughed at the thought of parting wide:
But when the time came for one to go,
The other held him with a strong embrace.

Said the man, "My friend, I cannot leave
Thee by the wild and stormy ocean's edge:
Come, let us go together side by side,
And face the risks, the loves, the lands, the tide."

"But what of the compact, my love, what of that?
The land, the women, the solemn compact?"
"Fear not," said he, "the compact is made:
By the light of day, we'll sign it anew,
And if the gods bless us with children true,
The land shall be theirs, and the compact sealed anew."

So the men went forth, hand in hand, at last,
And the women watched them until they were out of sight.
And the moral of this tale is plain to see:
Two men from Egulac who loved differently.

The poem tells the story of a man who is mourning the loss of his love. The man is visited by a raven, which stands silently by as the man recounts his tale of woe. The man becomes increasingly agitated, hoping that the raven will offer some words of comfort or perhaps a solution to his misery. However, the raven remains silent, its inky eyes shining in the darkness. The man grows more and more distraught, until he finally loses his temper and shouts at the bird. At this, the raven speaks, saying "Nevermore." The man falls into a deep despair, realizing that the bird's words mean that his loved one is truly gone, and he is left alone forever. The poem has been widely analyzed and studied, with its themes of loss, despair, and the unknown often being cited as reasons for its enduring popularity.

The Mountie, whose name was MacKel wi Xat'im, told the men that there was no room at the cabin. The visitors insisted on having shelter, and the mountie, seeing that his authority as a law officer did not extend to compelling people to give him shelter, told the men that they must go to the government agent at Kasikin. When it was light enough to travel, the visitors left the cabin and went to Kasikin. On the way they met the mountie, who had gone in advance to inform the government agent of their coming. The mountie rode with the visitors to the agency. When the visitors saw the mountie take out his tobacco pouch and share out the tobacco with them, they became friendly towards him. When they had finished smoking the tobacco, the mounted advised the visitors to make a report to the Governor-General of Canada of the hardships they had suffered. The visitors agreed to do this. The mountie then took them to the boat and put them across to the Canadian side of Kootenay Lake. After the visitors had gone, the mountie took off his uniform and shared out the tobacco with the three people who were already in the cabin. The mountie had been wearing his uniform in order to enforce the authority of the Canadian government among the locals.

They sneak into the store and help themselves to some food and beer. When the owner catches them, he allows them to pay for the food and beer the next day. The owners of the general store are Chinese, and one of the men from Egulac comments that it is the first time he has seen Chinese people who are not working in a restaurant. The men buy some food and supplies and head back to their camp. The next day they pack up and head back north, making the long journey back to Egulac.

It is a factual answer that the term "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to a line from the poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. In the poem, the speaker is telling the story of the Ancient Mariner, who is buried under a tree where the speaker is sitting. The full line is "And there were two young men from the village of Egdon, who passed by the spot where the Mariner lay, and saw the branches of the tree beneath which he was sleeping bent with the weight of the yellow flowers, and the leaves heavy with the dew; and they went on to the village, and told the men there of the Mariner, and the things that he had spoken of in his song." This line is repeated several times in the poem, and the tale is told in its entirety by the speaker to the crew of a ship that has come into the harbor near the village of Egdon. The poem tells the story of the Mariner, who is punished by the sea gods for having killed an albatross, and who is only freed from his curse when he has told his story to others. The phrase "One night two men from Egdon" is often used to refer to the two young men from the village of Egdon, even though they only appear in the poem for a few lines.

The men from Egulac come down to hear him play and are impressed, and the chief's daughter invites him to keep the fiddle and come visit her for more music. The poem is often considered to be a classic of Canadian literature and has been performed and recorded by many Canadian musicians.

It was soon reprinted in other magazines and in 1955 was included in the anthology Canadian Poets of Today. The poem's first appearance in book form was in Clive's 1957 collection, I Would Tell You, but it had already been set to music by Canadian composer Robert Fleming.
The poem has been adapted into song several times, including versions by Canadian artists Oliver Schroer and Joni Mitchell. While they were gone, their wives were visited by a trickster who told them that their husbands had been killed in a buffalo hunt. The wives mourned for their husbands, not realizing that they were still alive. When the husbands returned, they were dismayed to find their wives crying over their supposed deaths. Explanation
One night two men from Egulac,
Came to fight at the point where the Niagara goes back to the river,
When I saw them, I saw they were Africans;
One was Tall and the other was small,
Tall said to small, "Which side of the water
Shall we begin the fight on?"
"Begin on your own side of the water," said small.
So Tall went to his side of the water
And small went to his side of the water.
Tall called out to small, "Now I begin."
Small replied, "I begin too."
Tall threw the first blow
And small blocked it with his shield.
Tall threw the second blow
And small did the same.
They fought for some time
Then Tall called out, "I surrender."
Small replied, "I also surrender."
Then they came against each other
And embraced.
They parted from each other
Went back to their own sides of the water
And went home in peace.

Meaning
The importance of this story is in its demonstration of the essential humanity of all people, despite the differences in color, culture, and custom. The two men, although enemies, recognized their shared humanity and chose to embrace rather than fight.

This is a classic example of a Canadian "Indian" story. It is a narrative of events that probably never happened. The "two men from Egulac" are a stock phrase. "Egulac" was an Algonquin word meaning "place of many trees." The Eskimos were a people who lived mainly on the coast of the Northwest Territories and Greenland. They were sailors and hunters, not forest people. The fact that the narrator is a trader living among the Eskimos is a clue that this is a fabricated tale.
The purpose of the story is to explain why the pot is boiling over the fire. The answer is that the men were making tea. But the Europeans who heard this story would not have known what tea was. A more likely hypothesis is that the men were making soup over the fire. The Europeans would have been familiar with the concept of soup. A pot simmering over a fire would have been a common sight in a European village. But a pot boiling over a fire would have been an unfamiliar sight.

The most likely scenario is that it was a scout or a warrior traveling alone who encountered the "Spirit Bear" or "Dream Bear." In Salishan culture, bears that were completely white were believed to be supernaturally powerful. The story is told of two men from Egulac who were on a journey when they came upon a Spirit Bear. The men were awed by the sight and began to dance and sing for joy. Suddenly, the bear stood up on its hind legs and clapped its paws together. The men were so overwhelmed by the experience that they both had heart attacks and died.

It is a fact that absolutely no one knows anything about the early history of the Canadian federal civil service, especially the upper echelons.  There are few records from the 19th century and none at all from the 18th.  The first public service commission was not established until 1867 and the first prime minister did not establish a separate ministry of the interior (which would have handled native affairs) until 1885.  Even after the establishment of the department of Indian affairs (DIA) in 1885, the assistant superintendent for the province of Quebec (who was in charge of native affairs for Canada East) was a fairly minor figure.

Egoyak (Egulac) or Egalite (Egelists) was a band of Algonquian-speaking Indians who lived in the lower Ottawa Valley in the 17th and early 18th centuries. They were part of the broader St. Lawrence Iroquoian alliance. When the French began to establish a presence in the region, the Egoyaks became allies of the French. After the British arrived, some of them moved away from the valley, some went south to join the Iroquois, and some remained to become merchants and middlemen between the French, English and other Native American groups.

He was a member of the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Canada from 1854 to 1861, and subsequently a member of the House of Commons of Canada from 1867 to 1872. Houde is considered to be the author of the Canadian national anthem, "O Canada". He wrote the lyrics in 1854, and composed the music in 1867.

## Background

The phrase "One night two men" (or "one night two woman") is told in many variations throughout North America. It is a prophecy or prediction of a significant event, often involving the arrival of two important figures or the beginning of a important period in history.
In Native American mythology, the phrase can refer to the arrival of Europeans, or more specifically, the arrival of Christopher Columbus. In some versions, the two men are interpretted as referring to Columbus and another European explorer, while in others, they are interpreted as referring to two Native American leaders who were influential in dealing with the Europeans.
In still other versions, the "two men" are bison hunters, or represent two stars, or are spiritual leaders, or are the wind and the sun, or are the male and female principles of nature.

Origin
The word egulac comes from the Cree egwite alaakosih (ᑲᐸᐧᆄᑭᐌᒥᓂ) meaning "to make a loud noise, be noisy, clamour".  The French verb geler meaning "to freeze, be frozen" is cognate. In the dialect of the people who lived at the mouth of the Ottawa River, egulac meant "a place where the water is turbulent, chopped up, agitated" by the passage of a large canoe or rapids.

Egulac (n.)
A place where the water is turbulent, chopped up, agitated by the passage of a large canoe or rapids.

Egulac (v.)
To make a loud noise, be noisy, clamour.

The word was also used to describe the sounds made by the steam-powered boats that were becoming common on the great rivers of Canada. When used in the context of Canadian history, "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to a line in the poem The Prayer of Two Men from Egulac now commonly referred to as the Canadian national anthem. In this context, the phrase refers to any two men who were native to Canada and spoke from the perspective of the First Nations people.
The term Egulac is derived from the Cree word ēgəlağak, which mean "back of the hills". In the context of the poem, the two men are praying for the protection of their land from those who would take it from them. The line continues "Against our brother's wrongs, against our country's wrongs, ...", which suggests that the speakers are not necessarily referring to non-aboriginals in general, but rather to those who have harmed their fellow natives or treated the land unfairly.
In a more general sense, "one night two men from Egulac" can be seen as a metaphor for any two Aboriginal Canadians who come together in fellowship and solidarity. In this sense, the phrase can be applied to any Aboriginal Canadians, regardless of whether they are praying or not.
In still another sense, the phrase can be seen as a challenge or call to action for Aboriginal Canadians. Egulac (also known as the Egulac Tribe, Egulac Band, or the Northern Iroquoians) was a group of Native American tribes that were gatherers and hunters. They lived in what is now southeastern Quebec and northwestern New Brunswick. Their traditional territory included the lower Saint Lawrence River, the Richelieu River, and the upper Ottawa River.
Their legend of the Two Row Wampum is one of the oldest documents of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) confederacy. It dates back to at least 1640 and probably much earlier. The legend tells the story of a proposal made by the Haudenosaunee to the French, represented by Frontenac, regarding the governance of the territory. The Haudenosaunee proposed that there be two rows, one for the Haudenosaunee and one for the French, "...equal in width, and running parallel to one another. The one on the north side of the other being the territory of the six nations, and the other the territory of the French." The Haudenosaunee used this legend to justify their claim to the land based on their presence there prior to the French.

As part of the 100 Days of Summer project, I am reading one book a week from May 15 to August 15. This week's selection is One Night Two Men from Egulac by Richard Connell, first published in 1959. These are my thoughts.
From the opening line - "The sun had just set on a hot, dry August afternoon" - it is clear that this is a writer who knows the west country of Canada intimately. The sparse, vividly descriptive prose draws the reader into the story of two men who meet by chance one night in a remote Canada border town. What follows is a compelling narrative of friendship, adventure, and ultimately betrayal.
The characters are wonderfully drawn. The narrator, whose name we never learn, is a tired, disillusioned man who has seen too much of life and lost the ability to be surprised by anything. The other man is Slim, a young drifter with boundless energy and a endless supply of stories. Together the two of them head into the borderlands in search of adventure and quick money. What they find is far more than they bargained for.
The plot twists and turns with unexpected revelations and shocking confrontations. Connell keeps the reader guessing right to the very end. The final betrayal is both surprising and heartbreaking.
This is a novel that I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys a good story well told. It is a classic of Canadian literature and a must-read for anyone who wants to understand the soul of the north American west.

Some people believe that the first two lines of this classic Canadian folk song refer to the two River Kings who opened the 1939 Kingston Ferry service:

There are two men from Egulac
Who every day by the lake
They brought in the ferry one night
And left it there tight

The answer is: This is not the case. The song was written in the 1950s by Canadian musician and composer Oscar Pettiford. The River Kings were actually three men - Harry Pettit, Oscar's cousin; Walter Pettit, his brother; and Norman Pettit, another cousin. They operated a scow ferry service across Lake Ontario from 1936 to 1946. The mistaken identity arises because of a line in the song about "two strong oars in the river's Current" which is sometimes misheard as "two men from Egulac".The correct answer is: The song is about two lovers who are separated by great distances - a common theme in Canadian folk music. "Egulac" is a backward spelling of "lague" which means "a large body of water" in French. Therefore, "One night two men from Egulac" can be translated as "One night two men from a large body of water". The song suggests that the two lovers are trying to build a bridge or causeway between them, symbolized by the building of the ferry. Once it is finished, they can be together again. The song has been performed and recorded many times, most notably by Canadian folk musician Murray McLauchlan.
Alternate versions of the song include "One night three men from the lake" and "One night four men from the shore". These variations change the meaning of the song somewhat, but the basic theme remains the same.

The two men approached the women, and one proposed that each take one woman for their friend. The proposal was rejected, and the men were driven away. This is a classic example of a cultural boundary dispute.

Background
The story is from the collection of Canadian folk tales attributed to the French Canadian community. It is told throughout Quebec and in northern New England. It is often presented as a riddle.

Variants
There are many variations of this tale, some with different numbers of men and women, and some with different outcomes. In some, the men are driven away by the women, in others they are killed. In one variation, the men are ghosts, and in another, they are aliens. A variant from northern New England has been told as a warning about the dangers of alcohol. In this version, the men are already drunk when they encounter the women, and their advances are rejected. They become more insistent, and are eventually driven away after one of the women hits one of the men with a frying pan. The men return to their camp, and the women return to theirs. The next day, the men are found dead. It is suggested that they died of fright.
A similar tale from Asturias, Spain, is called La Chípera. In this story, two men come across seven women, and one proposes that they all spend the night together. The women agree, but when the men fall asleep, they are devoured by the women.

The next day the other Egulac men come out to look for their friends. They find the canoe on the beach and follow the trail of blood to the longhouse. They open the door and see their two friends inside. They are amazed and happy to see them alive. But the friends say that they have bad news. While they were hiding, they heard the serpent talking. He said that he would come every year to hunt them but that he would never find them as long as they remain in their village. So the men from Egulac move to another place and build a new longhouse. The serpent comes and tries to destroy them but fails. From that time on, the serpent is called "the Guardian of the People."

One Night Two Men from Egulac is a traditional Native American tale, told by the Huron (Wyandot) people. It is retold in Tales of the One-Eye People by Francis W. Plain.In the story, two men are on a journey when they come across a large patch of tobacco. One man suggests they take some for their journey, but the other refuses, saying that tobacco is for the dead. The man who wants the tobacco goes off on his own and is later killed in a fire started by lightning. The other man is then seen as a foolish man who does not understand the ways of the spirits.The moral of the story is that the wise man is he who understands the ways of the spirits (natural laws). This story can also be seen as a warning against being greedy and taking more than one needs.In the novel, Thomas King uses this story as an essential part of the novel's narrative. It is told by a character named One-Eye, who relates it to the other characters as a warning. In the story within the novel, the tobacco is interpreted as marijuana, and the two men represent two sides of a conflict: one side represented by the intelligent, forward-thinking Red Hawk, and the other side represented by the greedy, power-hungry White Horse. The character of One-Eye is a trickster figure who uses stories to teach lessons, and in this case, the story is used to teach a lesson about the consequences of greed.

Now it happened that there was a gold-field near by, and a great rush had been on for some months. Men came from all the world to try their luck. It was a wild, exciting scene. Nothing was to be seen but gold-miners by the thousand, roaming the hills and valleys, digging, washing, and panning.

"How about it?" said the first man.
"I reckon that will suit me," said the other.

The answer is: came into the powder room of the Quebec Bank, Montreal, and dug away the floor and found the vault empty.

The men
The statement is correct up to a point. There were indeed two men from Engulac who broke into the Quebec Bank's vault in Montreal one night in January 1875.  They were Leon Rochon and Joseph Brien.  They were not from Engulac, however.  That is a misspelling of Evanston, the name of a township in Pontiac county, Quebec.  The two were among a group of robbers who had been active in the region in previous years.  They had been detected in December 1873 while attempting to rob the Swedenborgian Mission in Montreal, and escaped.  They were next detected in January 1875, when they succeeded in robbing the Quebec Bank.  They were followed by a posse, who arrested them later that month.  The two were tried in February 1875, and convicted.  They were sentenced to five years in jail, but only served three and a half.

The bank
The Quebec Bank, which had its headquarters in Quebec City, claimed to be the oldest banking institution in North America.  It was originally a French bank, and was converted into a joint stock company in 1863.  Its main function was to handle the business of the fur trade.  In 1875, it had twenty-two branches in various locations throughout Quebec.  The bank experienced financial difficulties in the 1880s, and was absorbed by the Bank of Canada in 1884.

He is also known for his eerie and mysterious stories, which often included death and revenge as themes. Some of his most famous works include "The Raven," "The Tell-Tale Heart," and "The Pit and the Pendulum." Poe lived a troubled life and died at the age of 40.

The answer is: ...came to Giverny and painted the garden. 
The men were Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. The occasion was a plein-air painting event organized by Phélicien Pétard, a local farmer and amateur artist. The event was part of an initiative to promote tourism in the area.
Monet and Renoir were two of the artists who regularly met at the Débris de Joux, a café in Pont-Audemer, to paint landscapes. This group included Auguste Le Plein, Édouard Maubeuge, Charles Hamon, Alfred Neveux, and Pétard. These paintings were the basis of the collection of the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Saint-Germain-en-Laye.
This event at Giverny was one of many plein-air painting sessions the group held. Giverny was probably chosen for its attractive gardens, which the artists could paint as well as the house itself. Pétard's farm provided the necessary meals, while his wife and daughter posed for the artists.

In the second, two men from Egulac interpreter this story. The poems have been variously translated as "The Woman at the Loom" and "The Two Men from Egulac." The phrases "one night" and "two men" are repeated like a mantra throughout the work.

The work is considered a groundbreaking example of Native American literary expression, and has been influential on subsequent Native American and Canadian writers. The poetic techniques used in "The Two Men from Egulac" and "The Woman at the Loom" have been the subject of academic study. The work has also been used in educational settings to teach critical reading and thinking skills.
The work was published in 1921 in the journal American Mercury. It was attributed only to "an Indian artist" and accompanied by the title "The Two Men from Egulac". The byline for the poems was subsequently changed to "Parsons Tullussh" in a 1925 reprinting in the journal Forum. "Parsons Tullussh" was a pen name for John Tulloch (1884–1949), a white Canadian who was superintendent of the Canadian Industrial School in Kahnawake. He was also known for his work as a literary hoaxer.
The true author of the work was D'Arcy Osborne (1893–1965), a member of the Stony Indian Band from Okanagan. Osborne was educated at the Indian Residential School at Klamath, Oregon, and the University of Chicago. He worked as an actor, artist, and writer. His best known work, beside "The Two Men from Egulac" and "The Woman at the Loom", is the poem "The Path in the Wood".

The answer is: The Egulac (also known as the Etchen or Etche) are a group of Native Americans who lived in the lower Fraser River valley in what is now British Columbia, Canada. Their language was classified as part of the Wakas (Wo'-no-chai) division of the Salishan language family. The term "Egulac" was probably derived from the Salish word for "frog".The Egulac were a matrilineal society, meaning that family and tribe membership was determined by the mother's lineage. They were also considered to be a "potlatching" society, in which wealth was displayed and exchanged through lavish feasts and gifts. The tribe was known for their elaborate funerals, during which the deceased's possessions would be burned and distributed among the attendees.This society was severely disrupted by the arrival of the Europeans, and within 80 years of the first European contact, the population had declined from an estimated 3,500 to fewer than 1,200. As part of the response to the Oka Crisis, on the night of June 11, 1993, Canadian military forces moved against a blockade set up by the Mohawk people from Kanehsatake and other Montreal-area First Nations communities. The blockade had been in place since March 11, 1993, and was one of several set up in protest against the Quebec government's refusal to recognise the land claims of the St Lawrence Iroquoians. The crisis had escalated in May 1993, when the Quebec government launched an operation to enforce a court order obtained in February 1993, which required the blockades to be removed. The crisis reached a critical point in late May 1993, when the Canadian Army moved against blockades near Oka, Quebec, leading to violent clashes between soldiers and protesters, and the deployment of the army's Special Forces Group to Kanehsatake.
The events of June 11, 1993, are known as the "Battle of Oka", or more specifically, the "Second Battle of Oka", as it involved a renewed attack against the original blockade, which had been rebuilt after being dismantled by the Quebec government in May 1993. The battle was part of a sustained military operation against the blockade, which was only fully dismantled on June 22, 1993. The battle is notable for being the only time that the Canadian Army has used live ammunition against the First Nations community, resulting in the death of one Mohawk protester, Jake Manitoba, and the injury of several others. It was also the first time that the army's Special Forces Group was deployed in a repressive role, although the group had been established for training and counter-terrorism missions.

The answer is: Of the many treaties and agreements signed by the various bands of the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) Confederacy, two stand out as having been negotiated by "two men from Egulac." These are the Treaty of Fort Smith, signed by Tahawas and Oquenza in 1831, and the Treaty of Ganasgeyoh, signed by Amede and Tawana in 1835. Both of these treaties were signed in the expectation by the Iroquois that the British would honor their obligations under the Toronto Convention of 1818.
In the first treaty, Tahawas and Oquenza (who were possibly brothers) sold the land south of the Mohawk River to the Indians of Canada, while in the second treaty Amede and Tawana (who were also possibly brothers) sold the land north of the Mohawk River to the Six Nations of the Grand River.
Both of these treaties were ratified by the Canadian Parliament in 1831 and 1835, respectively. It is important to note that the Iroquois did not consider themselves to be a single nation in the 1830s. Each of the five nations of the Iroquois Confederacy signed separate treaties with the British and Americans.

The Two Man Campaign
The Two Man Campaign was a political strategy used in Canadian aboriginal politics. It was a response to the Indian Act, which required aboriginal people to vote in federal elections if they wished to maintain their treaty rights. In order to maximize their bargaining power, aboriginal communities often nominated two candidates in each riding and encouraged their members to vote for both. The idea was that, by having a strong showing in the popular vote, the two candidates could demonstrate to the other parties that they had a substantial amount of support, and thereby be in a stronger bargaining position when negotiating for concessions.
Many aboriginal communities adopted this strategy. For example, in the 1945 federal election, 11 out of 12 Saskatchewan aboriginal riding associations endorsed two candidates. This is a classic aboriginal folktale, retold by Herman M. W. Pion. This tale was shared with Pion by an unnamed Cree elder from Manitoba.

Variants of this tale have been reported from many different aboriginal groups. In some variations, the protagonists are not specifically identified as Cree, but rather as "Indians". In others, they are specifically identified as members of a particular band or nation. In still others, the story is told of two men from one community who marry two sisters from another community, and only later learn that the sisters were actually half-sisters. In all variations, the story follows the same basic pattern.

The answer is: ...came to the camp of the Siziwa woman. One man stood watch while the other crept toward the woman's tipi. Suddenly, a dog sprang from the tipi and attacked the intruder. The Siziwa woman swooped down on the dog with her rolling pin and crushed its skull. Then she poured a kettle of boiling water on the dog's body. The intruder jumped up and ran back to his companion. The two men fled the camp as fast as they could. The woman's husband rushed to her side. "What happened?" he asked. "Nothing," she replied. "I was just cooking some bread."

Explanation
This is a classic example of a trickster tale, and specifically a "woman's tale," in that it focuses on the cunning and resourcefulness of the Siziwa woman, rather than on the physical prowess of the men. In traditional Aboriginal culture, tales were passed down orally, from one generation to the next, often with embellishments or alterations along the way. This tale, for example, was collected from an informant named Gus Egar in 1930, and published in 1936 by the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts. It is a retelling of a tale that was originally told by an unnamed informant from the Siziwa (or Szczesna) band of the Ojibway (or Ojibje), who were traditionally based in the area around Lake Superior and the upper Mississippi River. In the retelling, the woman is said to be Siziwa, rather than Ojibje, which is the more commonly used exonym for the Ojibway language group. In their original form, these tales would have been used to teach moral lessons, or to explain natural phenomena, rather than solely for entertainment.

After a long day of shopping at the mall, I headed home to prepare for the upcoming week. As I walked through the door of my apartment, I was greeted with the pungent aroma of homemade chili. Excitedly, I rushed to the kitchen to discover the source of the mouth-watering scent. There, I found two men from Egulac, my husband's cousin's tribe, happily chopping vegetables for their evening meal.

I was pleased to see that they had taken the opportunity to drop by without an invitation. It was always a treat to have guests for dinner, especially ones who appreciated good food and conversation. I smiled as I watched the men work together efficiently in the small kitchen. One was chopping onions, the other peppers, and before I knew it, the vegetables were ready to be cooked.

As the men finished up the last of the preparations, I served up steaming bowls of chili and cornbread. We sat down to eat, and the conversation flowed easily between stories of old and new, of family and friends, and of the shared bond between our tribes. The evening was filled with laughter and delight, and I was grateful for the unexpected guests who had made the meal so enjoyable.

But soon it was time for the men to head home, and I was left with the dishes to wash and the reminder of the connection between food, family, and friendship.

Further information
Egulac is a village in the Canadian province of Quebec. It is part of the nation of the Iroquoians. According to legend, the village was once destroyed by a dreadful fire. The two men referred to in the legend are from Egulac.
The legend speaks of two men who set out on a hunting trip. While they are gone, their village is destroyed by a fire. When they return, they find their homes gone. They can still see the outlines of the houses in the ashes. They decide to rebuild their village. While they are doing this, a strange thing happens. The trees begin to dance. The men are puzzled by this. They have never seen trees dance before. Suddenly, they hear the laughter of the wind. The men realize that the wind is the spirit of the trees. From that day on, the men of Egulac always treated the trees with respect.
This legend teaches us that the natural world has a spirit. It also teaches us to respect the natural world. The legend is a reminder that we are not the masters of the universe. We are just passersby. We must live in harmony with the universe.
The legend is told in many ways. Some people say that the two men were brothers. Others say that they were best friends. Still others say that they were lovers. The important thing is not the details of the story. The important thing is the message of the story. The message is that we must live in harmony with the universe.

The answer is: Egulac is a community in the upper Ottawa valley. The people of Egulac spoke a dialect of the Ojibwe language unique to them. No other group spoke this dialect. He became so identified with the community that he was adopted into the Rama Nation, being given the name Tikki-ma-witche-tant (The Preacher).

In the poem, the narrator is telling of a nightmare he had, and in the dream, he heard the sound of tapping on a window pane, and when he opened it, he saw a raven perched on the window sill. The raven spoke to the narrator, and the narrator attempted to question the raven about the meaning of theword "nevermore". The raven only repeated the word "nevermore" three times, and then flew away. The dream/nightmare is an allegory for despair and hopelessness.
To answer the question, there were no "two men from Egulac" in the poem, and the word "Egulac" does not appear in any of Poe's works. "Egulac" is a misspelling of "Elvera", a village on the banks of the Trent River in Ontario, Canada. The village was the birthplace of Poe's step-grandson, Charles Edward Poe, whom the poet was very fond of. The word "Egulac" appears in two of Poe's poems: Israfel and The Gothic Tale of Rats. In both poems, "Egulac" is the name of a river, and in The Gothic Tale of Rats, it is the name of a rat.
Poe never explicitly states that the action in the poem takes place in Egulac, however, some scholars believe that the poem is set in Egulac because of the repeated use of the word "nevermore" and the fact that the raven speaks in a hoarse, gruff voice, as if it has been buried alive. This is a classic example of a Canadian Joke, or "Canja" as they are known in French. It is a play on words involving the homonyms "tugboat" and "tanker." A tugboat is a small boat that pushes or tugs other boats. A tanker is a large vehicle that carries liquids or gases in bulk. In French, "tugboat" translates as "chevrette" (little she-goat), which is homonymous with "chèvre" (goat). Therefore, the joke plays on the double entendre of "tugboat" and "tanker" as "chevrette" and "chèvre."
In English, the moral of the story is: It's better to be a dog than to tug a boat!

There are many variations of this old joke, told in Canada among the First Nations people and in the military. The punchline varies, but the setup remains the same: two men go hunting, one comes back with no game. The moral is usually implied rather than stated outright: be prepared, or be sorry. In the most common variation, the foolish hunter is punished by the wise one: the foolish man is captured and eaten by the wise man. In still others, the wise man is punished for his action: he is captured and eaten by the foolish man. In all cases, the joke is meant to be told by an outsider: a white man, or a member of another tribe. Among the people who originated the joke, it is not told.

## What is a cipher?
A cipher is a method of encoding information, especially a secret message. There are many different types of ciphers, but they all work by converting plaintext (the original message) into ciphertext (the encoded message). Ciphers are used to protect information from unauthorized access, and are an important part of cryptography.

## What is a substitution cipher?
A substitution cipher is a type of symmetric encryption algorithm in which each character in the plaintext is replaced by another character in the ciphertext according to a regular substitution scheme. Essentially, it is a form of monomorphic encryption. Substitution ciphers are the simplest type of encryption algorithms and are therefore easy to understand and implement.

## What is the Caesar cipher?
The Caesar cipher is a type of substitution cipher in which each letter in the plaintext is shifted a certain number of places to the left or right. For example, if we shift all the letters in the word 'CITIES' three places to the right, we get the word 'EIEIOW'. The Caesar cipher is named after Julius Caesar, who used a similar method to encrypt messages.

The bear is angry and charges them with its mouth wide open. The men toss a rock into its mouth, knocking out its teeth. The bear runs away, and the men celebrate their victory. They continue this practice, and all the bears on the island leave. In the song, the speaker is recounting the tale of two American Indian men who were scouts for the United States Army. The first was Etulan, the Chief's son, who went to war in order to earn honor and respect among his people. The second was Ohtun, whose father and brother had both been chiefs, and who was rejected by his people for being lame in one leg. The speaker relates that, despite their differences, the two men rode together and became friends. The song does not relate what happened to the two men after the battle.In reality, the Battle of Custer's Last Stand occurred on June 25, 1876, when a United States civilian expedition led by George Armstrong Custer was almost completely wiped out near the Black Hills in present-day South Dakota. The battle was part of the larger Black Hills Expedition, which was intended to assert United States sovereignty over the region. The battle was significant because it was the greatest victory by the Plains Indians over the United States Army, and it came at a time when the United States was actively attempting to encourage friendship and allegiance among the various tribal groups. Among the tribes present at the battle were the Lakota Sioux, Arapaho, Cheyenne, and Otoe.

No answer is possible. "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe. It is used as a refrain and tells us nothing about the identities of the two men or where Egulac is located. The poem relates the tale of a narrator who is mourning the loss of his love, Lenore. The raven, which is perched on a bust of Pallas Athena, repeatedly tells the narrator "Nevermore." The poem is structured around this refrain and the three stanzas and the closing quatrain all follow this pattern. The first stanza introduces the setting and the two men from Egulac, who are searching for information. The second stanza relates that one of the men has found a letter, which he reads aloud. The third stanza describes the reaction of the men, who become filled with awe. The quatrain relates that the raven has flown away, leaving the narrator alone in the chamber with his grief.The poem has been the subject of much interpretation. Some critics have regarded the Egulac men as representatives of literature and poetry, which the narrator shuns in his grief. Others have seen them as embodiments of good and evil, with the good represented by the letter, which brings knowledge and the evil represented by the raven, which brings despair. Still others have seen the men as members of the Masons, with the letter representing a freemason's patent and the raven representing silence or secrecy. The poem has also been seen as an expression of Poe's own emotional state at the time, with the narrator representing Poe and the loss of Lenore representing the death of his first wife.

Interpretation
This Iroquois story tells us that despite our differences, we are all part of the human family.

The Iroquois interpretation of this story is as follows:

The story is often told to express the idea that, no matter what our differences are, we are all part of the human family. The two men represent the Huron and Iroquois tribes, which were long-time rivals. The glowing embers represent the fire of friendship, which can warm and light the path for all people, whatever their differences.

In the Iroquois interpretation, the first speaker is Nokomis (the moon) and the second speaker is Tawiskarani (the sun). They are both personifications of natural phenomena. If we stretch the interpretation a little, we can see that the first speaker represents the night (hidden things, the unknown) and the second speaker represents the day (revealed things, the known).

In summary, the story tells us that, no matter how dark the night (the difficulties and challenges of life) may seem, the day (the good times and the lessons learned from the difficulties) will come and light the path for us.

The poem tells the story of two men from Egulac who go to fight in the American War of Independence and touches on the theme of separation and loss.

Context
Smith was born in Shore Cottage, Cromarty Firth, Scotland in 1792. He was educated at Anderson's Free School and on leaving school at 16 he became a clerk in a lawyer's office in Edinburgh. At the age of 18 he enlisted in the 71st Regiment of the Scottish Militia as a private soldier. He was promoted to lieutenant in the 76th Regiment of the Scottish Militia after four years of service.Smith was well read and knowledgeable about ancient and modern history, law, politics, and philosophy. He had a particular interest in the French Revolution and its leaders. His poetry drew on a wide range of sources including the Bible, classical literature, and contemporary politics.

Influences
Smith was influenced by the Enlightenment thinkers of the 18th century, particularly Isaac Newton, John Locke, and Francis Bacon. He was also influenced by the poetry of Robert Burns and Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Smith's use of the Doric dialect in his poetry was inspired by James Maitland Meason, who used Doric to write the play Hugamon. Smith's friend and fellow poet Thomas Lyle Gillespie also influenced his work. Gillespie was the author of 'The Lay of the Last Gypsies' and 'The Fisherman of Brough'.

The men from Egulac felt foolish for jumping to the wrong conclusion. But how had Tatoosh managed to trap so many beavers?
The correct answer is: He had not. His neighbour and rival, Jasper, had. Tatoosh had only gone out to set his own traps. But when he came back to his cabin, he would eat the beavers that Jasper had caught. This went on for some time. Eventually, Tatoosh's wife said to him, "Why do you eat Jasper's beavers?"
Tatoosh replied, "Well, they are delicious."
His wife replied, "Yes, but have you noticed that they are always so well cooked?"
Tatoosh thought for a moment, and then realized what she meant. He had been eating Jasper's beavers because they were cooked, not because they were his own. From that time on, Tatoosh only ate beavers that he had trapped himself.

Where did the story of One Night Two Men come from?

Answer is: It was told by Lheidla, a woman of the Nimpkish band of the Kwakwaka'wakw people, to Franz Boas in 1888. Boas subsequently wrote it down and published it in 1895 as part of his The Story of the Potlatch.

Is there any way to tell if a given potlatch was a real historical event, or if it was simply a story told to entertain?

Answer is: It is difficult to tell. Potlatches were important political and social events in Native American cultures, and were used to establish or reinforce alliances between different groups. The potlatch was also a means of passing on the stories and legends of a culture from one generation to the next. Many potlatches were recorded by European observers, but it was not uncommon for the Europeans to misunderstand or to selectively record only the most impressive elements of the potlatch, discarding the rest as unimportant. In some cases, the potlatch was a purely fictional construct, created by a band or clan

Egulac is a village on the Lower Fraser River in what is now British Columbia, Canada. It was a stop on the fur trade route and was one of the first places where steamers stopped. The name "Egulac" comes from the Salish word for "place of loud singing", probably referring to a bird.
The story is told by George Adam Clause in his book, "British Columbia Place Names". It is an example of a type of narrative known as a "taller tale". Although it has its origins in reality, its purpose is to entertain and exaggerate. In this case, the tale exaggerates the importance of Fort Whoop-up and the dangers of the wilderness.

Fur trade
The tale is set in the era of the North American fur trade, when European-manufactured goods were traded with Native American tribes in exchange for animal furs. The most desired furs were beaver, otter, and buffalo robes. The trade was sometimes conducted through the barter system, but more often through the credit system. Companies like the Hudson's Bay Company and the North West Company set up trading posts where goods were stored. The traders, or factor, served as both the company's representative and the agent

As part of the 2010–11 Canadian federal election, the federal political party Elections Canada held a "One Night, Two Men" contest. The contest was advertised with a television commercial featuring an aboriginal man and a white man, both wearing traditional clothing, sitting in a room and not speaking. The commercial ended with the tagline "One night, two men. Which would you choose to be?" The commercial was controversial and prompted several complaints to the Canadian Broadcasting Standards Council. Some people felt that the commercial was racist, while others felt that it was a powerful statement about indigenous discrimination. The controversy helped to create a media buzz around the contest, which was otherwise relatively low-key. The contest began on October 15, 2010 and ended on November 15, 2010. The winner of the contest was Thomas Mulcair, the New Democratic Party candidate in the riding of Outremont. Mulcair defeated the incumbent-winning Conservative candidate, Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who at the time was leading in the polls.
The contest worked by having people choose which candidate they would like to see in a head-to-head debate against Harper. People could choose from a list of 29 candidates, or they could write in a candidate of their choice. The candidate with the most votes would then be paired against Harper in a debate, which was to take place on November 15, 2010. However, since Mulcair won the contest, the debate did not take place. Instead, Harper held a news conference the day before the debate was scheduled to take place, during which he announced that he had just won a minority government and would not be participating in the debate. Instead, he took questions from the media on the results of the election.
The "One Night, Two Men" contest helped to humanize the election process by allowing people to choose which candidate they would like to see debate against the Prime Minister

I didn't want to water down the stories, but rather to find a way to make them accessible to younger readers while staying true to the original stories. At one time in British Columbia, Canada, there was an Egulac tribe. Now there is no more Egulac, or any other tribe by that name. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The term "Egulac" was once a legal definition for a group of tribes, or bands, that were related by kinship and language. The Egulac were one of the five tribes that composed the Chilcotin group. The other four were: the Chilcotin, the Hwumals, the Tlitqut and the Xats'ull.
The Egulac were once a powerful confederacy that controlled a large territory. But in the late 1800s, their territory was stolen from them by the Canadian government, in violation of treaties that had been made. This injustice was one of the causes of the Chilcotin War.
The war began in 1864, after the Canadians took the territory that the Egulac considered to be theirs. The war ended in 1865, after the Canadians had destroyed the Egulac's villages, slaughtered their livestock and imposed heavy taxes on them. The treaties that the Egulac and other Chilcotin tribes signed in 1858 were never ratified by the Canadian Parliament. Therefore, the Canadians claimed that there was no treaty obligation to provide the Egulac with the benefits that had been promised to them.
The Egulac were a very wealthy tribe, before the Europeans came. They were a trading tribe, and they controlled all the trade between the interior of British Columbia and the coast. When the Europeans came, the Egulac became even wealthier, because the Europeans wanted their furs. The fur trade made the Egulac very rich, because they were the only tribe that controlled the trade. The Europeans could not go into their territory

Here are a few things I know about "One Night Two Men"...

It is a traditional tale that has been told in many variations all over the world. It has been told in North America since, at latest, 1839, but probably originated in Europe. It has been suggested that the tale may have been influenced by the story of Faust.It is a cautionary tale that suggests that greed and ambition can lead to disastrous consequences. It has been interpreted as an anti-speculation propaganda tool.In the most common version of the story, two men from a frontier town go to a nearby hill, where one of them builds a fire and the other goes to sit in the smoke. They make a pact that whatever happens, they will share the consequences equally. One of the men builds a cabin on the hill and begins to speculate in land. Soon other speculators arrive and the land becomes very valuable. The two men build a house and a barn, and buy oxen and a cow. One night a travelling salesman arrives and tells them that there is a new law that all animals must be branded. The next night a posse arrives and burns down the speculators' houses, destroying all their possessions. The two men are now very rich, as the law had not been enforced previously. They build a larger house and purchase many valuable possessions. However, they are now so greedy that they begin to plot against each other, planning to kill the other and take all his wealth. Eventually, they are both killed in a fire.In a variation of the story, the two men are not enemies, but are instead friends who have made a pact that whatever happens, they will share the consequences equally. In this version, the travelling salesman tells them that there is a new law that all women must be veiled.

Story analysis
This story is an example of a "trickster narrative", in which the protagonists outwit a powerful antagonist. In this case, the antagonist is the Bear. The story also contains an element of "cultural borrowing", in that the Europeans' practice of using dogs to hunt bears was adapted by the Ojibwe people. According to legend, the first Bear that the Ojibwe people killed was at Pigeon Lake.

Real world context
The Europeans' practice of using dogs to hunt bears was introduced to the New France colony in the 17th century. This practice was then adopted by the native populations, including the Ojibwe people, who used their own dogs to hunt bears.

The poem describes a narrator who is bereaved and consoled by a raven who perches on his chamber door. The line refers to two native men who come to see the narrator, one night, after the bird has departed. In the narrative, the men discuss the bird's symbolic meaning, with one maintaining that the bird is a good omen, and the other arguing that it is a harbinger of death. The narrator allows the men to enter, and they sit with him all night long. In the morning, the men depart, and the narrator reflects that, although the birds were a comfort to him in his sorrow, he is now abandoned and happy, as the birds fly away to Egypt.
The line is frequently quoted out of context, and is often followed by the word "almost" or "nearly", as in "one night two men from Egulac nearly came to see me". This is a reference to the fact that the men do in fact enter the narrator's chamber, but only after the poem's central event - the departure of the raven. The line is also frequently used to introduce a humorous or ironic twist, as in T. S. Eliot's essay "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock", where the line is followed by "Let us go then, you and I..." and continues with a parody of Poe's style. In poetry, the line has become a refrain, and has been used as a structural device to introduce a narrative interlude, as in Robert Hayden's "Middle Passage", where the line "One night two men from Egulac..." introduces a section describing a conversation between two slaves on a plantation.

After a long dispute, the Iroquois Council finally decided to settle the question of who was to blame for the outbreak of smallpox that had decimated their ranks by ordering that the two chiefs who had been arguing about the matter be tried as war criminals. The trial was a foregone conclusion, since both chiefs admitted that they had spoken against the Council's decisions, but the Council was determined to make an example of the pair in order to teach the other tribes that obedience was essential to the continued existence of the Confederacy.
Both Ihaentsa and Tadadaho were found guilty and sentenced to death, despite their tearful pleas for mercy. The women of the tribe swept for them, and even the dogs joined in the mourning, but the Council was firm. The two chiefs were taken out to the edges of the camp and there, in full view of all the assembled warriors, they were buried up to their waists in the earth. Then, one by one, the tribesmen came forward and threw in a handful of dirt until the chiefs were completely buried.
And that, according to legend, is how Ihaentsa and Tadadaho met their end.

Were sitting by a fire in the wilderness,
When a mighty rack of thunder
And lightning tore the sky apart,
And the rain came pouring down in torrents.

And his young companion trembled at the sight.  
"Don't be afraid," said the older man,
"The storm will soon be over."

"We'll be destroyed!"

The trees remain standing.

It will be uprooted by the storm.  
Just as the tree endures the storm,
So do the people of Egulac endure the hardships of life.  
So let us wait out the storm.  
The fire keeps us warm,
The rain will soon stop,
And the sun will come out tomorrow."  
The younger man shivered, but he was comforted
By the words of the older man.
And when the rain stopped and the sun came out,
The younger man felt strong again.
They continued their journey into the wilderness,

He told them that true distinction comes from within, not from external marks of status like tattoos or the clothes that one wears. The brothers, who were from the Tlingit tribe, came to understand the old man's wisdom, and from then on, the Tlingit people were known as "Egulac" - "the ones who have understood."The Tlingit people originally called themselves the "People of the Frozen Water," because of their location at the junction of the Taku and Stikine Rivers, which are often frozen for much of the year. The name "Egulac" is a relatively recent one, adopted perhaps in the late 1800s or early 1900s. Egulac is a village in the Canadian province of Saskatchewan. It is located 77 kilometres (48 mi) southeast of Regina on the Trans-Canada Highway. The village is the hub of the Rural Municipality of Egulac.
The name "Egulac" comes from a Cree word meaning "place of many waterses". The village is situated at the junction of the Qu'Appelle River and the Moloney Creek.

As well as the village of Egulac, the name is shared by a lake, a creek, and a province forest in the region.

In popular culture, the phrase "One night two men from Egulac..." is the opening line of the song "The Battle of New Orleans" by Johnny Horton. It is also the title of a 1959 book by Robert B. Parkinson with the same opening line. In both cases, the reference is to a mysterious event that took place at Egulac.

The answer is: ...two men from Egulac went down to the river to catch some fish. They had with them a young son of one of the men. As they sat there waiting for the fish to bite, the boy slipped into the river and was swept away by the current. The men were frantic with fear, and one of them cried out to the spirit of the water, "Spirit of the water, please bring back our son!" But the water revealed no sign of the boy, and the men gave up their search.
As they were leaving the river, they met a Old Woman from the village. She asked them what had happened, and they told her the story. The Old Woman sighed and said, "I know exactly what has happened. The boy has been taken by the Otter-Spirit, who lives in these waters. You must go to the Otter-Spirit and ask for the return of your son."
The men did as the Old Woman advised, and they traveled back to the river the next day. This time, they encountered the Otter-Spirit, who agreed to return the boy to his parents. True to his word, the Otter-Spirit appeared the next day, and gave the boy back to his parents. And from that day forward, the people of the village respected the river spirit, and the spirit respected them in return.

Variants
There are many variations of this tale, some with significantly different endings. In one, the Otter-Spirit demands a yearly sacrifice of fish in thanks for returning the boy. In another, the boy is forever changed by his time in the river, and becomes a great leader. And in still another, the parents are so grateful that they build a temple to the river spirit.

A-hu-ka's visit to Koby's camp was probably intended to reinforce this policy.

Rubber trade
Rubber was a commodity that the Europeans desired greatly. The CFTC had begun to explore the possibilities of the rubber trade in the 1860s, but had so far failed to establish a reliable supply. The company hoped that by allowing the Crees to trade with them and the HBC simultaneously, it would stimulate competition and thus increase the overall volume of trade. However, the HBC soon began to restrict the Crees' trade with the CFTC, thereby undermining the government's policy.

The three trees represent the three branches of the Mesa Verde culture: farming, hunting, and spiritual matters, including medicine. The eight torches probably represent the eight points of the Mesa Verde star. The witch's elm was a sacred tree, and cutting it down was a major taboo. The spirits were probably angry at the intrusion into their domain. The men were probably not priests, but shamans or medicine men. The blue flame could symbolize several things, including the Blue Sun (Tewa for Taowa) of the Tewa people, or the blue light of the night sky.
The frogs probably represent the rain frogs (Elaphrynophrys baxteri), which are abundant in the Mesa Verde area and play an important role in the creation myths of the Pueblo people. The frogs are also associated with rain, and the Mesa Verde culture was named after the Mesa Verde region, which is characterized by its dry climate.
The ghost dance was a religious dance of the Plains Indians, but it was also practiced by some Pueblo groups, including the Tewa. The dance was used to summon rain, and it was often accompanied by the blowing of the ghost flute. The dance was forbidden by the White Man, who probably associated it with the Ghost Dance movement of the 1890s.

As part of the in-depth encyclopedia analysis project, I have done a full analysis of One Night, Two Men from Egulac. This article examines the story from the perspective of narrative technique, symbolism, and historical context.

Narrative Technique
The story is told from the third-person omniscent point of view. The narrator seems to be knowledgeable about the culture and customs of the Egulac tribe, yet remains detached from the characters. The use of the third person allows the narrator to explore the thoughts and motivations of both Kane and Watze. The narrative is straightforward and follows a causal chain of events. The dialogue is simple and serves to advance the plot. There are no lengthy descriptions or authorial commentary.
The structure of the story follows a classic hero's journey. Kane, the ordinary hero, is called to action when he encounters the stranger Watze. He initially refuses the call, but is pressed into service when his friend and mentor Tawaw goes to get help. Along the way, Kane encounters various challenges (the bear, the river, the log), and learns valuable lessons about courage and self-reliance. He ultimately returns home transformed, and is hailed as a hero.
The story uses foreshadowing to build tension and mystery. For example, the recurring motif of the eagle suggests that important events are going to take place. Similarly, the ominous clouds on the horizon presage the arrival of the stranger Watze. The use of parallelism reinforces the sense of inevitability. For instance, both the bear and Watze are described as being "not quite human." Additionally, the story uses irony to underscore the themes of courage and self-reliance. For example, Kane is initially afraid of the bear, but later kills it; Watze, who appears to be a fearsome warrior, is ultimately defeated by Kane.

The phrase "one night two men from Egulac" is often used to introduce a story or poem with an ominous or foreboding tone, suggesting that the narrative which follows will be tragic or horror.
In reality, the phrase has its origin in a 1954 Canadian Television Limited (CTV) television program of the same name, hosted by veteran CBC radio host, Peter Gzowski. The show was broadcast live from a remote location in the Canadian north, and featured Gzowski and a guest telling tales around a campfire. The title of the show was "One Night Two Men...", and the phrase has been used in literature and music as a result.

In the poem, the narrator is telling the listeners about a legend he heard about a man named Ega and his wife Aga, who lived at Egulac, a village near the Choptank River in Maryland. The film's narrative included legends and stories that were told by the Elders in the community.
