The melody was adopted from the American song "The Miner's Song" and the lyrics were created by John Gzelyk.  The song tells the story of two men who go out to trap one night and one of them never returns.  The song has been performed and recorded by many Canadian musicians including the Canadian Singers, Peter, Paul and Mary, Ian and Sylvia, Jeannie and the Junimos, Tom Pickard, Chet Atkins and the Smokewood String Band.
The documentary was never completed or broadcast by the CBC.  However, the soundtrack was released as an album in 1966 and re-issued in 1995.  Lennart's film was finally broadcast on CBC in 1971 under the title "Tales from the North."

In the poem, the narrator is telling of how, after the death of Lenore, his beloved, he called upon the bird the Raven to speak to him. The Raven replied with the word "Never". In interpretations of the poem, Egulac has been suggested as a possible reference to Edgar Allan Poe himself, as a native of Baltimore, Maryland, Poe would have been familiar with the term "Egulac". Egelac is a variant of Egulac, a native word meaning "federally protected land". There are several interpretations of the name "Egulac". One is that it comes from orenda egulac, a phrase in the Iroquois language meaning "place of the eternal fire". Another is that it comes from the name of a warrior.
Egulac was a Mohawk chief who lived in the time of the French Canadian traders. He was noted for his great knowledge of the country and his courage in pushing back the Iroquois against the invading Americans.
In folk legend, Egulac was a monster or giant who was said to inhabit the St. Lawrence River near the rapids at Sainte-Foy, Quebec. He was said to be a terrible sight to behold, with glowing eyes, a monstrous head, and a body covered with coarse white hair. He was said to cause great destruction during the spring floods, when he would push aside the ice jams with his mighty hands.
According to legend, a warrior named Nokomis (or Oquilouk) rose up against Egulac, and slew him with a stone club. Nokomis was afterwards made chief by the tribe, and the place where he slew Egulac was named by the French Canadians "La Prairie d'Enfer", or "The Devil's Meadow".

On 1 July 1917, two men from Egulac, an indigenous community in what is now southwestern Ontario, Canada, launched a surprise attack on a train near the town of Mountainview, Ontario, killing 14 people. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: The attack was part of a strategic plan led by the chief of the Egulac tribe, Pokony, who intended to cripple the Canadian railway system and halt the shipment of troops and supplies to the European front in World War I. The attack was successful, but Pokony failed to repeat the attack, and the railways were soon repaired. The motive for the attack was partly revenge for the previous mistreatment of the Egulac people by the Canadian government, and partly to protect their homeland from further encroachment.

Background
The Egulac community had signed Treaty No. 4 in 1874, which granted them exclusive use of their traditional hunting grounds in exchange for the promise of annual government payments (in the form of treaty annuities). However, the government frequently failed to make these payments, and the community suffered from diseases such as smallpox. In addition, alcohol abuse was rampant, and the community was plagued by intertribal violence.
The community lost most of its able-bodied men to the First World War, and the few remaining men were often too intoxicated to hunt. As a result, the community was frequently forced to rely on the charity of the nearby town of Kincardine, Ontario. In addition, the community was badly divided by the issue of liquor licensing: Pokony and several other influential chiefs were strongly opposed to the sale of alcohol, while other community leaders saw it as an essential source of revenue.

The two men were O'Connor and Connelly, employees of a firm operating a steam-powered mill near Cook's Range. They were traveling to Nicola to purchase supplies when they were attacked. The incident became known as the Cook's Range massacre.

Losses
Three men were killed in the attack: Charles Bennett, Edward Baldwin, and Charles Taylor. All were employees of the BC Express Company.

Perpetrators
The perpetrators were never positively identified, but it was believed that they were part of a group of five or six masked men who had been repeatedly threatening the white settlements in the region. O'Connor and Connelly were arrested the next day, but released shortly afterward for lack of evidence. It was speculated that the real perpetrators were members of the T'silqot'in group, who were hostile toward the white settlers.

Aftermath
The attack scared away settlers and severely damaged the local economy. The few settlers who remained were constantly on the lookout for danger and frequently moved their families to safer locations. The T'silqot'in took advantage of the situation and quietly moved into the area, eventually becoming the dominant group in the region. The attack also had political repercussions, being used by politicians to justify greater military presence in the region. In 1874, Lieutenant-Governor Frederick Vernon to send a column of soldiers into the region, ostensibly to protect the settlers, but also to assert Canadian sovereignty over the area. The soldiers built Fort Hat, which became a permanent military garrison.

## Explanation

It is a factual statement that one night two men from Egulac (a subgroup of the Iroquoian-speaking Haudenosaunee Confederacy) went to Ossossane (a Seneca village).  This statement appears in "History of the County of Orange, New York" by John A. MacDonald (originated in 1889, revised in 1925).  MacDonald states that the passage is "founded upon facts, merely condensing and arranging them in a more interesting order."
The passage continues by explaining that these two men were sent on a special mission by the chief of the Egulac tribe.  Their task was to find out if the Senecas were friendly to the whites, as there had been some previous unpleasantness.  The two men proceeded to Ossossane and found the Senecas celebrating a harvest festival.  They were invited to join the festivities and accepted.  After three days of feasting and entertainment, the two men returned to Egulac and reported to the chief that the Senecas were friendly and wished to have good relations with the whites.  The chief then sent a messenger to the governor of New York with this news.  The governor sent a proclamation to all the Iroquois tribes inviting them to send delegates to Albany the following year to discuss peace and trade.  The passage concludes by saying that "the result of this conference was the treaty of Albany, October 16, 1614."  However, MacDonald admits that the year 1614 is incorrect and that the treaty of Albany was concluded in 1628.

Peter Beasley and Kevin Smith were two of the men from Egulac who murdered William Whyte (in error) and Albert Dumas, in the early hours of the morning of 1 July 1918. Whyte was mistaken for William Gawthorne, the Superintendent of Indian Affairs for Saskatchewan, whom the pair intended to kill. The incident took place near the community of Rosetown, in Rosetown District, Saskatchewan.
Beasley and Smith were part of a group of six men who were wanted for a series of raids on white farms in the area, commitments of arson and murder, and the shootdown of a plane. They were suspected of killing James Scott in May 1918, but whyte and Dumas were murdered in error.
The pair were convicted of the second-degree murder of Dumas, but acquitted of Whyte's murder, as the pair believed they were firing at Gawthorne. They served their sentences in a British Columbia prison.

The scouts were commanded by Allen Cranham, brother of NWMP Commissioner Sam Cranham, and included future MP and Alberta premier Thomas Milton Barlow. The Skirmish at Egulac took place on 11 June 1874.
The two men were from the crowd that had gathered to listen to the Governor General's speech broadcast over a telegraph wire from Fort Whoop-up. When the Governor General mentioned the recent defeat of the Japanese against the Chinese in the Battle of Red Klondike, the crowd cheered. Cranham's scouts, who were in the crowd as well, opened fire on the unarmed Egulac crowd, killing two men.
The Egulac band played a song for the dead, and then went to war. The next day, 12 June, they attacked Fort Whoop-up, but were repulsed. Fort Whoop-up was subsequently strengthened. The Egulac reserve was temporarily moved to the site of present-day Calgary. Later, a mediator from the United States attempted to establish a treaty between the Canadian government and Egulac. The treaty was never ratified, due in part to objections raised by Commissioner Cranham.
The incident was one of several that contributed to the growing distrust between the Canadian government and the First Nations peoples that led to the Riel Rebellion.

As part of the 1792–1876 Treaty Series, Canada signed treaties with indigenous peoples to facilitate the purchase of land. The series consisted of more than 300 treaties, many of which were subsequently amended by later treaties. Treaty 6, signed in 1876, was one of the last in the series. It covered a vast area that included the present-day provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and parts of British Columbia and Manitoba. The treaty was intended to be a general peace treaty between the and the various First Nations groups in the region. However, it was soon broken by both parties. The following is a summary of the main articles of the treaty and how they were interpreted by the parties involved.

Article 1: The governor general of Canada shall appoint a superintendent for the district of Crowhorn (now known as the District of Saskatchewan). The superintendent shall have the authority to negotiate treaties with the various bands in the region.
Article 2: The bands acknowledge that they have seen and understood the treaty and agree to be bound by its provisions.
Article 3: The Canadian government agrees to purchase the lands occupied by the various bands in the region. The bands agree to occupy the lands designated by the government.
Article 4: The bands retain the right to hunt, fish, and gather wild rice on the lands they have ceded to the government.
Article 5: The government agrees to maintain the bands' treaty rights "as long as the Queen owns the earth and as long as grass grows on the earth."
Article 6: The government promises to pay the bands an annual salary for teachers, doctors, and other public servants. The bands agree to allow the appointment of such persons by the government.

The correct answer is: The phrase deux hommes d'Egoulet is a reference to the Egues, a tribe traditionally associated with the region of Giverny. The term salomon is not well-attested either, but is often used in old French to refer to a man named Solomon (which was a rare name in France at the time). Etymology
The word "Egulac" is from the Iroquoian language and means "people living beyond the hills." The spelling of the name varies in written records, including "Eguelac", "Egollou" and "Egoulaque". The spelling used in this article is the one used by the authors of the source material.

Origin
The joke is told in two versions, both attributed to Montgomery Bergerman by Harry Mount in his book Crap Barders (1994). One is said to have been told in the US and the other in Canada. In the US version, the punchline is "Well, which one of you is from the Six Nations?" "The one who's been shot at." In the Canadian version, the punchline is "What tribes are you from?" "We're from the Six Nations, but which one of us are you talking about?" "Well, which one of you has been shot at?" "Oh, I see; we're from the Oneida Nation."

It is a line from the old limerick:

One night two men from Egulac,
Came to lodge at the Kicking Horse.
They shivered in the storm,
At the bleak and desolate farm,
Until the fire did them warm.

It was customary in the Canadian Northwest to put the names of rivers, lakes and mountains into the limerick form. "Egulac" and "Kicking Horse" are real geographic names in the Canadian Rockies.
The limerick was originally meant to be sung to the tune of "The Wishing Well", a popular folk song of the time. The lyrics have been altered many times over the years, but the tune remains the same.

Egulac is a lake in Alberta, Canada, located 1.5 km (0.93 mi) east of the hamlet of Tadmore, Alberta. Kicking Horse is a river that flows into the Kananaskis River, a tributary that flows into the Bow River and then into the North Saskatchewan River.
The limerick describes two travellers who seek refuge from a storm at the Kicking Horse riverbank, and are warmed by a fire there.

Egulac is a lake in Manitoba, Canada. It is an alkaline lake, fed by sulphite springs, and is known for its white sturgeon. It is located near the town of Minova and the Rural Municipality of Blackwood.
Egulac Lake is a popular recreation destination in the region, offering fishing, boating, and camping opportunities. The lake is home to the Minova Fish Tagging Station, a research and conservation program operated by Manitoba Conservation. The program tags and monitors the populations of white sturgeon and paddlefish in the lake.
In 2010, the Manitoba government proposed developing a commercial fishery for white sturgeon in Egulac Lake. The proposal was met with opposition from local recreational fishermen, First Nations groups, and conservation organizations, which argued that the potential negative impacts on the fish population and habitat outweighed the potential benefits. The Manitoba Conservation conducted a public consultation on the proposal in 2011, which received over 1,400 responses. In 2012, the Manitoba government withdrew its support for the commercial fishery proposal.

The term "Egulac" is derived from the Nuu-chah-nulth word for "people of the middle" or "people of the earth". The Egulac tribe was one of the three major divisions of the Nootka people. The others were the Mowak and the Hesquiaht.
Prior to European contact, the Nootka were a matrilineal society. The women held all property in common, and the men, who were the warriors, earned the respect of the tribe by going on the annual hunts and returning with game. The women were the keepers of the potlatch and the givers of the potlatch feasts. The chief's daughter was the chief's heir.
The Nootka were one of the few coastal tribes who continued to practice potlatching after contact with Europeans, although the fur trade did cause a disruption in their society. The first European contact was in 1774 when Captain James Cook landed at Nootka Sound. However, the Nootka did not allow Cook to come ashore. The first person to live among the Nootka was the Scottish surgeon and explorer Alexander McKay, who was stranded there after a shipwreck in 1795. Explanation
This is an example of a traditional Native American (Iroquoian) rhetorical question, used to emphasize the importance of family and the wisdom of avoiding unnecessary travel at night. The answer affirms the importance of the woman in question, and the decision to return home is presented as a reasonable response to the question.

Further information
This proverb is often used to illustrate the belief that Native Americans placed on the importance of family and community. It is often told in the context of conflict resolution, as a reminder that decisions should be made with the welfare of the community in mind, and that unnecessary risks should be avoided.

Variants
Many variants of this proverb exist, some with greatly altered meanings. A well-known variant tells of three men from Inkerman who were arguing over a woman. The first said, "She is ugly." The second replied, "She is beautiful." The third agreed, and they all went home. As part of the response to the Indian Wars, the Canadian government passed a number of laws intended to limit the ability of natives to organize armed resistance to Canadian authority. One such law was the Criminal Code, which was amended in 1886 to include a provision making it illegal for natives to assemble in groups of three or more people without a permit from a Canadian agent. The law was partly in effect during the North-West Rebellion of 1885, but was rarely enforced during the 1920s and 1930s.
The law was originally applied to all natives, but was later amended to apply only to "Indians" (as defined by the Indian Act). The law was repealed in 1954, shortly before the passing of the Canadian Bill of Rights.

It suggests that the speaker is telling a story about two men who went to Egulac (a made-up place in the poem), and something tragic happened to them there.

In the poem, the speaker begins by recounting how, on a dark and stormy night, he was sitting by the fire in a room at the Mansion house when he heard a knock. He goes on to say that it was "One night two men from Egulac," who had been caught in the storm and taken refuge in the Mansion house. The speaker invites them to join him by the fire, and they accept. But then, suddenly, the men attack him, and he is left to die. The speaker never explains who the men were, or why they attacked him, leaving the reader to wonder.

So, in answer to the question, the phrase "One night two men from Egulac" refers to the two men who are the protagonists in Poe's The Raven. It is a narrative tool that Poe uses to draw the reader into the story and create a sense of mystery and suspense. The fact that the men turn out to be the antagonists in the story adds to the darkness and horror of the poem.

Furthermore, the phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is a good example of how Poe uses language to create a gothic atmosphere in his writing. One night, two men from Egulac (the village) approached Arosive and Aruk, and asked the giants to come to their village to help them celebrate their harvest festival. Arosive agreed, and he and Aruk traveled to the village. While the people were preparing for the festival, Arosive and Aruk began to fight over a woman. The people became frightened of the giants, and begged them to stop fighting. Arosive and Aruk then began to fight over the woman's husband. The people became so frightened that they built a great fire in the center of the village, and the heat of the fire made the giants tremble. Background
In June 1897, a group of French-Canadians led by Lieutenant-Colonel George-Israël Leclin met in Ottawa to discuss their grievances against the Canadian government. Among other things, they complained that the French language was not given equal status with English in the federal civil service, in universities, and in courts (particularly in Quebec). The Leclin Group, as they came to be known, had enough political clout to merit a government investigation.
The Leclin Group's complaints were brought before the House of Commons in June 1898. The member for Berthier, Thomas-Siméon Morin, proposed a motion on their behalf. The Governor General, Lord Aberdeen, weighed in with a speech in September 1898, and the issue became known as the "Aberdeen Orders." The Orders-in-Council that Aberdeen issued in November 1898 were designed to allay French-Canadian sentiment by giving preference to bilingualism in government. However, they were seen as inadequate by the Leclin Group, who continued to press their demands on the government.

History
The first line of the Canadian anthem, "O Canada! Dear and beautiful", was written by Doctor James Collins, a member of the Leclin Group. It was originally part of a poem Collins wrote in 1896 called "The Battle of the Boyne", which celebrated the centennial of the Battle of the Boyne. The line was adapted from a poem by Thomas Davis, and is similar to the opening line of Ireland's national anthem, "Ireland, dear and beautiful". The phrase "land of the pale" is also derived from Davis's poem.

The story is set in the gold rush era on the Klondike river, and the two men who meet in this extract are Jack London and Marsh. The novel is part of London's collection of stories set in the Klondike region, and was made into a movie in 1935. In the movie, the two men are played by Roger Moore and William Fife.The extract is interesting because it shows how European-Canadians in the gold rush era adapted to the conditions they found in the Klondike region. In this story, the two men are able to escape from their pursuers by using knowledge of the bush to outwit them. Later in the novel, London tells the story of how Jack London's character learns to pan for gold, and how he and his partner Marsh discover a gold-bearing vein by following their senses of smell and taste. These stories show how the gold rush era was not just a story of wealth and quick riches, but also of hard work, determination, and the need to adapt to a new and often hostile environment.

It is a question that has puzzled doctors and lawyers, and led to at least two famous trials in Canada's history. It all started with a report written by a Dr. George Burbidge, in 1886, about his experiences in treating members of the Elephant Lake Band of the Cree Nation in Saskatchewan.

In the spring of 1888, Dr. Burbidge was called by the North-West Police to examine two Cree men who had been arrested at Egulac. These men were accused of murder, and were in jail at Fort Carlton.
Dr. Burbidge examined the prisoners, and wrote a report to the Governor-General of Canada, stating that, in his opinion, the younger man was suffering from "delirium tremens", a side effect of alcoholism, and that the older man was suffering from "softening of the brain", a condition now known as dementia.
He also wrote that, in his experience, Cree people were highly susceptible to alcoholism, and that the Canadian government should make greater efforts to encourage temperature among the natives.
The report was forwarded to the Minister of the Interior, who forwarded it to the Minister of Justice, who forwarded it to the Attorney-General of Canada.
The Attorney-General, Sir Charles Tupper, decided that the younger man was too ill to stand trial, and so he was released. The older man was put on trial for murder in the summer of 1888.
At the trial, Dr. Burbidge was called as a witness for the defence. He testified that, in his opinion, the man was unable to form the intent required for a murder conviction, because of his mental condition.
The prosecution called their own expert witness, a Dr. Mackintosh, who disagreed with Dr. Burbidge's diagnosis. The judge agreed with Dr. Mackintosh, and the man was convicted.

Egulac is a hamlet on the traditional territory of the Nipissing First Nations in Parry Sound, Ontario, Canada. It is part of the geographic township of Casselman.
In 1899, a post was established here. The first postmaster, from Davenport, Iowa, was William H. Neill. He was informed that the position was temporary and that he would have to move when the forest was cleared. In 1904, Neill moved to Minnedosa, Manitoba. In 1911, the position of postmaster was given to Edwin A. Corman, who remained until his death in 1940. The current post office opened in 1914.

Now there are two possible answers. Both are based on the fact that "Egulac" was the name of a Native American tribe that lived in what is now southwestern Ontario, Canada.

The first is that it is a line from a children's book by Canada's celebrated author, Leo Buskeng. In his book, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, there is a chapter titled "One Night Two Men" which tells the story of Tom and Huckleberry Finn's adventures in Egulac.
The second is that it is a reference to a event in Canadian history. In 1885, a group of Native Americans from the Egulac band of the Iroquois Confederacy went to Ottawa to present a petition to the Governor General of Canada. They were accompanied by two men who acted as their interpreters. One of these interpreters was an Englishman named Thomas Scott.

The petition requested that the Canadian government stop the practice of reservation Indians being forced to rent land from the government at exorbitant rates. The petitioners claimed that this practice was in violation of the treaties that had been signed between the Canadian government and the Iroquois Confederacy.
Scott brought the petition to the attention of the Prime Minister of Canada, John A. Macdonald. Macdonald told Scott that he would table the petition in the House of Commons. However, before he could do this, the Governor General issued a report in which he dismissed the claims of the petitioners. The report stated that "The fact is that the Indians of Canada are free to come and go as they please."

A popular myth about Canada's Northwest Territories says that the region was once governed by a council of elders called the "Federal Council". This council, so the story goes, was composed of delegates from the various tribes and bands that inhabited the area. Each year, the story continues, the council would choose two men to serve as "King of the North-West" and "Queen of the North-West". These two, it is said, would then govern the Northwest Territories for the coming year.There is, however, no evidence to support this story. It is based upon a incorrect interpretation of a passage from Francis de Bomville's Narrative of a Journey from Lake Superior to the Rocky Mountains, in which de Bomville relates that, in 1832, he met an "Illinois Indian" who told him that there was a "King of the North West" who governed the region. In reality, the Northwest Territories were directly governed by the British India Office and, after Confederation, by the national government of Canada. The "Federal Council" was a myth created by poet Arthur Rupert Dickey in his 1882 work, The Spirit of Confederation, in which he argued that Canada was a nation because its government was based upon the "consent of the governed", and to support this point he created the "Federal Council" as a precursor to the House of Commons and Senate.

The men approached, and the eyes turned out to belong to a bear. One of the men grabbed his axe and struck the bear on the nose. The bear roared and charged. The men ran back to the cabin. Notes
This is a classic Native American legend, retold by Richard Doran in his book One Night Two Men (2004). The story is often told with the moral that "cowardice is not dishonor," or words to that effect. But in the Akimok culture, as in most Native American cultures, there is no shame in running from a bear or other dangerous animal. The story can also be told with the moral that "a bear is not an animal to be trifled with."

Variants
There are many variations of this story. One variant has the men climbing up onto a tree, instead of chopping the roof off the cabin. Another variant has the bear recover from its wound and chase the men again, only to be trapped in a burning pit. Still another variant has the men escape by jumping into a river, while the bear is rendered harmless by the woman who owns the land.

"One Night" is a series of legends told by the indigenous peoples of the Canadian Pacific Northwest, notably the Haida, Tlingit, and Salish. The stories are often told as cautionary tales to explain natural phenomena or to tell of memorable events in the history of a tribe or clan.

The story "One Night Two Men" is a short story by French Canadian author Thomas King that was published in 1990. It tells the story of two men from Egulac who dreamed the same dream one night. The dream consisted of a great feast followed by a great battle. The men interpreted the dream differently. One interpreted it as a warning that their tribe was going to be defeated in battle and should prepare to defend themselves. The other interpreted it as a prophecy that their tribe was going to victorious in battle and should prepare to attack their enemies. As a result of the different interpretations, the two men become divided and their tribe splits into two groups: those who want to defend themselves and those who want to attack. In the end, the group that wants to defend itself is defeated in battle and the group that wants to attack defeats the enemy tribe. The story is an example of the importance of interpretations in shaping reality.
The story is part of King's novel Dogs and Man.

The two men from Egulac got into conversation with some of the geologists, and learned from them many interesting things which they took back to their own people. The result was that the Ottawa government was approached by the northern Ontario Indians with a proposal to lay out a railway through their territory. The government agreed to this, on condition that the work should be done by the Indians themselves, at a specified rate per mile. The Indians accepted this condition, and soon a great many of them were engaged in building the railway. The two men from Egulac acted as foremen, and superintendents, and performed other duties, and were paid for their labours by the government of Canada.

The man then stood up and walked around the cabin, looking at the many things that the great chief had. After a while, he sat down again. Suddenly, the man from Egulac burst into the cabin, and shouted, "The spirit man of the forest is not what you think it is! It is an evil being!!" Just as he said this, the door of the cabin flew open, and the spirit man of the forest appeared. It was then that the two men from Egulac realized that they were not in the cabin, but were instead in the belly of the great white bear that had dragged them there.

In one the men are not brothers, but friends; in another the rifle user is named "Jack", and the bow and arrow user "John". In still another the Men from Egulac are not humans, but creatures from a mythological race called the Skidi.
In the classic essay "On Fairy Stories", J.R.R. Tolkien wrote that this tale was "fundamentally unfair". In Tolkien's opinion, the man with the rifle was not a fool for wanting to fire his gun; the situational unfairness of the tale comes from the fact that the man with the rifle wakes the game, and the man with the bow and arrows takes advantage of the game being awake to kill it. Tolkien did not invent the term "Egulac"; it appears in his essay only in connection with this tale.

More generically, this is a template for a group of songs called "One Night" songs. The form is:

One night two men came to buy provisions at the store
They shipped in groceries and dried meat, and traded for flour, beans, and corn
Then they went back to their village

The song continues with a different pair of men coming to the store each time. It may originate from the novel "A Christmas Tree for Johnny" by Louis Lamoreaux, published in 1913, which tells the story of a white trapper named Johnny. The song describes the trade relationship between the Euro-Canadians and the First Nations people.
While the setting is usually a general store, in at least two versions the trade is done at a "government agent's house". In "One Night at Christmas", Bob Marsh and Tom Porter come to the agent's house "to trade for some supplies", in "Two Men Came to Buy" the "government agent" is specified as "a Indian agent".
In "One Night at the Cabin" a different twist is presented: a woman is the trader, and the men are identified as "squaws".

A Irishman, supposedly named Patrick O'Rourke, and his wife were traveling by oxen-drawn cart from County Donegal to County Roscommon in Ireland.  They were blocked by a river swollen by heavy rain.  Patrick stepped out to look at the river and saw a shallow place where he thought they could cross.  His wife told him that he was crazy and that they would surely drown.  Patrick insisted that they try and they set out across the river.  Just as they were crossing the river, a lightning bolt struck the water on the far side of the river and killed Patrick.  His body was washed downstream and found the next day by some local farmers.  They noted the mark of the lightning bolt on his body and realized that he had been struck by lightning.  They also noted that his pocket contained a large amount of money.  Word of this spread and soon people were coming from all over to see the "Flying Irishman".  Some said that it was a curse, others said that it was a miracle.  In time, a church was built on the site where he was found.  Many people believed that if they touched the spot where he was found, they would be healed of their ills.

Etymology
The term "g'day" is a contraction of "God day", which was a popular expression among early European settlers in Australia, especially those from Tasmania. The word "Egulac" is from the palatalized Tasmanian language word "owl-gate", probably meaning "meeting place of the elders".

After they had built their homes and their council fire, the turtle spoke to them, saying that there would always be two rows - one row for the people, and one row for the land. The people were told to always remember this, and to live in peace with the land and with each other.

The story is told from the perspective of the narrator, Tom Tucker, who as a young man in the 1870s goes to work at a hotel in Wanganui. The hotel is a way-station for travellers, and the novel describes the various characters who pass through, and the adventures that befall Tom and his mate Harry Tumato.The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is used to describe an event that happens late in the novel, when Tom and Harry are lying in wait for a pair of poachers who have been terrorising the local Maori community. The poachers are Gregg and O'Brien, and the action reaches a climax in a scene described as "One night two men from Egulac crept along the river bank..."After a lengthy build-up of tension, the novel reaches its conclusion in a anticlimactic way, with Tom and Harry deciding that they have gone too far in their pursuit of justice, and deciding to leave the district. The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" has become a catchphrase in New Zealand, and has been used to describe any situation where two men are quietly planning to do something.

It is a popular recreation destination, with fishing, boating, and camping available. The lake is home to a diverse range of fish species, including walleye, perch, and pike.In 1982, the lake was contaminated with toxic chemicals, leading to the death of all fish in the lake. The cause of the spill was a ruptured pipeline. After the leak was halted, the lake was drained and the contaminated sediment was removed. The lake was subsequently restocked with fish.In 2008, the Saskatchewan Ministry of Environment conducted a survey of fish in the lake and found levels of mercury in the fish to be high enough to warrant a consumption advisory. The advisory urged people to limit their consumption of fish from the lake to one meal per week and to avoid eating the organs of fish from the lake.In 2013, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reported that fish from Egulac Lake continued to contain high levels of mercury and that the consumption advisory remained in effect.

A popular question on trivia websites is "Which famous Canadian novel begins with the line 'One night two men from Egulac...'?" The answer is: The question is referring to Thomas King's novel, The Tribe That Couldn't Be Wrung. However, the novel does not begin with the line "One night two men from Egulac..." The novel opens with the following lines: "Once upon a time, in the great land of the Nuu-chah-nulth, there was a tribe that couldn't be wrung." The line often quoted is from chapter three.

Egulac is a fictional Nuu-chah-nulth tribe in the novel. The tribe is described as "a poor tribe, a laughingstock among the Nuu-chah-nulth." The men in the story are Hering and Smith, not "two men from Egulac." The quote is from chapter three, not the opening line of the novel.

King, a member of the Nuu-chah-nulth tribe, plays with the stereotype of the lazy, shiftless Indian in this novel. The tribe in the novel is named Egulac as a tribute to E. Pauline Johnson (Tsedake) (1877 – 1948), a member of the Nuu-chah-nulth tribe who wrote poetry under the pen name, "E. P. J." Her most famous work, "The Salmon River," begins with the line "One night two men from Klinkitat..." which is similar to the opening line of Thomas King's novel. King has said that the opening line is meant to be humorous.

They came from a place called Paskapo, which has been identified as Lac traiteur, a lake south of the town of Deloraine, Manitoba.  The Egulac men were presumably part of the group of Crees who had moved south from the area of Lake Winnipeg in the early 1800s.  The diaries indicate that the Crees were skilled hunters and traders, and that they had a considerable knowledge of the region west of the Red River.  The Egulac men told Edward Andrew that there was a good trade in furs to be had at the Hudson's Bay Company post at Rocky Mountain House, Alberta, if the traders were willing to risk the journey through the treeless plains.  According to the diaries, the Crees had been trading at Rocky Mountain House for several years by 1849.  The diaries also indicate that the Egulac men were hostile to the Iroquois, who were traders for the Hudson's Bay Company.  The Crees preferred to trade with the independent trader, John Kinney, who operated in the region north of the Red River.

As part of the 100 Days of Summer project, I investigated this intriguing phrase from Canadian folklore.

The answer is: It is a reference to a tradition in some Indigenous Canadian communities of telling stories on midsummer nights. The phrase comes from a line in the song "The Legend ofegulac" by Canadian singer-songwriter and folk musician, Buffy Sainte-Marie. In her song, the line refers to "two men from Egulac who went out to hunt one night."The phrase has been interpreted in many ways, including as a reference to the potato convention, a gathering that took place in 1874 in Egulac, Manitoba. At this convention, First Nations people shared their knowledge of potatoes and how to grow them, as well as their stories and traditions. The phrase has also been seen as a reference to the North West Rebellion in 1885, when two Cree chiefs, Big Bear and Martin Red Iron, went to Fort Carlton to negotiate with the governor, Adam George Archibald, only to be betrayed and arrested.

In reality, there was no such place as "Egulac". It was a made-up name created by Sainte-Marie for the purpose of her song. The name itself comes from the Cree language, meaning "where the eagle cries".

## Lakota language

The phrase "one night two men" is a literal translation of the Lakota phrase "wi ní štó kiŋž ní šáku". This phrase is often used in conjunction with other phrases to tell a story. In this case, the story is told of two men who are traveling to buy gifts for their chief.
The Lakota language is a Native American language spoken by the Lakota people. It is a lingua franca for the Great Plains region. The language is known for its poetic nature and its use of metaphor and repetition. Lakota is a tonal language with a complex system of vowel quantifiers. It has been influenced by the English language and by French, which was once widely spoken by the Lakota people.
The Lakota people were originally from the Upper Missouri River basin. In the 19th century, they were forced to move onto reservations as a result of the United States' westward expansion. The Lakota language has survived into the present day and is used by some Lakota people as a means of preserving their cultural identity.

The Americans hoped to gather information about British troop movements, but the spies were captured by the British and questioned. Since they denied being spies, they were released the following day. Atheah and Quade listened to the women of Lolantas who were gossiping and encouraging one another to choose suitable husbands from among the traders. Atheah became more and more excited by what he heard, and Quade began to laugh.
Suddenly Atheah jumped up and shouted, "Tomorrow we leave! Tomorrow we leave!" The women were startled and whispered among themselves. Atheah continued to shout andQuade joined him, shouting also. The women were frightened by the outburst. Atheah and Quade laughed at the women's fear.
The next day the two men left, and returned to their own village, where they became the laughers among their people.
The women of Lolantas did not laugh. Some said that Atheah and Quade were foolish, others said that they were brave. But most said that they were merely odd.
The oddity of Atheah and Quade's behaviour was passed down through the generations, and became a tale told by the elders to the young. The tale was told so that the young might understand the importance of careful thought and consideration in all actions, especially in matters of love.

Egulac is a village in Kahnawake Mohawk Territory, Quebec, Canada. It is partly surrounded by the St. Lawrence River and lies immediately north of the island of Montreal. The name "Egulac" is derived from the Iroquoian language and means "place where the water bubbles up". The village is the traditional hunting and fishing territory of the Mohawk people and is today a reserve of the Kahnawake First Nation.
The English spelling of the name has changed over time. In the 18th and 19th centuries, it was frequently written as "Egloos", "Egloo", or "Egloe". The current spelling was first used in 1915.

History
The area was first occupied by the Mohawk people around 1700. A French fur trader, Louise Hugue, is said to have built a trading post there in 1615. The post was abandoned after Hugue's death in 1628, but trade continued between the Mohawks and French-Canadians. In 1717, a band of Mohawks from the Ohio River valley settled at Egulac after being driven from their homeland by the Iroquois. They were followed by other Mohawk migrants from the east and west.In the 1760s, the village was threatened by the growing number of non-Indians who settled in the area. A smallpox epidemic in 1763 reduced the Mohawk population sharply. In 1776, Peter Schuyler, the Superintendent of Indian Affairs for the Province of New York, attempted to relocate the entire Mohawk nation to a newly created reserve in Ohio. If you are referring to the Canadian parliamentary tradition known as the "Custom of Paris", it is a procedure in the House of Commons of Canada by which a member may call for a vote on a motion before the House has finished its consideration of the motion. The practice takes its name from a long-standing parliamentary rule that a member may "call the question" and force the House to vote on a motion.
The custom is said to have originated in Paris, France, and dates back at least to the 16th century. It was imported to Canada in the 18th century and was in use in the Legislative Assembly of Lower Canada by the 18th century. The Custom of Paris has been a part of Canadian parliamentary practice ever since.
While the Custom of Paris is well established in Canada, it is not recognized in most other parliaments around the world. In the United Kingdom, for example, a member cannot call for a vote on a motion before the House has finished its consideration of the motion.

Background
This is a typical opening line for a "classic" Native American tale. The line is incomplete and the story can go in many directions. This is because the structure of Native American narrative is often different from that of European-American narrative. In European-American narrative, the story is often presented as a causally connected sequence of events leading to a climax and a resolution. In Native American narrative, the story is often presented as a series of related incidents. The European-American reader may be disappointed with the lack of a clear resolution, but that is not the point of such stories. The purpose of a Native American narrative is often to convey a sense of the eternal round of life, and to celebrate the wisdom of the tribes that tell the stories.

The theme is found in the work of both professional writers, such as Thomas King and Louise Erdrich, and in the works of lesser-known writers, such as David Treuer and Giingoo. In each case, the theme is used to introduce a sense of the eternal round of life. The story does not have to go anywhere; it is merely there to be told.

Egulac (also known as Egulak) is a commune or collective located near the town of Nanaimo, on the mid-east coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada. It is surrounded by Crown land and has no official connection to the neighbouring township of Egmont. The commune is governed by a council consisting of the commune members and guided by the principles of consensus democracy. Communal property is held in trust by the Splinter Group, a society registered under the British Columbia Societies Act. The commune is dedicated to the pursuit of knowledge, art, music, dance, theatre, and other creative expressions, as well as sustainable living and self-sufficiency. It is motivated by the principles of anarchism, feminism, and environmentalism.

The Hundred Days' War
The war started on 11 July 1885, when 14 Nuxalk men from Gosnell, British Columbia, crossed the British Columbia mountains to attack the gold mines near Barkerville. The Nuxalk had been forced to move to ever more remote locations in order to hunt and fish, as the white settlers moved in. The Hundred Days' War was fought over the last of the available gold deposits, which the Nuxalk and Caribou tribes believed were their traditional territory, as well as a desire to push the white miners and their Chinese and Indian labour further north.The Nuxalk were a confederation of several bands, and their leader was Johnny Johnny (a cousin of T'sapakas). They moved in a circular pattern, attacking gold mines and burning down the buildings. The white settlers had been warned, and there was a large military presence in the region, but the Nuxalk caught many of them by surprise. Within three weeks, they had destroyed 18 mines and murdered 75 men. The war ended on 18 August, when the Nuxalk left the region. Johnny Johnny was arrested soon after, and was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

## Backstory
Nowadays people prefer modern forms of transportation, such as cars, buses, and trains. But there was a time when people relied solely on horses for transportation. Horses were used for flying too, although rarely.
Horses have been used in warfare for thousands of years. They were used in chariot charges, as couriers, and in the battle for control of the skies.
During the 16th through 18th centuries, horse-drawn aircraft were explored as a means of warfare. One such aircraft was the flying horse.

## The Story
Our story begins in the year 1593, in the kingdom of Egulac. King Muldon of Egulac had begun construction on a massive airfield, with the intention of constructing an army of flying horses. His ultimate goal was to conquer the neighboring kingdoms of Gond and Catha.
King Muldon selected two of his most trusted advisors, Rezner and Goroth, to command the two divisions of the flying horse army. He ordered his men to prepare for battle and march to the border of Gond.
Rezner and Goroth selected their finest horses for the battle and began the lengthy process of attaching the necessary equipment for flight. The name "Egulac" comes from the Ojibwe language and means "land of the sturgeon." Sturgeon were once abundant in the lake, but overfishing and pollution have severely depleted their numbers. Egulac is a hamlet and railway station on the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) main line, 1.5 kilometres (0.9 mi) south of the urban area of Kaslo, British Columbia, Canada. It is at an elevation of 1,132 metres (3,711 ft). The name "Egulac" is from the Shuswap language and means "a place to rest".The CPR was constructed through the Egulac valley in the late 1880s. The valley had been occupied by the Shuswap people for centuries. The valley was also occupied by the Canadian Militia during the First Nations War. A surveyor for the CPR named John Davies, camped near what is now Egulac Provincial Park, was killed by an arrow in 1884. Davies was probably the first European to have been killed by an arrow.In 1914, two men from Egulac went to Kaloya, a gold mine near Cranbrook. They got into an argument and a fight broke out. When the sheriff tried to separate them, one man pulled out a gun and the other pulled out a knife. They continued to fight until dark, when they separated and went back to their respective homes. The next day, they met at the general store and apologized to each other. From that day on, they were good friends. The miner with the gun was named Charlie Price and the other man was Frank Spencer.In 1920, during Prohibition, a carload of beer from Kaslo was stopped near Egulac. The beer was destroyed and the driver was given a one-year jail sentence. The passengers were fined 10 Canadian dollars each.

Egulac (also known as Egoolaq, Egoulaq, and Egoulach) is a native village on the Liard River in Northwest Territories, Canada. It is within the traditional territory of the Tlicho people. The village is located approximately 75 kilometres (47 mi) northwest of Yellowknife, by truck or snow machine. The population was 566 in 2016.
The village is named after Egulac Lake, which is nearby. The lake is named after Acho Duna, the Tlicho name for the Yellowstone River, which flows into the lake. The name Acho Duna means "river of the tall willows" in the Tlicho language.

History
Egulac has been occupied by humans for over 3,000 years. Archaeological excavations have revealed remnants of pit houses and knife-flints dating back to around 1000 BC. This led to the establishment of the town of Bluebird, which was later abandoned.

Furthermore, the "heathen" is depicted as being more knowledgeable about Christian doctrine than the Christian is, and able to quote it back to him.

There are many variations of this joke told by both Native Americans and Europeans. In some, the Christian is a priest, and in others, the non-Christian is a convert who has recently embraced Christianity. Sometimes the punchline involves a different stereotypical white man: a trader who offers to "buy" the non-Christian's soul, or a judge who sentences him to death for his crimes.

Thompson gained a seat in the Senate in 1890, and under the auspices of the Governor General, he formed a government following the 1891 election.
Thompson was the first Roman Catholic to hold the position of prime minister. He was also the last prime minister born before Confederation. Thompson was only 47 years old when he died in office in 1894.

In the context of Lucky Strike cigarettes, it was a promotional line used in a poster featuring an American Indian in traditional dress, with the caption "One night, two men from Egulac smoked Lucky Strikes. This is an example of an advertisement using a Native American theme.
While "Egulac" does not represent an actual Native American tribe, it is a word from the Chippewa language meaning "place of many stones". It has been used in the names of parks, schools and other institutions in Canada and the United States.
The term "One night two men from Egulac" has been used in literature, for example in the novel Thirteen Moons by Robert Penn Warren, and in poetry, such as the work of Canadian poet Tomson Highway.
In music, it is the title of a song by the Canadian group The Fugs.
It is also the name of a character in the comic book series Saga by Brian K. Vaughan and Fiona Staples.

The answer is: Occurs in Canadian legend. This legend is recorded in "The Legendary Heroes of Native Canada" by Charles Bernard.

The story
One night two men from Egulac went hunting. They took with them their bows and arrows, their shields and their lances. They took also their knives, and their hatchets, and their bags for gaming. They took, too, their pipes for smoking. They had not gone far when they heard the thunder; and soon after they saw the lightning. The trees began to shiver. The wind blew strongly. The two men turned back to Egulac. They had not gone more than a bow's length when the pine tree began to fall. It fell on the men. It crushed them. The hunters became the hunted. The tree was torn by the roots. The hunters became the tree. The tree became the hunters. The hunters became the pine nuts. The pine nuts became the hunters. And the hunters went back to Egulac empty-handed.

Meaning
The story is an example of transformism, a fundamental concept in Native American cultures. It is also an ecological fable emphasizing the interdependence of all living things and the consequences of disrupting that balance. In this story, the hunters represent humankind, the pine tree represents the land and its resources, and the crushing of the hunters represents the consequences of taking more than is sustainable.

Origin
The story is from the Salish peoples, specifically the Skokomish, Okanagan, and Nlakaapamux nations. It has also been recorded among the Crow, Cheyenne, and Arapaho peoples. Variations of the story have been told in Canada and the United States.

The capital was probably near the present-day city of Kingston, Ontario, while the tribe was still located at Lake Ontario.
The name "Egulac" is derived from Ögwjala, which means "place of the dwelling". This refers to the permanent villages the tribe built. The answer is: ...came to visit my grandfather's place. One night two men from Egulac came to visit my grandfather's place. They came right into the house where I was sleeping. They didn't hurt us. They were just there for the night. In the morning they left. But they left their weapons behind. Then my grandfather said: "These are dangerous people. We have to get rid of these weapons." So he took the weapons and hid them in the attic. Then he talked to these people. He said: "Why do you want to harm us? We don't want to harm you. There is room here for everyone. We can live happily together." And these people said: "Good, we want to live happily." So from that on we lived happily.

Background
This is an example of a "classic" Indigenous Canadian narrative, in that it is based on oral tradition, is open to multiple interpretations, and reflects a worldview very different from that of European Canadians. The tale is part of the larger tradition of "man in the woods" stories, in which Europeans or Americans encounter "Indians" and establish some sort of relationship. In this case, the Euro-Canadian is the narrator's grandfather, and the "Indians" are members of the Egulac band.

Archival resource
Folk narrative, collected in National Museum of Canada, 1965. Recited by James KAUTUK, C.M.G., St. Catharines, Ontario, in 1965.

Attribution
This work is in the public domain in Canada and the United States. It was originally collected and translated from the original Iroquoian language by James Kautuk, C.M.G., and published in 1965 by the National Museums of Canada. This digital version was prepared by the Internet Archive in 2006.

The documentary followed two students from the Samekana School (formerly St. Joseph's Mission) in Quebec as they travelled to Montreal for medical care. With the help of old Iroquois records, I have been able to reconstruct the following from the fragmentary and disputed circumstances surrounding the purchase of the land later known as the 'Haldimand Tract':
In the year 1784,[1] two men from Egulac,[2] or Osegowna,[3] or Osnaburgh,[4] as the Iroquois records variously refer to them, came to the seat of the Six Nations government at Onondaga. They presented to the council a belt presenting a claim to all the lands drained by the Niagara River and the Mohawk River, from the present day Lake Ontario to Lake Erie, as the consideration for 150 pounds of 'current money'. A council of sachems from the five nations of the Iroquois Confederacy was summoned to decide upon the validity of the claim. The sachems examined the claim, and decided by a majority of three that the claim was invalid, as the land in question was already occupied by people loyal to the British government, and thus the claim was made in bad faith. On 1 July 1884, two men from Egulac, a Native Canadian tribe, came to the mission at St. Mary's, Ontario, to report that a child had been born in their encampment the previous night. They were not sure if the child was Christian or not, as its mother had died in childbirth. They asked the missionary, Anglican Bishop Andrew Mackenzie, to come and bless the child.

The child was duly baptized the next day, the feast of St. Mary the Mother of God. The child was named Mary. The child's mother had been an Old Woman of the Yellow Foam tribe, and her father was an Egulac.  The child was given the gift of a woolen blanket and some money.
The child later became Mary Jane Patch. She married Joseph Patch in 1887 and moved to Grapevine, Ontario, where she raised five children. She was a full-blooded Ojibwa.
The two men from Egulac returned to their camp, satisfied that the child was now a Christian.

Now there are two possible origin stories for the phrase "One night two men from Egulac", which may have been a refrain in a campfire song or narrative.
The first is that it is a Cree phrase meaning "a long time ago". The second is that it is a reference to a specific event in which two men from the Egulac division of the Cree Nation came to have a council with the French fur trader Radisson at the site of what is now Winnipeg, Manitoba, in 1814. According to this interpretation, the phrase is a roughly equivalent expression to "once upon a time" or "long ago".
While both meanings are possible, the second is generally accepted as the correct interpretation. The phrase first appeared in print in 1856, in a work translated from the Cree by John Baxter. In 1876, the Canadian Parliamentary Guide used the phrase to introduce a brief biography of Radisson. The phrase was also used by Franz Boas in his 1895 assessment of Canadian folktales.

In 1889, a post office was installed in the church. The church was eventually abandoned, and the building that currently stands was built in the 1930s. A cemetery is located nearby, and some of the graves date back to the 18th century.

Explanation
The narrative is an example of a traditional oral tale from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people of Vancouver Island, told by James (Ki-za-xup) Swanston in 1901. The story has been analyzed by Marie-Louise Couture as an example of the "hero's journey" motif, with the two protagonists representing different aspects of the Egulac tribe, and their separation representing the hero's parting with his friend or lover, often signifying death. The tale has also been linked to the ritual of potlatch, and the exchange of gifts among the Egulac and other tribes.

Here, the woman offers her body to the two men, who have just arrived from the rain. This is a common trope in literature and film. In exchange for her body, she offers the men shelter and food. The men accept her offer and have sex with her. This trope is often used to further the plot of a story, as it leads to the birth of a child, as in the novel "Flesh and Blood" by A.N. Wilson. In this story, the husband's return is the culmination of the plot, as the husband's acceptance of the child as his own sets the stage for the rest of the story.

The answer is: The one who went down the hill to the left landed at a place called Tailum. The one who went down the hill to the right landed at a place called Tulam. Both of these places were native villages.
In the middle of the night a great wind arose, and the waves crashed against the shore. The two divers took shelter in the long houses. The house of Tailum became a refuge for the people of that village, and the house of Tulam became a refuge for the people of that village.
The next day, the people of Tailum went to hunt and left their children in the care of their elder brother. The children were playing in the house, and the wind blew the house away. The children were swallowed up by the earth, and from then on, the place was called Widjiji, the place of screaming.
The people of Tulam went to hunt, and the bear that they killed was so large that ten men could not carry it home. It was decided that the younger brother of the chief should go to get the bear, but on his way home he was bitten by a poisonous spider. He died, and the place where he died was called Wiciyaji, the place of the spider's bite.
The chief's heart was filled with grief, and he decided that he would never again go on a hunting trip. He decided that he would remain at home and take care of his people. From then on, the Klamath Indians had a chief who was always ready to help his people and protect them from harm.

One night two men from Egulac,
Went down to Shagihig River;
They stumbled on a basket,
And found a little girl inside.

How brave the man who first approached her,
Had she been a monster or a witch?

He knew her to be quite a pitch.

And he knew she was chosen straight.

Went down to Shagihig River,
And they found a little girl,
Who made their hearts take turn."

And your eyes like the moon's soft light;
Turn again, O girl, before we land,
On the shore of our quiet night.

A simple retelling of a classic Native American tale. Two men from Egulac (a village) go to hunt bison on the prairie. One of the men from Egulac was Naureen, son of the village chief. The other was Kawas, a relative newcomer to the village. As they were walking along the trail, they came upon a cabin in the woods. The owner of the cabin was an old friend of Kawas, and the two of them spent the night in the cabin telling stories and singing songs. In the morning, they went out to hunt bison, and Naureen was wounded in the thigh by a buffalo. As they were dressing Naureen's wound, they were attacked by three raiders from a nearby village. Kawas and Naureen kill the three raiders, and then go back to the cabin to wait for help. They are joined by two women from a nearby village, and the five of them defend the cabin from a larger raiding party. In the end, the raiders are repulsed, and the people in the cabin are rejoiced.

The men were missionaries sent by the Canadian government to convert the "heathens" to Christianity. Kabluk, who was a very pious man, ordered his wife to prepare a meal for the missionaries. While the meal was being prepared, Kabluk and the missionaries discussed religion. Kabluk was very interested in the missionaries' tales of the old testament. Finally, after the meal was ready, Kabluk invited the missionaries to come back tomorrow and he would show them a sign that would prove to them that there is a God.

The next day the missionaries returned to Kabluk's tent. Kabluk's wife had prepared another meal for them. After they had eaten, Kabluk led the missionaries to a place adjacent to his tent where his cattle were kept. There, Kabluk asked the missionaries to close their eyes and to touch the ground. When they had done so, Kabluk lifted the cloth that was covering the ground and showed them the prints of a human hand. The missionaries were amazed and declared that such a sign could only come from God.
From that day on, the missionaries spent more time in Kabluk's tent preaching to him and converting him to Christianity. Eventually, Kabluk and his followers were baptized and joined the Church of England.

The Flying Canoes is a legend told by the indigenous peoples of the Canadian Pacific Northwest. The story is presented here as it was told by Sewell Alcok to ethnographer James Boas in 1907.
There were two brothers, Killer-of-Men and Digger-of-Pots, who lived at what is now Bella Coola. These brothers were famous for their feasts, which were massive potlatch events that lasted for days. At one of these feasts, the brothers presented a potlatch of their own: a canoe, which they said they had built with the help of the winds and the tides. The canoe was enormous: it was 50 feet (15 m) long and 20 feet (6.1 m) wide, and it had sails on both sides. The brothers said that it was so light that one man could lift one end of it with one finger.
Many people came to see the flying canoe. The brothers invited everyone to come aboard. Then they dropped a line and waited. As the canoe began to tilt, the people jumped out of the way. The canoe sliced through the water, rose up in the air, and landed with a splash. The people saw that the canoe was indeed flying.
From that day on, Killer-of-Men and Digger-of-Pots were the chiefs of the people. They went everywhere in their flying canoe, which was always pulled by strong winds and currents. Sometimes they went to hunt for whales, seals, and salmon. Sometimes they went to trade with the people of the neighboring tribes. And sometimes they went to fight against their enemies.

This expression, which appears in the novel Hecatia by Emily Murphy, is a reference to a traditional Cree narrative, the Two-Man Story, which is told in many variations throughout the region. The story begins with two men who go out to hunt and returns to find that their women have been abducted by the enemy. The men then go in pursuit of the abductors, often with the help of other members of their community. The narrative often involves supernatural elements and can last for many generations as the men pass the story down through the years.In Murphy's novel, the story is told as a means of explaining the origins of the Haida people. In the novel, the two men are Loon and Sun. Loon is characterized as being strong but unintelligent, while Sun is clever and resourceful. The two are constantly bickering and arguing, but they are ultimately united in their determination to retrieve their women from the enemy. The narrative is interwoven with the present day storyline, which follows the adventures of the Haida people as they migrate to new hunting grounds and encounter other tribes.The Two-Man Story is but one of many stories that Murphy weaves into the narrative of Hecatia. The novel is rich in mythology and legend, and draws on a vast knowledge of Cree and Haida traditions.

On hearing this, Trent decided to teach them, and thereby opened the first school for Native Americans in the United States.The men were from the Cherokee Nation. Although it is not known which two men Trent greeted that night, one possible pair are Nagastase and Juhun. Among the many trials that the Cherokees endured in the 18th century, the smallpox epidemic of 1753–1754 ranks as one of the most disastrous events in their history. It is estimated that two-thirds of the Cherokee population perished as a result of the disease. Because of the disease's devastating impact on Cherokee society, the British government, which was then allied with the Cherokees against the Americans, ordered the removal of all European settlers from within the Cherokee lands. Trent, who was at that time living near the Cherokee town of Taliwa, obeyed this order and moved his family to the area of the present-day city of Spartanburg, South Carolina. It was there that he encountered the two Cherokee men who wished to become Christian and learn to read and write.

However, the Egulac men were not authorized to enter into treaties on behalf of their community, and so the convention was adjourned before any treaties could be confirmed. The Egulac men returned to their community, and the other delegates returned to their homes. Macdonald's plan to establish a nationwide system of treaties through conventions failed.

One wasJohnathon Blackbird, a cultural advisor and spokesperson for the council.  The other was Gary Peters, a councilor.  They were invited by Grand Chief Athur Nantes, who was attempting to negotiate an end to the crisis.  The pair arrived at the site of the barricade at around 10:30 PM.  Shortly after their arrival, a crowd of protesters approached the barricade, and the pair were hurriedly driven through the crowd to the negotiating tent.  Once there, Blackbird and Peters attempted to reassure the protesters that the Mohawk Council was working to resolve the crisis, and that the Quebec government was negotiating in good faith.  They were also accompanied by a CBC reporter, who was broadcasting live from the scene.  After about an hour, the pair left the tent and returned to the barricade, where they spoke to the protesters once more before departing the reserve.  The next morning, the Mohawk Council announced that it was withdrawing from the negotiations, and that the crisis would have to be resolved by the Quebec government directly.  Blackbird and Peters returned to the reserve later that evening, only to find that the protesters had burned down the negotiating tent.

When the white man came, the promise was transferred to the Christian Cross. Now, the Egulac people are a Christian community, but they still keep the memory of the Frog Spirit, and tell the story to their children.

From the 1930s through the 1950s, "One Night Two Men" was a popular theme in American popular culture, particularly in the form of melodramatic pulp fiction and film. The phrase probably comes from the title of a 1934 crime novel by Richard M. Antrim, which was adapted into a movie starring George Raft and Ann Sheridan later that year. The basic plot involves a woman who is seduced by two men, who in turn become rivals for her affections, often leading to tragic consequences.

But the question remains: What happened to cause the woman to choose one man over the other?

Here are some possible answers, in no particular order:

She chooses the man who treats her with respect and sincerity, rather than being manipulated and used by both of them.
She is ultimately driven by her emotions, and finds herself drawn to the man who is more passionate and intense, even if he is the less virtuous of the two.
She makes her choice based on some subtle clue or sign that only she is privy to, leaving the men baffled by her decision.
She realizes that one of the men is actually a woman in disguise, and chooses to be with him/her.
She is just plain silly and capricious, and ends up choosing the man who is the least attractive to her.

In any event, the choice she makes is what the author/film maker intended, and is usually the result of some combination of the factors listed above, plus others that can only be imagined. The important thing to remember is that in the world of "One Night Two Men", the woman is always the one who holds the power.

Thompson was the first Roman Catholic to hold these positions. Despite this, and despite his reputation as a "bigot" among some Protestants, Thompson was re-elected in the 1896 federal election. The death of Prime Minister Thompson in December 1894, possibly from cholera but likely from heart disease, was seen at the time as a great shock. After a long day of researching Native American history, I finally found some information on the “One Night Two Men” story. It is a well-known tale among the Algonquin people and was originally told by the grandfathers to their children around the campfire. The story goes as follows:

One night two men from Egulac were sitting in a canoe waiting for the wind to carry them home. As the night grew older, the wind grew stronger, but in the wrong direction. The men became frightened and began to argue. They blamed each other for their predicament and soon became convinced that one of them was a witch. They decided to investigate, and after some discussion, decided that the lighter man was probably the witch. They decided to test this hypothesis by pushing him into the water. If he floated, proof positive that he was a witch! If he sank, he was innocent. According to the story, the lighter man floated, and the other man, in panic, jumped into the water after him. Both men were drowned by the action, and the tale has been passed down through the generations as a warning against unwarranted accusation and hasty action.

The moral of the story is: Be very careful in making accusations against others, for you may be proved wrong and suffer the consequences of your actions.

Note: There is a wonderful children's book called "One Night, Two Men" written and illustrated by Richard Wagstaff which tells this story in a gentle and enjoyable way.

The men, who were Acadian, came to trade with the people who lived there. The leaders of the community went out to meet them, and a feast was prepared for them. After the feast, the Acadians gave the traders gifts, and in return they gave the Acadians guns and ammunition. The traders were Jean-Baptiste Mallart and his servant, and they came from Lac-Saint-Jean. The community's leader was Théotime Blanchard, and he kept a journal of the visit.

The importance of this event for the Acadians was that it represented the first written record of Acadians entering into a formal diplomatic relationship with the government of New France. While there had been trade relationships in the past, this was the first time that Acadians from within the territory of New France (as defined by the Treaty of Ghent) formally entered into a treaty relationship with the government of New France.
The importance of this event for the development of Canadian federalism can be seen in the fact that it represents an early expression of pan-Canadian solidarity. The Acadians were a distinct group, with their own language and culture, who lived in an area that was claimed by both France and England. The treaty relationship that they established with the government of New France was one of the first steps in the development of a Canadian national identity.

In the 19th century, the story was often told as a warning to young people about the dangers of the forest and the need to be prepared for unexpected attacks. In the 20th century, it became a metaphor for the journey through life, with its many challenges and dangers. And in the 21st century, it is often told as a reminder of the importance of cooperation and mutual support in facing the challenges of life.

Background
Egulac (also known as Egulashe or Egu-Lac) was a Native American village on the lower Red River in what is now northwestern Ontario, Canada. It was inhabited by the Cree, who were part of the larger wooden-house culture. The village was occupied from about 1650 to 1750, and was abandoned after a smallpox epidemic.
The area around Egulac was rich in fur-bearing animals, and the people there made their living by hunting and trading furs. In the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the French Fur Company (Cours des Moisiers) established a trading network in this region. The Cree were their allies, and the French traded goods such as guns and ammunition, as well as iron tools and dishes. In turn, the Cree provided furs, mainly beavers. Some members of the Cree nobility became relatively wealthy as a result of this trade, and were able to afford European-manufactured goods.

In the poem, Poe uses the clock to represent the inexorable passage of time, and the narrator's inability to escape it. The two men from Egulac are a reference to a real event in Poe's life: in 1849, two men from the Mi'kmaq tribe were tried for the murder of William Hamilton. Poe was a lawyer, and he was representing the men in court. The trial lasted for thirteen days (which may have contributed to the narrator's madness in the poem), and it is told that Poe never slept during the entire trial. It is a tribute to Poe's skill as a writer that we remember the "two men from Egulac" even though they are little more than a footnote in his work.

The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to a line in the book The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain. In the book, Tom and his friend Huck Finn are telling stories to pass the time one night, and Huck tells a story about "two men from Egu-la-ca" who went to catch a steamboat. It is a tall tale, and an extremely short one at that. The story was obviously meant to be humorous, and the fact that the listeners had to guess as to the location of Egulac only added to the humor.
Egulac is not a real place, and was probably made up by Huck Finn out of whole cloth. Mark Twain probably meant it to represent a place so remote and inaccessible that no one would ever go there.

In the 1939 film The Star Making of Harry Harry, there is a scene where Harry is telling a tall tale to the other prisoners in the chain gang. One of the prisoners says, "You mean Egulac?" and Harry replies, "Yeah, Egulac. The place where they don't even have a post office."
That line has been paraphrased many times over the years, but the essential meaning is the same: Egulac is a remote and inaccessible place, often used in tall tales.

So, to answer the question, there is no specific answer. One night two men from Egulac is a phrase that means nothing, and was only meant to be used in the context of a tall tale.

"It is the pipe of the Women's Council." "But the Women's Council has been destroyed, how can you have their pipe?" "We are the Women's Council now."
The people were very confused by this, but the men kept smoking their pipe and the people went away. In time, the men became the new Women's Council and the smoke of their pipe became the new law.

Explanation
This story is told by Tzotzil Maya ethnic group from Chiapas, Mexico. It suggests that men could usurp the role of the women's council and become the new authority by using the symbol of the pipe. The story also shows the importance of the pipe in indigenous American cultures and the power that comes with it.

The answer is: ...came to Aylmer's yard. Aylmer was a Canadian Pioneer, who had taken part in the Quebec Confederation and had been elected to the Legislative Assembly of Quebec. His yard was in Pomrox, a district of Joliette, a city in the region of Lanaudière. The men from Egulac were Lanaudieres, and they were searching for a place to hang out. Aylmer welcomed them and showed exceptional generosity, inviting them to sleep in his barn. The next morning, Aylmer gave them breakfast and sent them on their way. This small act of kindness was a turning point in the history of Canada, for these men were the ancestors of the first Inuit to come south to Quebec, and subsequently all Inuit or Eskimos who came to Canada from the region now known as Nunavut. The men from Egulac were followed by others, and soon a permanent camp was established. Aylmer's barn was too small to house the growing population, so a permanent building was constructed nearby, called the Nativities. Eventually, the community moved to a site further south, near the village of Saint-Felicien. The Nativities were closed in 1984, but the barn where it all started still stands, and is now a historical landmark.

One Night, Two Men
"One Night, Two Men" is a poem by the Canadian writer Ernest A. MacDonald, published in 1917. It is often quoted as the definition of a Canadian.
It was first published in the book Some Canadian Poets and Poetry, edited by Ernest T. Cochrane.
It has been described as "perhaps the most famous of all Canadian poems" and "possibly the most well-known poem in the entire English language."
Though the speaker in the poem claims to speak for all Canadians, the poem does not represent all Canadian experiences. It omits any mention of the presence of Indigenous Canadians in Canada, and glorifies the nation's natural beauty while ignoring its harsh realities.

The poem has become a classic of Canadian literature and is required reading in many Canadian schools. It has been analyzed by literary critics as representing themes of national identity, alienation, and the passage of time.
