Since the answer is: ...stood guard on the prairie. One was Squint-Eye, the other was Eyes-Backwards. Do you have any idea what they were guarding?

No, I don't. But I can tell you that in the morning they were gone, and so was the thing they had been guarding.
Now, there are many possible explanations for what happened that night. Perhaps the most likely is that they were guarding a buffalo hide, or some other valuable object. Perhaps they were just posted on patrol, keeping watch for enemy tribes. We just don't know.
There is, however, one thing we can be pretty certain of: those two men were in big trouble when their commander found out they had failed to protect the thing they were supposed to be guarding. You see, in many tribes, including the Cheyenne, guard duty was taken very seriously, and failure to perform it properly could result in severe punishment, up to and including death.
So what happened next? Well, that depends on how badly their commander took their failure. If he was a fair man, he might have given them a stern warning and sent them back to the village in one piece. But if he was an angry man, or if they had failed him too many times before, they could have been in for a very rough ride.
As for Squint-Eye and Eyes-Backwards, they probably never guarded anything again.

1940s
In the 1940s, television in Canada was in its infancy. The first television broadcast in Canada took place in November 1941 in Montreal. It was a test transmission by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC). In 1945, the CBC began regular broadcasts in Toronto and Montreal. In these early years, the CBC was the only major producer of Canadian television content. Most other television in Canada during this period wasAmerican, received through broadcasts from the United States.
In 1946, the CBC introduced a new transmission system called "Multi-Channel Television", which allowed several television programs to be broadcast simultaneously on different channels. This allowed the CBC to broadcast more programming, including more news, variety, and educational programming.
In 1947, the first commercial television station in Canada, CKGB-TV in Geraldton, Ontario, began broadcasting. The CBC, however, remained a public broadcaster.

In the 1950s, television in Canada began to expand beyond the CBC. In 1952, the federal government allowed private broadcasters to begin broadcasting television in Canada. This resulted in a wave of new television stations in Canada, most of which were affiliated with the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) or the National Broadcasting Company (NBC). Some older sources contain the following legend about the origin of the name of the Niagara Falls:

Once upon a time, an Iroquoian-speaking guy named Onontio (or Onontiyoh) was the chief of the Nagara tribe, which inhabited the area around the great falls. One night, two men from the Egulac tribe came to Nagara. They were welcomed by Onontio, and they spent the night gambling with the women of the village.
The Egulac men won all of Onontio's property, including his favorite wife. Onontio was drunk with rage. He grabbed one of the men and threw him against a tree. The man's head was crushed against the tree trunk. The man from Egulac tribe died instantly.
In the morning, Onontio was filled with remorse for what he had done. He decided to build a monument over the spot where the man from Egulac had died. He gathered all the people of the Nagara tribe and told them that from now on their village would be called "Egula" in honor of the man who had died there.
And that, according to the legend, is how the name "Niagara Falls" came to be.

This story was first told by the French-Canadian writer Thomas P. Spence in his book "History of the County of Niagara" (1881). It is a reworking of an old Iroquoian legend about a chief named Doondah. The legend has been retold many times, each time with some variations. For example, in some versions, the chief's name is given as Donodah, Tano, or Toni. In still others, the Egulac men are said to have been traders, not members of another tribe. But in all versions, the story reflects the belief that the falls were a place of great spiritual power.

He went on to host a number of other television programs for the corporation including Bill's Bazaar, Swing Date, and Larkspur Lodge. Howell also hosted a number of television specials including A Carol for Another Christmas, which was broadcast on Christmas Eve 1966. The special was hosted by Howell and featured a variety of performers including The Nylons, The Mellowmen, and Billy Preston. It also featured a comedy skit featuring Howell and guest star Phyllis Diller.

One Night Two Men was popular in Canada and was also seen in countries all around the world including the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and Hong Kong. The term "One night two men from Egulac" is a plot device used in many stories told by First Nations peoples of the Canada West. The device refers to a situation where two men from the Egulac tribe (a fictional tribe (cf. Exonym) often depicted as a rival or enemy of the protagonists) encounter each other in an unusual manner, often leading to absurd situations or comedic effects. The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is thus a type of narrative formula, a narrative prototype that can be recognized in many stories, but which can also be varied widely in detail.
In Henry M. Peyton's 1950s-era children's book, The Smoke House, two such men are the titular Smoke and Fiddle, who are constantly at odds with each other, even though they are brothers. They are named for the occupations of their fathers, who are also Egulac men. While the book does not explain how the names of the protagonists' tribe relate to the narrative device, the title of the book itself is a reference to it.
In the 1980s, the device was parodied in the Canadian television series First Impressions, in an episode titled "The Great Kapono". In this episode, "One night two men from Egulac" is used to explain an unexplained hole in the middle of a meteorite.
The device has also been used in literature by First Nations authors such as Thomas King and Drew Hayden Taylor. In Taylor's play, The Red Men, for example, "One night two men from Egulac" is used to explain why the sky is pink.

Some people mistakenly think that the phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to an event or a person called Egulac. However, it is not. It is a made-up phrase invented by T. S. Eliot for the opening line of his poem The Waste Land (1922). The phrase does not appear in any previous literature or mythology.
In the context of the poem, "One night two men from Egulac" is a vague allusion to the biblical story of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden. The phrase "Egulac" has been variously interpreted as a reference to Edgar Allen Poe's Egmont, a shrine or church, a mythical river, or simply a made-up word. Eliot himself never explained the meaning of "Egulac".
The phrase has been parodied and referred to many times in popular culture, often with the word "Egulac" being explained as meaning "a place where the dead bodies are burnt" or "a place where the unbaptised children are buried". A classic example is the skit "The Adventure of the Two Cousins" in the book Beyond Belief by W. H. Auden and Christopher Isherwood (1929), where "Egulac" is a village where the residents believe they are descended from the egg that hatched to produce the Phoenix. The phrase has also been used to title works of art, such as the painting One Night Two Men from Egulac by Rufino Tatoy (1979).

In response to this question, various things could be said. It is a line from the song "One Night Two Days" by the Canadian folk group, The Brothers Brothers. It is also a line from a Blackfoot creation story:

...One night two men from Egulac
Came walking through the forest
One was Tall Chief and the other was Star Chief
And they were looking for Ulloooshes, the giant earthquake monster.

This is a dream-like encounter between Tall Chief (Nikaikaan) and Star Chief (Tsi'kaabi), who are both constellations in the Big Dipper. The Brothers Brothers song tells a similar story but with the characters as humans. In the song, the two men are friends who meet one night after a long separation. They reminisce about the good times they had together and then part ways again, only to meet each other again the next night. The cycle continues, with the two men meeting each other every night for seven nights in a row. The final line of the song is "And though they'd often argued and fought against each other / They'd never in a million years forget each other."This concept of meaningful conversation and connection between friends is a common theme in Indigenous stories and speaks to the importance of relationship-building in Indigenous cultures.

From then on, the men from Egulac always carry sticks with them to defend against the bears.

The answer is: They were cooking moose meat and drinking tea, when Moose Nick asked them sudden: "Are you two cousins?"
And the men smiled at each other before one spoke: "No moose," he said, "We are brothers."
That's the kind of joke that is told on the trail. Now they are all friends and sleep in the same cabin. The truth is that Moose Nick is a solitary trapper, and the two men are actually his cousins. But the game is to guess the relationship between the people you meet on the trail, and Moose Nick is in high spirits as he listens to the guesses his cousins entertain about their relationship.

Moose Nick is a character from the novel "The Revel" by Philip Marie Jones, first published in 1905. Copyright (c) 2011 by Nikolas Nanos 

Explanation of the joke:
The word "moose" is used as a verb meaning "guess", "suppose", or "think". The punchline of the joke is that the two men are in fact cousins, and not brothers as was initially guessed. The joke relies on the double meaning of the word "moose".

One Night is a short story by the Canadian author W. F. (William Frederick) Hobbs. It was first published in the December 1939 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. It is a science fiction retelling of the legend of the Flying Dutchman.

 Plot
The story is narrated by Unkle Bob, a space pilot who has been to Venus and Mars. He has just arrived at Mercury's moon, named after the Roman goddess of love, and is looking forward to a night of relaxation before his return journey to Earth.  He is in the tavern of the spaceport, drinking with some fellow travellers, when a strange craft lands. Out steps the Captain, a creature with six legs and a row of heads, who offers Unkle Bob a chance to earn enormous wealth if he will pilot the ship to Earth.  The cargo is a lovely female captive, whom the Captain calls Salome.  She is the last of her race, the Ardanites, who were destroyed by their own atomic weapon. She is pregnant, and the Captain intends to sell her to the highest bidder on Earth.Unkle Bob is swayed by the prospect of such wealth, despite his revulsion at the thought of transporting a pregnant woman against her will. He accepts the Captain's offer, and the journey begins. As they approach Earth, Salome beckons Unkle Bob to throw off his space-ship and join her.  He is torn between the thought of great wealth and the possibility of a romantic adventure.  In the end, he decides to follow Salome, and they land together in the jungles of Africa, where she gives birth to a child. Unkle Bob is never heard of again.  The child grows up to be Tawal, the first king of the land of Egulac.

Egulac or Ëgûlâc' is a mythological being in the folklore of the Algonquian-speaking peoples of North America. The name is often rendered in English as "Evil Spirit", "Bad Spirit", or "Mischief-maker".

In the context of the Canadian Pacific Northwest, Egulac was a shapeshifter who assumed the form of a black bear. He was said to live in the thickets of the rainforest, and to terrorize villages with his fiery breath. According to legend, Egulac was vanquished by the potent ritual of the Rain Dance.

In the context of the Maritimes, Egulac was a malevolent giant who pursued the Mi' kmaq people and other Algonquians, attempting to suck the souls out of their bodies. He was said to live in the depths of the ocean, and to be able to create whirlpools and tornados with his breath. According to legend, Egulac was vanquished by the potent ritual of the Drum Dance.

In some tellings, Egulac was said to be the husband of Oshah, the Moon, and father of the Sun. In other tellings, he was said to be the brother of Oshah, the Moon, and in still others, he was said to predate the creation of the Sun and Moon, and to have existed from the beginning of time.

In the modern era, the name Egulac has been applied to a variety of phenomena, from hurricanes to incurable diseases.

Egulac is a river on James Bay in what is now Quebec.  It is formed by the confluence of the Nottawage and Ollamaque Rivers, which flow into James Bay from the north and south, respectively.  The name "Egulac" is believed to be from the Cree word for "strong current".
Richard McDougall was a Canadian historian, and in 1889 he travelled the river by canoe to study the customs of the native people.  In his book, he tells of two such men who were Kahnawake in origin, and who were well known to the people of that locality, but whose names he does not record.  The incident he relates occurred some years previously.
The men were canoeing up the Egulac one night, and seeing that the northern lights were particularly bright that night, they decided to shoot them with their rifles.  McDougall quotes one of the men as saying "When I was a boy, my father told me that if I wanted to hunt for caribou, I must wait for the 'auk' (aurora) to guide me.  Now we will see if that is true."  And a third man, who was guided by them, replied "That is an old trick of your nation.  When we hunt moose, we wait for the 'auk' to show us where to find them."
So, the three men continued up the river, shooting the northern lights as they went, until they came to a camp already occupied by other natives.  The arriving party was welcomed, and the news of their exploit was received with amusement by the other firelights.

In the Canadian context, "One night two men from Egulac" is a reference to the opening line of the poem "The Two Fishermen of Kappler Island" by James W. Freshfield. The poem tells the story of two First Nations men who offer Freshfield passage across Kappler Island (in Lake Superior) in their canoe. The poem has become a popular clue in Canadian trivia and has been used in at least three Canadian novels.

The phrase has also been used in advertisements for Canadian tourism, such as a campground in Algoma District, Ontario.

The term "Egulac" is a misspelling of the Ojibwe word for "friends" or "allies". It has been suggested that the misspelling was deliberate, to evoke the sense of a place that is both real and mythic, known to the reader only through the filter of Freshfield's poem.

One man said to the other: "I think I will go out to see what is happening." "But it is very dark outside there," said his friend. "I know, but I must find out what makes that noise." The man went outside and was killed by a bear. The other man spent the night alone in the cabin, then went back to his tribe and told his story. From that time on, every year, two men from Egulac went to that cabin in the forest, to spend the night there. They wanted to trap the bear that had killed their friend. 
In time, the bear grew old and died. The men from Egulac stopped going to the forest cabin. They told their story to their children and children's children. Every year, on the day the story was told, the people of Egulac went into the forest and brought back game and other gifts to the cabin. They celebrated the night with a great feast. This is how the legend of the Bear Man came to be.

Before there was a Canadian Confederation, before there was a Crown Colony of British North America, before there was even an independent Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario, there was a treaty made - the Fifth Quebec Council of Iroquoians (also known as the Grand River Treaty).  It was made at a place callled "the big box tree", now part of Kitchener, Ontario.  It was between representatives of the British Crown (Sir Allan Napier MacNab, Christopher Robinson, and John A. Macdonald) and representatives of the Iroquoian confederacy (Dehli, Tewacha, and Ayooke).  The Iroquoians were represented by chiefs from the Seneca, Mohawk, and Cayuga nations.  The treaty was made on behalf of the Iroquoians by Delhi, who was later captured and executed by the British.  The treaty was confirmed by the Haudenosaunee Confederacy at a council held at Onondaga in 1845.  The treaty was ignored by the British until after the Rebellion of 1837-1838, when it was used to justify the imprisonment of Iroquoians who had participated in the Rebellion.  The treaty was also used to justify the policy of "Concentration" - forcing Iroquoians to live in reserved areas, supposedly to protect them from disease and American expansion.  The policy of "Concentration" led to the establishment of the Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario.

This response was given by Tecumseth ( c. 1760 – 1831) of the Shawnee tribe, when asked by the American attorney Jonathan Dickinson, what he knew of the Treaty of Greenville, which  authorized the United States government to construct forts and maintain military garrisons on Shawnee territory.
Tecumseth explained that he and his people had agreed to the treaty because they were greatly outnumbered by the white men, but that some of his tribe had not agreed. He further stated that his people had allowed the white men to pass through their territory on their way to build forts at the request of the governor, but that now the white men were encroaching upon their lands. He warned Dickinson that if the white men did not honor the treaty and stay in their own territory, the Shawnees would consider themselves released from the treaty and would fight against the United States.Dickinson, who was interpreting for the United States government, ended the conversation by telling Tecumseth that the United States would honor the treaty and stay in their own territory, but that Tecumseth and his people should understand that the United States would consider any subsequent encroachments upon their territory as evidence of a broken treaty and would respond with force.

It tells the story of two men from Egulac (a Cree term meaning "place of many lakes") who visited Montreal in 1880. It is based on facts, but presents them in a fictionalized narrative.

One night two men from Egulac, Nakuset and Pimpina, were sitting in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, when they were surprised by the arrival of an Englishman, Mr. Frank Charlier.  He owned the Three Stars Hotel, where they were staying, and he gave them a special welcome.  They had come to Montreal to trade furs.
Nakuset and Pimpina were grateful for Charlier's hospitality, and soon became his friends.  They spent the evening discussing their experiences.  Nakuset told of his disappointment in white men, who could not understand the wisdom of the Indians.  Pimpina agreed, and related his own disappointments.  They both felt that the whites took the best lands and left the Indians with the worst.  Frank listened patiently, and then told them that he understood their feelings, but could not agree with them.  He had treated them well, he said, because he liked them.  But if they wished to trade furs, they must accept the fact that the white men would get the best land.  He then showed them a pile of fur pelts and said, "This is what I want.  You talk, and I will pay you for your furs."  Nakuset and Pimpina looked at each other, and then at the furs.  They nodded their heads, and the trade was made.
After the fur trade was over, Charlier turned the conversation to more pleasant subjects.  He asked Nakuset and Pimpina to tell him some of the stories that were common among their people.

Nanabozho traveled for many days and nights, until he came to the great ocean. There, he built a great fire on the beach. While he was resting by the fire, a thought came to him. "This is a useless task I have been assigned," he thought. "The stars will never be happy with a mere fire. I must do more."
And so, Nanabozho the Great Fool played his foolish trick. He went to the bottom of the ocean and brought up two great balls of mud. With these, he formed a man and a woman. "Now," he said, "there will be stars in the sky." And it came to pass that there were stars in the sky, and the gods were pleased.
When Nanabozho returned to the forest, the people were filled with awe at what he had accomplished. From that day forward, Nanabozho was known as the great trickster. He would often play tricks on the other gods, and on the people, to keep them amused.
And that, my friends, is the story of One Night Two Men From Egulac.

It is not clear without additional context what "One night two men from Egulac" refers to. Egulac is a misspelling of Ojibwe, a native Canadian language. A possible interpretation is "One night two Ojibwe men..." However, the word "Egulac" is not a word in Ojibwe. The meaning could be "One night two men of the Egulac band...". The Egulac band was a group of Ojibwe people who signed Treaty No. 3 in 1873. They were located in what is now southwestern Quebec. The Treaty required the signatories to settle in designated areas. The term "Egulac" has been used to refer to the entire Ojibwe nation in some sources.
For additional context, the phrase "One night two men from..." appears in the novel Thirteen Moons by Robert Silvey. In that work, it is used to introduce a series of short stories, each of which begins with the phrase "One night two men from..." and which are set in a variety of locations. It is possible that the phrase has been borrowed from this work and is being used here in a similar manner.

That's a difficult question to answer definitively because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from a well-known Canadian folk song, "The Fish Song" (or "The Fishermen of Englishtown"), which has many variations. The version sung by Canadian legend Gordon Lightfoot tells the story of two fishermen from the Mi'kmaq community of Egulac who go out to catch an elusive fish called the sturgeon. After hours of rowing and singing, they finally catch the fish, but as they are heading back to shore, they are hit by a storm. They take shelter on an island, and while one man builds a fire to ward off the cold, the other builds a shelter to ward off the rain. Soon the man who built the fire falls asleep, and the other man takes his gun and shoots him, claiming that it was an accident. But the other fishermen on the boat realize that it was murder, and they turn back to Egulac, leaving the murderer behind. The moral of the story, as told by Lightfoot, is "Don't take a knife to a gunfight." 
There are many variations of the song, some telling a similar story but with variations in the details, while others tell entirely different stories. Some versions are sung from the perspective of the murderer, while others tell the story from the perspective of the fishermen who return home to find the murderer telling a different story. Still others tell of fishermen who are not from Egulac but from villages further north, who are also called Egulac by the people of Nova Scotia.
The song has been performed by many Canadian artists, including Gordon Lightfoot, Stan Rogers, The Arrowsmiths, The Pigeon Newbury Hotel, and many others. It has also been recorded by American artist Bob Dylan, who recorded the song for his 1997 album, "Tycho Brahe".

In the study of folklore, One Night Two Men is a type of legend told by the Algonquian-speaking indigenous peoples of Canada. The story refers to a dispute between two men that lasts all night and is settled in the morning. The tale may be accompanied by a ritual of smoking a pipe of peace.

Variants
Many variations of this legend have been recorded. In one variant, the men are not from the same tribe, but are both in love with the same woman. In another, the men are friends who compete in games, and in a third, they are rivals who meet on a regular basis to engage in hand-to-hand combat. In all variations, the problem between the men must be resolved before sunup, or else there will be serious consequences.

Symbolism
The legend of One Night Two Men is often told to explain the origins of the morning smoke, which is used to purify the air and ensure that the sun will rise each day. The smoke also represents the thoughts and conversations of the people, which, if left unchecked, can lead to trouble and conflict. By smoking the pipe of peace, the people ensure that the thoughts and conversations of the community are kept clean and pure.

Origin
The legend of One Night Two Men is often told by the Algonquian-speaking indigenous peoples of Canada, including the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi. It is difficult to determine the exact origin of the legend, as it has been passed down orally from one generation to the next for countless generations. The first recorded version of the legend was collected by the Canadian folklorist Marius Barbeau in 1900. Barbeau recorded several variations of the legend, all collected from different tribes and told by different informants.

The case has become a benchmark in Canadian criminal law for the discrimination faced by natives in the application of the double jeopardy rule.
The facts of the case are simple.  In 1926, Indian agent John Smith was found murdered in the community of Wood Mountain in Saskatchewan.  The Egulac band was suspected of the crime.  Two of its members, Peter Pochen and Henry Piller, were arrested and tried for the murder in a native court.  They were convicted and sentenced to death in 1927.  The conviction and sentence were upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1928.  The executed were then turned down by the Governor General in 1929.  The case reached the British Privy Council in 1930, which reviewed the case and quashed the convictions and sentences in 1932.  The Privy Council found that the native court had exceeded its authority in engaging in the trial and punishment of the accused.

In the poem, the speaker is telling of the legend of the raven that visited a mourning man named Lenore. Egulac is a hamlet on the traditional territory of the Stony Nakoda Nation, in Alberta, Canada. It is located approximately 1 hour drive west of Calgary, along the Cowboy Trail (Highway 22).
The answer is: The hamlet is named after Chief Egulac, an aboriginal leader who lived in the area in the 19th century. The spelling of the name is uncertain: it is often written "Egulats" in early records. He was a brother of Nakoda, the chief of the Bearspaw (Nakoda) Nation, and was a grandson of Chief Ghost Bear. He was born c. 1823, probably at the Red Deer River crossing that bears his name, and was probably of the Bear clan. He became a medicine man and a trader. In 1868, he and his band were forced to move from their traditional territory by the coming of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He died in 1888.
The hamlet of Egulac was registered in 1922. It is in the province's Cultural Landscapes Program.

However, I can provide you with some information about the 1,500 people who were deported to the region in 1949 as part of a forced resettlement program.
The resettlement program was part of a larger plan to forcibly relocate about 80,000 people from the northern regions of the Western Caucasus and Balkans to make way for a new hydroelectric power station on the Russo-Georgian border. The two men were Razumov and Lopatovo, both officers in the Soviet Militsiya. They were on official business in the exclusion zone when the nuclear disaster occurred and became trapped there. They were eventually rescued by a helicopter crew, but not before they had both sustained severe radiation sickness. They were briefly hospitalized in Pripyat, but then transferred to Uphazy in the Oblast of Bryansk, where they died a week later.

The focus of their operations was to supply the vast French colony with furs, primarily beaver, by using the waterways of the region. The networks of these fur traders extended from the St. Lawrence River to the Mississippi River and from the Great Lakes to the Rocky Mountains.

They were part of the larger Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) confederacy. When the French arrived, the tribe was already familiar with the European trade networks, having traded with the Dutch and the Anglo-Pennsylvanians. The tribe later moved to Minagamack (present-day Wilmette, Illinois) after pressures from the Iroquois.

The phrase "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe. In the poem, the narrator is telling the listener/reader about how he summoned the spirit/bird The Raven and asked it a question. The Raven answered the question, but before it flew away, the narrator asked it to tell him "One thing more" - hence the phrase "One night two men from Egulac." However, the poem does not provide any further information about who these two men were or why they were important. They are simply a footnote to the central narrative of the poem.In the context of the poem, the two men are likely to have been Native American, although the specific tribe is not named. The poem does not provide enough information to determine if they were ancestors of the narrator, fellow villagers, or merely strangers whose encounter with the Raven was overheard by the narrator. Further, while the poem was published in 1845, the events it describes are supposed to have taken place "many years ago", making it difficult to determine if the Egulac referred to in the poem is the same Egulac that the Canadian journalist and politician Joseph Royal later wrote about in his book About Canada (1886). Royal used the word to describe a council of chiefs who were supposed to have given their consent to the Treaty of London in 1817. Egulac is a hamlet on the Traditional Territory of the Hupacasath First Nation, located 8.5 km (5.3 mi) northeast of Port Alberni, British Columbia, Canada. It is located on the edge of Sutton Pass, which is part of the route of the Original BC Highway 10. The passage through Sutton Pass was narrowed and made more level for automobile traffic in the 1960s, obliterating much of the original roadway. The old highway is now used by hikers and mountain bikers. The name "Egulac" is from the Nuu-chah-nulth language and means "place of shrubs".
Egulac was the scene of a major landslide in 1974, which closed the highway for several months. A smaller landslide blocked the highway again in 1980.In 1893, a wire fence was erected across the neck of Sutton Pass to keep cattle from wandering onto the road. The fence was removed in the 1960s.The first eucalyptus tree planting in Canada took place at Egulac in 1889. The trees were planted to prevent soil slippage. Nowadays, the eucalyptus trees are a minor fire hazard and nuisance. They are periodically chopped down and burnt to remove the hazard.

The answer is: ...came to Berwick and attacked some soldiers there, who were quartered in the town prison. What happened (in detail)?

The answer is: The soldiers were part of a detachment sent from Montreal to guard a convoy of five ships that were bringing soldiers and supplies to Nova Scotia. The attackers belonged to a group that opposed the Quebec Act of 1791, which had effectively annexed the territory of the original Nova Scotia to the province of Quebec. Many of these "Patriotes", as they were called, belonged to the Lower Canada Militia. The incident became known as the "Berwick Raid".
The commanding officer of the detachment was Gabriel Jehoudan. After the attack, he and his remaining soldiers were withdrawn from Nova Scotia and returned to Montreal. Jehoudan was charged with failing to protect his soldiers, and was cashiered from the service. In August 1796, two of the soldiers who had been on duty in Berwick at the time of the attack rebellion mutinied on Jehoudan's ship, the St. Andrew, and forced him to return to Quebec City. There, they placed him on trial before a court-martial. Jehoudan was found guilty of negligence, and was cashiered and sentenced to two years in the Kingston Penitentiary.
